lessons.title: The pulse: the heartbeat under every song
lessons.summary: Find the steady beat in music you know, keep it with your body, and lay a simple rhythm over it.
objectives: You will find and keep the pulse of a song with a clap or a step
You will explain the difference between the beat and the rhythm
You will perform a four-beat body-percussion pattern over a steady pulse
lessons.body:
Every song you have ever danced to — at a wedding, in church or mosque, at a party on your street — sits on something you can feel before you can name it: a steady beat. This term is about musicianship, the skills that every singer and player shares. It starts with the heartbeat.

## What to do

1. Play a song you like and tap your foot. Do not think, just tap. That tap is the **pulse**.
2. Count along out loud: **1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4**. Notice where the count feels strongest — that is beat 1.
3. Open a free metronome (any metronome app, or the one built into a search engine) and set it to **80 BPM**. Step on the spot in time for one minute.
4. Build this body-percussion pattern and loop it over the metronome: **beat 1 stamp · beat 2 clap · beat 3 stamp · beat 4 clap**.
5. Now keep stamping on every beat and clap a *different* pattern with your hands — for example, two quick claps on beat 2. Your feet are the pulse; your hands are the rhythm.
6. Record 30 seconds of it on your phone.

## Understand it

**Pulse (or beat)** is the steady, even tick that runs underneath music, like a clock. It does not change when the tune changes. When a crowd claps along at a concert, they are clapping the pulse.

**Rhythm** is the pattern of long and short sounds placed *on top of* the pulse. The words of a song have a rhythm: say "Na-ija, we go dey a-lright" and you can hear some syllables are quick and some are held. Many different rhythms can sit on the same pulse.

A simple test: if you can march to it evenly, it is the pulse. If it skips, bunches up or pauses, it is a rhythm.

**Tempo** is how fast the pulse goes, measured in **beats per minute (BPM)**. A resting heart is roughly 60–80 BPM. A slow worship song may be around 60–70 BPM; much Afrobeats sits near 100–115 BPM; a fast fuji or highlife dance groove can be quicker still. Musicians also use Italian words: *adagio* (slow), *andante* (walking pace), *allegro* (fast), *presto* (very fast).

**Metre** is how beats group together. Most pop and gospel music counts in **fours** — a strong beat 1, then 2, 3, 4. A waltz counts in **threes**. You can feel the group because beat 1 usually gets the strongest sound — often the kick drum or the lowest bass note.

In much West African music, several rhythms play at once over one shared pulse — a bell, a shaker, drums, hand-claps — each repeating its own short pattern. This layering is called **polyrhythm**, and it is why a talking-drum player and a shekere player can sound completely different and still lock together. You cannot layer anything until the pulse is rock steady, which is why we start here.

**Common mistake:** speeding up. Almost everybody rushes when they get excited or when a pattern gets harder. A metronome is not a punishment; it is a mirror.

## Key words

- **Pulse:** the steady, even beat underneath music
- **Rhythm:** the pattern of long and short sounds on top of the pulse
- **Tempo:** the speed of the pulse, measured in beats per minute (BPM)
- **Metre:** how beats are grouped, such as in twos, threes or fours
- **Polyrhythm:** two or more different rhythms played at the same time over one pulse

## Read and watch

- [Rhythm](https://musiclab.chromeexperiments.com/Rhythm/) — Chrome Music Lab
- [BBC Bitesize KS3 Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zmsvr82) — BBC
- [Learning Music](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/) — Ableton

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** keep the metronome at 60–70 BPM and only stamp the pulse for the first day. Add the claps when your feet stop drifting.
- **If you already can:** keep the pulse with your feet and clap a rhythm in **threes** across it (clap every third half-beat). Hold it for 16 beats without losing the stamp.

## Learning online

You need only a phone. Use any free metronome app (or a metronome website) and your phone's voice or video recorder.

- **Evidence to upload:** one video or audio clip, 30–45 seconds, of your stamp-clap pattern over the metronome at 80 BPM. The click must be audible in the recording so your instructor can hear whether you stay with it.
- **At the live Saturday class:** have your camera on and your metronome app open. You will be asked to clap the pulse while someone else claps a rhythm, then swap — so have a clear space to stand and stamp.
- If your connection is weak, keep video off and use audio only; stamping and clapping carry well over a voice call.

## Before the next session

Find three songs you know and estimate their tempo: tap along with a metronome app until the clicks line up, then write the BPM next to each title. Bring the list.

checks.prompt: A crowd claps along evenly at a concert while the singer's words come in quick bursts and long held notes. What is the crowd clapping?
options: The rhythm of the words
The pulse of the song
The tempo marking
The melody line
checks.answer: The pulse of the song
whys: The words are uneven — long and short — so they are a rhythm, not the steady clap.
Tempo is how fast the pulse goes; you cannot clap a speed, only the beat itself.
The melody is the tune — the ups and downs in pitch — not an even clap.

checks.prompt: A song is at 120 BPM. How many beats go by in 30 seconds?
whys: That is how many seconds, not beats.
That is how many beats in a whole minute.
That would be 120 BPM for two minutes.

checks.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between pulse and rhythm, using a song you know as the example.
checks.rubric: Pulse described as steady and even; rhythm described as a pattern of long and short sounds on top; a real song used correctly.

lessons.title: Writing rhythm down: note values and time signatures
lessons.summary: Learn the symbols for long and short sounds, count them in 4/4 and 3/4, and write and clap your own four-bar rhythm.
objectives: You will name and count semibreves, minims, crotchets and quavers and their rests
You will read a time signature and fill a bar correctly
You will write and perform a four-bar rhythm in 4/4
lessons.body:
Last week you felt the pulse and played rhythms over it. But a rhythm you cannot write down lives only in your memory. This week you learn the alphabet that lets a musician in Kano send a rhythm to a musician in Port Harcourt — and have it come back exactly the same.

## What to do

1. Copy the note-value table below into your notebook with a drawing of each note.
2. Say each rhythm aloud with **"ta"** for a crotchet, **"ti-ti"** for a pair of quavers and **"ta-a"** for a minim, while tapping the pulse on your knee.
3. Draw four empty bars of 4/4. Fill each bar with exactly **four beats** of notes and rests — use at least one of each value.
4. Clap your four bars over a metronome at 70 BPM. Repeat until it is clean twice in a row.
5. Enter the same rhythm in Song Maker's percussion row, or write it in your notebook and photograph it.

## Understand it

In most music we read, the **crotchet** (quarter note) is worth one beat. Every other value is a multiple or a fraction of it:

| Note | British name | American name | Beats in 4/4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| hollow oval | semibreve | whole note | 4 |
| hollow oval with stem | minim | half note | 2 |
| filled oval with stem | crotchet | quarter note | 1 |
| filled, stem and one flag | quaver | eighth note | ½ |
| filled, stem and two flags | semiquaver | sixteenth note | ¼ |

Quavers next to each other are usually **beamed** — joined by a line instead of separate flags — so two quavers look like a little bridge.

Every note has a matching **rest**, a symbol for silence of the same length. Silence is part of rhythm: the gap before the chorus drops is written down just as carefully as the notes.

A **dot** after a note adds **half its value again**. A dotted minim is 2 + 1 = 3 beats. A dotted crotchet is 1 + ½ = 1½ beats.

Music is divided into **bars** (measures) by vertical **bar lines**. The **time signature** at the start tells you what fills a bar. In **4/4**, the top number says *four beats in a bar* and the bottom number 4 says *each beat is a crotchet*. In **3/4**, there are three crotchet beats per bar. Each bar must add up exactly: in 4/4, a minim + crotchet + two quavers = 2 + 1 + ½ + ½ = 4. ✔

Some time signatures group beats in threes of quavers. In **6/8** and **12/8**, the pulse you feel is a **dotted crotchet**, divided into three quavers. Much West African drumming is felt this way. The well-known **standard bell pattern** played on an agogo or gong is often written in 12/8, striking on pulses 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10 and 12 of the twelve quavers. Try clapping it slowly while counting the twelve.

**Common mistakes:** forgetting that a minim is two beats (not one long one); writing bars that add up to 3½ or 4½; and confusing the minim (hollow) with the crotchet (filled).

## Key words

- **Crotchet:** a one-beat note in 4/4; the American name is quarter note
- **Minim:** a two-beat note; half note
- **Semibreve:** a four-beat note; whole note
- **Quaver:** half a beat; eighth note
- **Rest:** a symbol for silence of a set length
- **Time signature:** two numbers at the start of the music saying how many beats are in a bar and which note gets one beat
- **Bar:** one group of beats between two bar lines; also called a measure

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Song Maker](https://musiclab.chromeexperiments.com/Song-Maker/) — Chrome Music Lab

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use only crotchets, minims and crotchet rests for your four bars. Add quavers once those are steady.
- **If you already can:** write your four bars in 3/4 *and* in 4/4, using a dotted minim and a dotted crotchet, then try clapping the 12/8 bell pattern against a 4-beat stamp.

## Learning online

Everything here can be done with paper, a pen and a phone.

- On a laptop or phone, use the musictheory.net **rhythm** exercises to drill note values for ten minutes — they are free and need no account.
- **Evidence to upload:** a clear photo of your four written bars **and** a short recording (20–30 seconds) of you clapping them over a metronome at 70 BPM. Say "one, two, three, four" before you start so we hear your count-in.
- **At the live Saturday class:** have your written bars in front of you. A classmate will clap your rhythm from your photo without hearing you first — so check that it adds up before you upload.

## Before the next session

Finish the musictheory.net note-value exercise until you score at least 8 out of 10 twice. Bring the four bars you wrote.

checks.prompt: In 3/4 time, which group fills exactly one bar?
options: A minim and two crotchets
A dotted minim
Two minims
A semibreve
checks.answer: A dotted minim
whys: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 beats — one beat too many for 3/4.
That is 4 beats, which fills a bar of 4/4.

checks.prompt: What is a dotted crotchet worth when a crotchet is one beat?

One and a half beats
Two beats, like a minim
Three quarters of a beat
checks.answer: One and a half beats
whys: That is a crotchet without the dot.
That would be a minim.
A dot adds value; it never makes a note shorter.

lessons.title: Pitch and melody: high, low, steps and leaps
lessons.summary: Hear and describe how a tune moves, then make an eight-note melody with a clear shape and a home note.
objectives: You will describe pitch as high or low and a melody's movement as steps or leaps
You will draw the contour of a melody you know
You will compose and sing or play an eight-note melody that ends on its home note
lessons.body:
Rhythm is *when* sounds happen. Pitch is *how high or low* they are. Put a rhythm and a set of pitches together and you have a **melody** — the part of a song people hum on the way home.

## What to do

1. Sing "Happy Birthday" slowly. Draw a line in the air with your hand as you sing — up when the tune goes up, down when it goes down.
2. Now draw that line on paper. This is the melody's **contour**.
3. Open a free phone keyboard app or Chrome Music Lab's Melody Maker. Play the same note eight times, then play eight notes going up one at a time. Hear the difference between staying, stepping and leaping.
4. Make your own eight-note melody using only five neighbouring notes (C D E F G on a keyboard). Use mostly steps and **one** leap. End on C.
5. Sing it to "la" or play it, and record it.

## Understand it

**Pitch** is how high or low a sound is. It depends on how fast the sound vibrates: a fast vibration (a small bird, a whistle) gives a high pitch; a slow one (a big drum, a bass guitar) gives a low pitch. This speed is measured in **hertz (Hz)**; the A that orchestras tune to is 440 Hz.

A **melody** is a series of pitches with a rhythm, heard as one musical idea. Melodies move in three ways:

- **Repeat** — the same pitch again.
- **Step** — to the next note up or down (C to D, or G to F). Stepwise melodies are smooth and easy to sing; many hymns and lullabies move mostly by step.
- **Leap** — jumping over at least one note (C to E, or C up to the next C). Leaps make a melody exciting and memorable, but too many make it hard to sing.

A strong melody usually mixes steps with a few leaps, and after a big leap it often turns back by step — like a ball that bounces up and settles.

The **contour** is the overall shape: rising, falling, arch (up then down) or wave. Many choruses rise towards their highest note at the emotional peak.

Most melodies have a **home note** (the **tonic**). It is the note that sounds finished. Sing "Happy Birthday" but stop before the last note — you can feel it pulling you home. Ending on the tonic gives a melody a sense of arrival; ending elsewhere leaves it sounding like a question.

**Range** is the distance from the lowest to the highest note. A song for a whole congregation or class usually keeps a small range so everybody can sing it.

Yoruba and Igbo are **tonal languages**: the pitch of a syllable can change the meaning of a word. This is one reason the talking drum (dùndún) can "speak" — it copies the rise and fall of speech. Songwriters in these languages often shape melodies so they do not fight the natural tones of the words.

## Key words

- **Pitch:** how high or low a sound is
- **Melody:** a sequence of pitches with a rhythm, heard as one tune
- **Step:** movement to the next note up or down
- **Leap:** a jump of more than one note
- **Contour:** the overall shape of a melody
- **Tonic:** the home note, where a melody sounds finished
- **Range:** the distance between the lowest and highest notes

## Read and watch

- [Melody Maker](https://musiclab.chromeexperiments.com/Melody-Maker/) — Chrome Music Lab
- [BBC Bitesize KS3 Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zmsvr82) — BBC
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use only three notes (C, D, E) and repeat-step movements. Make sure it ends on C.
- **If you already can:** write two four-note phrases — the first ending on G (a "question"), the second ending on C (an "answer") — and include one leap of five notes or more.

## Learning online

You need a phone keyboard app or Chrome Music Lab (free, works in any browser), plus your voice.

- **Evidence to upload:** a recording of your eight-note melody, played or sung, and a photo of the contour drawing for it. Write the note names under the drawing.
- **At the live Saturday class:** you will be asked to play or sing your melody once, and the class will draw its contour without seeing yours. If they match, your melody has a clear shape. Unmute only when called, so the group hears you cleanly.

## Before the next session

Choose one song you love. Draw its chorus contour and mark the highest note. Bring the drawing.

lessons.title: Reading notes: the staff and tonic sol-fa
lessons.summary: Read pitches on the treble staff and in tonic sol-fa, then sight-sing a short tune from both.
objectives: You will name notes on the treble staff, including middle C
You will sing a melody using sol-fa names (do re mi fa so la ti)
You will translate a short tune between staff notation and sol-fa
lessons.body:
Walk into almost any church choir practice in Nigeria and you will see something like *d : r | m : – | s : f | m : –*. That is tonic sol-fa, and many great Nigerian choristers learnt to read music from it before they ever saw a staff. This week you learn both systems, because a complete musician can move between them.

## What to do

1. Draw a five-line staff with a treble clef. Label the lines **E G B D F** and the spaces **F A C E**.
2. Add **middle C** on a short ledger line below the staff. Write C D E F G A B C going up.
3. Sing up and down the scale using **do re mi fa so la ti do**, matching each to C D E F G A B C on a keyboard app.
4. Read this tune in sol-fa and sing it slowly: **d d s s l l s – f f m m r r d –** (it is "Twinkle, Twinkle").
5. Write the same tune on your staff with C as do. Check each note on the keyboard.
6. Make up a four-bar tune in sol-fa and write it on the staff too.

## Understand it

**The staff** (or stave) is five lines and four spaces. Each line and space is a different pitch; higher on the staff means higher in sound.

The **clef** at the start tells you which pitches the lines mean. The **treble clef** (𝄞) curls around the second line from the bottom, marking it as **G** — which is why it is also called the G clef. It is used for higher voices and instruments: sopranos, altos, flutes, and the right hand of the piano. The **bass clef** is used for lower sounds; we will meet it later.

Memory helps for the treble clef:
- Lines, bottom to top: **E G B D F** — *Every Good Boy Deserves Football*.
- Spaces, bottom to top: **F A C E** — spells *face*.

Notes above or below the staff sit on short extra lines called **ledger lines**. **Middle C** sits on one ledger line just below the treble staff. The musical alphabet uses only seven letters, **A to G**, then starts again — the note after G is A.

**Tonic sol-fa** names notes by their *job in the key*, not by fixed letters: **do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do**, often written d r m f s l t d'. "Do" is always the home note (the tonic). If a song is in C, do is C; if it moves to G, do becomes G and every syllable moves with it. This is called **movable do**, and it is why sol-fa is so practical for choirs: the same patterns feel the same in any key. Rhythm in sol-fa notation is shown with marks such as colons for beats and dashes for held notes.

Staff notation is better for showing exact pitch to instruments; sol-fa is brilliant for training your ear and singing in harmony. **Solfège**, used in many countries, is the same idea.

To translate: decide which letter is do, then count up. With do = C, so is G (C D E F **G**: the fifth note) and la is A.

**Common mistakes:** reading the treble clef with bass-clef names, forgetting middle C needs a ledger line, and treating do as always C.

## Key words

- **Staff (stave):** the five lines and four spaces that music is written on
- **Treble clef:** the G clef, marking the second line as G, used for higher sounds
- **Ledger line:** a short extra line for notes above or below the staff
- **Middle C:** the C near the middle of a piano, on a ledger line below the treble staff
- **Tonic sol-fa:** a system naming notes by their place in the key: do re mi fa so la ti
- **Movable do:** the rule that do is always the home note of whatever key you are in

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Teoria: music theory tutorials and exercises](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** learn only the five line notes this week, plus middle C. Sing everything in sol-fa first, then find it on the staff.
- **If you already can:** write "Twinkle, Twinkle" twice — once with do = C and once with do = G (remember G major has F sharp, which you will meet next week) — and sing both in sol-fa.

## Learning online

You can do this with a notebook and a phone. If you do not have staff paper, rule five lines with a pencil.

- Drill note names daily with the musictheory.net **note identification** exercise for treble clef — five minutes is enough.
- **Evidence to upload:** a photo of your staff with labelled notes and your own four-bar tune written in both sol-fa and staff notation, and a recording of you singing your tune in sol-fa.
- **At the live Saturday class:** you will sight-sing a short sol-fa line the instructor posts in the chat. Keep a glass of water near you and a keyboard app open for your starting note.

## Before the next session

Score at least 15 correct in a row on the treble-clef note identification exercise. Write down your best streak and bring it.

lessons.title: Scales and keys: the ladder every tune climbs
lessons.summary: Build a major scale from its pattern of tones and semitones, hear the minor and pentatonic scales, and find the key of a song.
objectives: You will build a major scale from any starting note using tones and semitones
You will hear the difference between major, minor and pentatonic scales
You will identify the key and home note of a simple song
lessons.body:
Last week, do was the home note. But why does do–re–mi sound the way it does? Because of the distance between the steps. This week you learn the pattern that makes a major scale — and once you know it, you can build one on any note.

## What to do

1. On a keyboard app, play every key — white and black — from one C to the next C. That is 12 different notes, each a **semitone** apart.
2. Play only the white keys from C to C. Count the gaps: where are there no black keys between? (E–F and B–C.)
3. Write the major scale pattern: **T T S T T T S** (T = tone, S = semitone).
4. Build the scale starting on G using that pattern. You will need one black key. Name it.
5. Play C natural minor (C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C) and the C major pentatonic (C D E G A C). Describe each in one word.
6. Play the **black keys only** for a minute. Notice that almost anything sounds pleasant — find out why below.

## Understand it

A **semitone** is the smallest distance on a keyboard — from one key to the very next, black or white. A **tone** is two semitones. Most white keys are a tone apart because a black key sits between them; **E–F** and **B–C** are only a semitone apart.

A **scale** is a set of notes in order, going up or down, from one note to the same letter an **octave** higher. What makes a scale major or minor is its **pattern of tones and semitones**.

**The major scale:** T T S T T T S. Starting on C it gives C D E F G A B C — all white keys. Starting on G: G (T) A (T) B (S) C (T) D (T) E (T) **F♯** (S) G. The F must be raised by a **sharp (♯)** to keep the pattern. Starting on F you need **B♭** — a **flat (♭)** lowers a note by a semitone. The set of sharps or flats a key needs is its **key signature**, written at the start of each line of music.

**The natural minor scale:** T S T T S T T. Starting on A it uses only white keys: A B C D E F G A. Because A minor and C major share every note, they are called **relative** keys. Minor often sounds darker or more serious, but not always sad — many joyful Nigerian gospel and Afrobeats songs are in minor keys.

**The pentatonic scale** has five notes. The major pentatonic is do re mi so la (C D E G A). It leaves out fa and ti, the two notes that sit a semitone from a neighbour, so there are no semitone clashes — which is why playing only the black keys (F♯ G♯ A♯ C♯ D♯, a pentatonic set) sounds pleasant. Pentatonic scales appear in music all over the world, including many West African songs, spirituals and folk tunes.

**Key** means the scale a piece mainly uses and its home note. "This song is in G major" means G is the tonic and the notes come mostly from the G major scale. To find a song's key by ear, hum the note that sounds most like "the end", then find it on a keyboard — that is usually the tonic.

**Common mistakes:** counting a white-to-white move as always a tone (E–F is not), and writing F♯ as G♭ in G major — every letter appears once in a scale.

## Key words

- **Semitone:** the smallest step on a keyboard, from one key to the very next
- **Tone:** two semitones
- **Scale:** a set of notes in order between one note and its octave
- **Sharp / flat:** a sign that raises (♯) or lowers (♭) a note by one semitone
- **Key signature:** the sharps or flats written at the start of the staff for a key
- **Pentatonic:** a five-note scale; the major pentatonic is do re mi so la
- **Relative minor:** the minor key that shares every note with a major key, such as A minor and C major

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Shared Piano](https://musiclab.chromeexperiments.com/Shared-Piano/) — Chrome Music Lab
- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** build only C major and G major this week, with the pattern written next to the keyboard picture.
- **If you already can:** build D major (two sharps) and F major (one flat), then sing a well-known chorus and work out its key on the keyboard.

## Learning online

A free keyboard app or the Chrome Music Lab Shared Piano is enough. If you have nothing but a phone, draw a two-octave keyboard on paper and point as you sing.

- **Evidence to upload:** a photo of your written G major scale with T and S marked between every pair of notes, and a recording of you playing (or singing in sol-fa) C major, then C natural minor, then C pentatonic, saying each name before you play it.
- **At the live Saturday class:** the instructor will play scales over the call and you will type "major", "minor" or "pentatonic" in the chat. Use headphones if you can — the difference is clearer.

## Before the next session

Pick one song you know and find its home note on a keyboard app. Write down the note and whether you think the song is major or minor, with your reason.

lessons.title: Chords and harmony: three notes that change everything
lessons.summary: Build major and minor triads, play the I–IV–V–vi chords of a key, and fit a chord pattern under a melody.
objectives: You will build major and minor triads from root, third and fifth
You will name chords I, IV, V and vi in C major
You will choose chords that fit under a short melody and perform them
lessons.body:
A melody on its own is a single line. Put other notes underneath it, at the same time, and you have **harmony** — the thing that makes a choir sound full and a song feel happy, hopeful or heavy. Harmony is built from **chords**.

## What to do

1. On a keyboard app, play C, E and G together. That is a **C major chord**.
2. Lower the E to E♭ and play again: C, E♭, G. That is **C minor**. Describe the change.
3. Build triads on each note of C major using only white keys: skip-a-note, skip-a-note (C–E–G, D–F–A, E–G–B …). Mark each as major or minor.
4. Play the four chords **C – G – Am – F**, one per bar, four beats each, along with a metronome at 80 BPM. Loop it eight times.
5. Sing "do re mi re do" over a C chord, then over F. Which fits better? Use your ear.
6. Record your loop with you humming any melody over it.

## Understand it

A **chord** is two or more notes played together. The most common chord is the **triad**: three notes stacked in thirds — a **root**, a **third** above it and a **fifth** above the root. On white keys, build one by taking a note, skipping one, taking the next, skipping one, taking the next: C (skip D) E (skip F) G.

The *third* decides the chord's character:
- **Major triad:** the third is **4 semitones** above the root (a major third), and the fifth is 3 semitones above that. C–E–G. It sounds bright and settled.
- **Minor triad:** the third is **3 semitones** above the root (a minor third), then 4 more to the fifth. A–C–E. It sounds darker or more reflective.

Build a triad on every note of C major and you get: **C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am**, and **B diminished** (B–D–F). Musicians number them with Roman numerals — upper case for major, lower case for minor: **I ii iii IV V vi vii°**.

Three chords do most of the work in a major key:
- **I** (C) — home, rest.
- **IV** (F) — moving away, warmth.
- **V** (G) — tension that wants to return to I.

Add **vi** (Am), the relative minor, and you have the **I–V–vi–IV** progression (C–G–Am–F), heard in a huge number of pop, gospel and Afrobeats songs across the world. Highlife guitar often cycles between I, IV and V with a bright, rolling pattern.

A **chord progression** is the order chords follow. The movement **V → I** is the strongest way to end a phrase; this is called a **perfect cadence**. Ending on V (**imperfect cadence**) sounds like a comma, not a full stop.

To fit chords under a melody, look at the most important melody notes in each bar (usually those on strong beats) and choose a chord that *contains* them. If the bar's melody leans on E and G, C major (C–E–G) fits; if it leans on A and C, try F (F–A–C) or Am (A–C–E). Your ear decides between them.

**Consonance** is when notes blend restfully; **dissonance** is when they clash and want to move on. Both are useful — music without tension is music without a journey.

## Key words

- **Chord:** two or more notes sounding together
- **Triad:** a three-note chord of root, third and fifth
- **Root:** the note a chord is built on and named after
- **Chord progression:** the order in which chords follow each other
- **Cadence:** a chord move that ends a phrase, such as V to I
- **Harmony:** notes sounding together to support a melody

## Read and watch

- [Chords](https://musiclab.chromeexperiments.com/Chords/) — Chrome Music Lab
- [TheoryTab](https://www.hooktheory.com/theorytab) — Hooktheory
- [Learning Music](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/) — Ableton

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use only C, F and G. Play just the root note of each in the bass with one finger while you count four beats.
- **If you already can:** play the loop in G major (G–D–Em–C), then add a seventh to the V chord (G7: G–B–D–F) and describe what it does to the pull back home.

## Learning online

A keyboard app or Chrome Music Lab Chords is all you need; both are free.

- **Evidence to upload:** a recording of your C–G–Am–F loop played eight times over a metronome at 80 BPM, with you humming a melody on top, plus a photo of your chart of the seven triads in C major marked major, minor or diminished.
- **At the live Saturday class:** the instructor will play a melody line and you will vote, in the chat, which of C, F or G fits each bar. Bring your chord chart so you can check the notes quickly.

## Before the next session

Find the chords of one song you like on Hooktheory TheoryTab or by ear. Write the progression in Roman numerals and bring it.

lessons.title: Song structure: verse, chorus, bridge — and a look back
lessons.summary: Map the sections of a real song and use everything from weeks 1–6 to describe what changes between them.
objectives: You will name the sections of a song: intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, outro
You will recall and use pulse, rhythm, melody, scale and chord vocabulary to describe a song
You will draw a timed structure map of a song you choose
lessons.body:
Halfway through the term, it is time to step back. You now have six tools: pulse, rhythm notation, melody, reading notes, scales and chords. This week you use all of them at once to look at how whole songs are built — and you will find out which tools you have truly kept.

## What to do

1. **Retrieval warm-up (no notes!):** on a blank page, write from memory: the major scale pattern; the treble staff lines; the notes of C, F and G major chords; what 3/4 means; the difference between pulse and rhythm. Then check against weeks 1–6 and correct in a different colour.
2. Choose one song you know well, about three to four minutes long. It can be gospel, Afrobeats, highlife, a choir piece — anything with words.
3. Listen with a timer. Each time the music changes section, write the time and a label (Intro, Verse 1, Chorus …).
4. For each section, write one line about what changes: lyrics, melody height, rhythm, instruments, loudness.
5. Draw the structure as coloured blocks along a timeline — the same colour for sections that repeat.
6. Count the chorus's tempo in BPM and guess its key, using week 5.

## Understand it

Most songs are built from **sections**, repeated and contrasted so the listener knows where they are.

- **Intro** — sets the mood and tempo before the singing begins.
- **Verse** — tells the story. The melody and chords usually repeat each time, but the *words change*.
- **Pre-chorus** — a short build that lifts the energy towards the chorus.
- **Chorus** — the main message. The *words and melody are the same* each time, and it is often higher, louder and fuller. It usually contains the **hook**, the catchiest line.
- **Bridge** — appears once, usually after the second chorus, with something new — different chords, a different melody — so the last chorus feels fresh.
- **Outro** — the ending, often fading or repeating the hook.

A very common pop shape is **Intro – Verse – Chorus – Verse – Chorus – Bridge – Chorus – Outro**. Musicians use letters to describe form: a song of verses and choruses might be written **A B A B C B**.

**Call and response** is a structure at the centre of much African music: a leader sings a line (the call) and a group answers (the response). You hear it in juju, in fuji, in church and mosque, at football matches, and in Afrobeat, where Fela's voice would be answered by his singers. It also shaped gospel, blues and jazz across the Atlantic.

Groove-based styles may be organised differently. Afrobeat songs are often long — ten minutes or more — building by adding and removing layers over one repeating groove rather than by changing chords. That is still structure; it is just structure of **texture** (how many parts are playing) rather than of verse and chorus.

**What changes between sections?** Use your six tools:
- **Pulse and tempo** usually stay the same — that is what holds the song together.
- **Rhythm** may get busier in the chorus (more drums, quicker words).
- **Melody** often sits higher in the chorus.
- **Harmony** may switch to a different chord pattern for the chorus or bridge.
- **Dynamics** (loudness) and **texture** usually rise in the chorus.

**About the warm-up:** recalling something from memory, then checking, makes it stick far better than re-reading. Anything you got wrong is not a failure — it is a map of exactly what to practise.

## Key words

- **Verse:** a section with new words each time, telling the story
- **Chorus:** the repeated section with the same words and the main message
- **Hook:** the catchiest short line or riff in a song
- **Bridge:** a contrasting section that usually comes once near the end
- **Call and response:** a leader's phrase answered by a group
- **Texture:** how many layers of sound are playing and how they fit together
- **Dynamics:** how loud or soft the music is

## Read and watch

- [TheoryTab](https://www.hooktheory.com/theorytab) — Hooktheory
- [BBC Bitesize KS3 Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zmsvr82) — BBC
- [Learning Music](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/) — Ableton

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** choose a song with a very clear chorus, and only mark Verse and Chorus. Add other labels once those are right.
- **If you already can:** map an Afrobeat track by Fela and an Afrobeats track by Burna Boy or Tems side by side and write a paragraph comparing how each one builds energy.

## Learning online

All you need is a phone or laptop to play the song and a notebook.

- Use any music app or a legal streaming service to play your song; pause and scrub back to pin each section's start time.
- **Evidence to upload:** a photo of your corrected retrieval warm-up (show both colours — we want to see what you corrected) and a photo or screenshot of your coloured structure map with times and one line per section.
- **At the live Saturday class:** be ready to share your screen or hold your map to the camera and play 20 seconds of your chorus. Others will say what changed from the verse using the week 1–6 words.

## Before the next session

Redo only the items you got wrong in the warm-up, on Thursday, from memory again. Bring your score both times.

lessons.title: Listening like a musician: Nigerian sounds, and checking the AI
lessons.summary: Listen closely to highlife, juju, fuji, Afrobeat, Afrobeats, gospel and choral music, and test an AI tool's description of them against your own ears.
objectives: You will describe a recording using pulse, tempo, melody, harmony, texture and instruments
You will tell apart highlife, juju, fuji, Afrobeat and Afrobeats by their features
You will check an AI tool's music claims against listening and reliable sources
lessons.body:
Nigeria has one of the richest music histories in the world, and you have been hearing it your whole life. This week you listen on purpose. You will also ask an AI tool to describe these styles — and then do what a good musician does with any confident voice: check it.

## What to do

1. Find one track (legally, on a streaming service, radio, or a family collection) for each of: **highlife**, **juju**, **fuji**, **Afrobeat**, **Afrobeats**, and either **Nigerian gospel** or **choral music**.
2. For each, listen to one minute twice. Fill a row in a table: tempo (slow/medium/fast, and a BPM guess), main instruments, how the vocals work (solo, call and response, choir), texture (thin or thick), and one word for the mood.
3. Ask a free AI chatbot your guardian allows: *"Describe the musical features of juju and Afrobeat, and name two key artists for each."*
4. Underline every claim the AI makes. Mark each ✔ (you can hear it or it matches Britannica), ✘ (wrong), or ? (cannot check).
5. Write down one thing the AI got wrong or left vague, and one thing your ears noticed that the AI did not mention.

## Understand it

**Listening like a musician** means using vocabulary, not just "I like it". Go through the elements: pulse and tempo; rhythm (busy or sparse, on the beat or off); melody (range, steps or leaps); harmony (how many chords, how often they change); instruments and **timbre** (the colour of a sound — why a trumpet and a voice singing the same note still sound different); texture; dynamics; structure.

Some features of the styles this week (what to *listen for*, not a rule every song follows):

- **Highlife** grew in Ghana in the early twentieth century and spread to Nigeria, where bandleaders such as Bobby Benson, Victor Olaiya, Rex Lawson and Stephen Osita Osadebe made it their own. Listen for bright, interlocking guitar lines or dance-band horns over a relaxed, swinging groove and clear major-key chords.
- **Jùjú** is a Yoruba style that took shape from the 1920s–30s and was made famous by I. K. Dairo, Ebenezer Obey and King Sunny Adé. Listen for the **talking drum**, layered guitars (King Sunny Adé added the pedal steel guitar), and call and response singing, often praising people and God.
- **Fújì** was developed in the late 1960s and 1970s by Sikiru Ayinde Barrister from Yoruba Muslim *wéré* music sung during Ramadan. It is driven by **percussion and voice** — several drums, often with little or no guitar — with a lead singer and responding chorus.
- **Afrobeat** was created by **Fela Anikulapo Kuti** with drummer **Tony Allen** in the late 1960s and 1970s, mixing highlife, jazz, funk and Yoruba music. Listen for very long songs, a repeating groove, horn sections, interlocking guitar riffs, and politically sharp lyrics, often in Pidgin.
- **Afrobeats** (with an s) is the twenty-first-century pop sound of artists such as Wizkid, Davido, Burna Boy, Tiwa Savage and Tems. It is shorter and song-shaped, usually built in a computer, with a mid-tempo groove, layered percussion and log-drum or synth bass. It borrows from Afrobeat but is a **different** genre — mixing the two up is one of the most common mistakes, including by AI tools.
- **Gospel** (for example Sinach's "Way Maker") and **choral** music (from church choirs to composers such as Ayo Bankole) lean on harmony between voices, often learned in sol-fa.

**Using AI critically.** A chatbot writes fluent, confident sentences, but it predicts likely words rather than listening to music. It can mix up names, dates and genres, invent song titles, and describe a style in vague words that would fit anything ("energetic rhythms"). Treat it as a starting point: check specific claims against a reliable source such as Britannica, and check musical claims against your own ears. If you cannot hear it, do not repeat it.

## Key words

- **Timbre:** the tone colour of a sound that lets you tell instruments apart
- **Genre:** a style of music with shared features
- **Talking drum:** an hourglass drum (dùndún) whose pitch is bent by squeezing its cords
- **Groove:** the repeating rhythmic feel that makes people move
- **Afrobeat / Afrobeats:** Fela's 1970s fusion, and the separate 21st-century pop genre
- **Verify:** to check a claim against evidence before trusting it

## Read and watch

- [Highlife](https://www.britannica.com/art/highlife) — Encyclopaedia Britannica
- [Afrobeat](https://www.britannica.com/art/Afrobeat) — Encyclopaedia Britannica
- [Fela Anikulapo Kuti](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Fela-Anikulapo-Kuti) — Encyclopaedia Britannica

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** compare just two styles — Afrobeat and Afrobeats — and fill the table for those only.
- **If you already can:** add a seventh column for an older family recording and interview the relative who owns it: what did that music mean when they were your age?

## Learning online

You need a phone or laptop, a way to play music legally, and (only with your parent or guardian's permission) a free AI chatbot. If you cannot use an AI tool, your instructor will paste an AI answer in the class chat for you to check.

- **Evidence to upload:** a photo of your six-row listening table, and a screenshot of the AI answer with your ✔ ✘ ? marks on it (marking on a printout or a notebook copy is fine).
- **At the live Saturday class:** bring one 20-second clip from your table to play, and the AI's worst mistake. We will build a class list of "things AI got wrong about Nigerian music".

## Before the next session

Listen to one full Fela track from start to end without doing anything else. Note the time at which each new instrument enters.

lessons.title: A real brief: a jingle for your community
lessons.summary: Take a brief from a real person in your community and write a short jingle or chant that delivers their message.
objectives: You will gather a brief from a real person: message, audience, length and mood
You will write a memorable hook using the melody, rhythm and chord tools from this term
You will present a first draft and collect feedback from the person who gave the brief
lessons.body:
Musicians do not only make music for themselves. Much of the music in Nigeria — radio jingles, church and mosque events, school songs, campaign chants — is written to a **brief**: somebody needs a message carried, and music carries it. This week you get a real brief and answer it.

## What to do

1. **Find a client.** Ask a real person — a teacher, a pastor or imam, a market association, a youth group, a clinic, your NGG centre lead — if they have a message that a short song could help with. Examples: hand-washing, a clean-up day, a reading club, voting registration for adults, saving water.
2. **Take the brief.** Ask them five questions and write down the answers: *What is the one message? Who is it for? Where will it be heard? How long can it be? What feeling should it give?*
3. **Write the hook first:** one line of words, said aloud until the natural rhythm is clear. Write that rhythm in notes (week 2).
4. Set it to a melody of no more than six notes, ending on the tonic (weeks 3–5). Keep the range small so anyone can sing it.
5. Choose two to four chords to sit under it (week 6) — or a body-percussion groove if your client wants a chant.
6. Make a 15–30 second draft, record it, and play it to your client. Write down exactly what they say.

## Understand it

**A brief** is an agreement about what the music must do. Working to one is a professional skill: the question is not "is this my favourite song?" but "does this do the job for these listeners?"

**Write for your audience.** A jingle for primary-school children needs simple words, a small range and lots of repetition. One for traders in a busy market must cut through noise — strong rhythm, a short hook, maybe a call and response so people join in. Choosing the language matters too: English, Pidgin, Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo or a mix should be the client's choice, because they know their listeners.

**What makes a hook stick?**
- **Short:** one line, often four to eight syllables.
- **Repetition:** say it at least three times in 30 seconds.
- **Rhythm that matches speech:** stress the important syllables on strong beats. "WASH your HANDS be-FORE you EAT" puts the stresses on beats.
- **A shape:** a clear contour with one leap on the key word makes it memorable (week 3).
- **Resolution:** end on the tonic so it sounds finished, or deliberately on V so it feels like an invitation to sing again.

**Respect the tones.** If you write in a tonal language such as Yoruba or Igbo, check that your melody does not turn the word into a different meaning — sing it to a fluent speaker.

**Be honest about what you use.** Your melody must be your own. Borrowing the tune of a famous song for a public jingle can break copyright, even if the words are new. Free sounds in BandLab are licensed for you to use in your own music.

**Feedback from a client** is information, not a verdict. Write down what they say in their words. Separate *what* they want changed ("it is too fast for the children") from *how* they suggest fixing it ("use a different song") — you are the musician; the solution can be yours.

**Safety and permission:** only work with adults your parent or guardian knows, meet in public or online with them aware, and do not publish anyone's name or face without permission.

## Key words

- **Brief:** a short agreement about what a piece must do, for whom, and how long
- **Jingle:** a short, catchy piece of music that carries a message
- **Client:** the person or group the music is made for
- **Hook:** the catchiest line, built to be remembered
- **Copyright:** the legal right of a creator to control copies of their work

## Read and watch

- [Song Maker](https://musiclab.chromeexperiments.com/Song-Maker/) — Chrome Music Lab
- [BandLab](https://www.bandlab.com/) — BandLab
- [BBC Bitesize KS3 Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zmsvr82) — BBC

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** make a spoken chant over a stamp-clap groove from week 1, with a three-note sung hook at the end.
- **If you already can:** write a verse and a chorus, include call and response so a group can join, and make a second version in a different language for a different audience.

## Learning online

You can do the whole brief online. Interview your client by phone or video call, or send the five questions on a messaging app.

- Make your draft in Chrome Music Lab's Song Maker or BandLab (both free; BandLab needs an account — ask your parent or guardian), or just sing over a metronome into your phone's recorder.
- **Evidence to upload:** a photo or typed copy of the brief (all five answers), your 15–30 second draft recording, and the client's feedback in their own words.
- **At the live Saturday class:** you will pitch your jingle in 60 seconds — say who it is for and what the brief asked, then play it. Classmates will give one "keep" and one "change".

## Before the next session

Make one change your client asked for and record version 2. Keep version 1 — you will compare them next week.

lessons.title: Capstone part 1: compose your piece
lessons.summary: Plan and write a 16-bar piece with a clear structure, melody, chords and rhythm, written so somebody else could perform it.
objectives: You will plan a 16-bar piece with at least two contrasting sections
You will write the melody and chord symbols in staff notation or sol-fa
You will record a complete first performance of your piece
lessons.body:
This is the start of your capstone. Over the next three weeks you will compose, rehearse and perform an original piece. You can grow your week 9 jingle into it, or start fresh. Either way, this week the piece goes onto paper, all the way to the last bar.

## What to do

1. **Decide the frame:** time signature (4/4, 3/4 or 12/8), key (C, G or F major, or A minor), tempo in BPM, and mood.
2. **Plan the structure** as 16 bars in two or more sections, for example **A (8 bars) + B (8 bars)**, or **A A B A** (4 bars each). Write it as boxes.
3. **Chords first:** write one chord per bar for the A section using I, IV, V and vi. End section A on V (a question) and the final bar on I (an answer).
4. **Melody:** compose over the chords, putting chord notes on strong beats. Make the B section contrast — higher, or a different rhythm, or call and response.
5. **Write it down** in staff notation (on paper or in MuseScore, which is free) or in sol-fa with chord letters above. Add tempo, dynamics (p, mf, f) and a title.
6. **Perform it once, start to finish,** and record it — mistakes and all.

## Understand it

**Composing is choosing.** You already have every tool. The job now is to make decisions and write them down clearly enough that another musician could perform your piece without you in the room.

**Plan big, then small.** Professional composers rarely start with note one. They decide length, structure and mood, then fill in. Sixteen bars at 90 BPM in 4/4 is about 43 seconds — long enough to say something, short enough to finish well.

**Unity and contrast.** A piece needs repetition so it hangs together, and change so it stays interesting. In **A B** form the B section contrasts; in **A A B A** (sometimes called 32-bar song form when each section is eight bars) the A returns at the end, which gives a satisfying feeling of coming home.

**Motif.** A **motif** is a short musical idea — two to four notes or a rhythm — that you repeat and develop. Develop it by:
- **Repetition** — exactly again.
- **Sequence** — the same shape starting on a different note (C–D–E, then D–E–F).
- **Rhythmic change** — same notes, new rhythm.
- **Inversion** — turn its direction upside down.

**Phrases and cadences.** Music breathes in **phrases**, usually two or four bars, like sentences. End a middle phrase on chord V (an **imperfect cadence**, like a comma) and the final phrase with **V → I** (a **perfect cadence**, a full stop).

**Writing it clearly.** Check every bar adds up to the time signature (week 2). Put chord symbols (C, G, Am, F) above the staff where they change. Mark tempo at the top (♩ = 90) and dynamics below the notes: **p** (piano, soft), **mf** (mezzo-forte, moderately loud), **f** (forte, loud), and hairpins for **crescendo** (getting louder) and **diminuendo** (getting softer).

**Use your voice and body.** This course is instrument-agnostic: your piece can be for solo voice, voices in parts, body percussion with voice, or a phone keyboard. Choose what *you* can perform well next week.

**The first performance is a test, not a verdict.** The recording will show you which bars are awkward to sing, which rhythms are unclear on paper, and where the melody needs a breath. That is exactly what week 11 is for.

## Key words

- **Compose:** to create and fix an original piece of music
- **Motif:** a short musical idea that is repeated and developed
- **Sequence:** a motif repeated starting on a different pitch
- **Phrase:** a musical sentence, often two or four bars
- **Perfect cadence:** the chord move V to I that ends a piece
- **Crescendo:** getting gradually louder

## Read and watch

- [MuseScore](https://musescore.org/) — MuseScore
- [Song Maker](https://musiclab.chromeexperiments.com/Song-Maker/) — Chrome Music Lab
- [TheoryTab](https://www.hooktheory.com/theorytab) — Hooktheory

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** write 8 bars in A A form with three chords (I, IV, V), all crotchets and minims. Finish it completely before adding anything.
- **If you already can:** write 16 bars in A A B A, use a sequence in the B section, add a simple second part (a harmony line a third below, or a bass line of chord roots) and notate it in MuseScore.

## Learning online

You can compose entirely at home. MuseScore is free on a laptop; on a phone, use paper and Chrome Music Lab's Song Maker to hear your ideas, then photograph the written version.

- **Evidence to upload:** your plan (structure boxes, key, tempo, time signature), the complete written score or sol-fa sheet, and one recording of a full run-through.
- **At the live Saturday class:** have your score ready to share on screen or hold up. In breakout groups, a classmate will try to read the first four bars from your score — if they cannot, that shows you where to make it clearer.

## Before the next session

Listen to your recording twice. Mark the score in a different colour wherever something felt awkward, unclear or too hard. Bring the marked score.

lessons.title: Capstone part 2: rehearse, revise, and remember
lessons.summary: Revisit the term's core skills through your own piece, improve it with feedback, and rehearse it to performance standard.
objectives: You will recall and apply pulse, notation, scales and chords to diagnose problems in your piece
You will give and use specific peer feedback to make at least two revisions
You will rehearse to a steady, confident run-through using deliberate practice
lessons.body:
A piece is rarely finished the first time it is written. This week you go back through the term — pulse, rhythm, melody, reading, scales, chords — not by re-reading, but by using each one to test and improve your own composition. Then you practise it the way performers do.

## What to do

1. **Retrieval check on your own score.** Without notes, answer six questions about your piece: What is the pulse in BPM? Does every bar add up? What is the tonic? Which scale does it use, and does any note fall outside it? Which chord is in each bar, and do they contain the strong-beat melody notes? Where are the cadences?
2. **Swap feedback** with a classmate (or a family member if you learn at home). Use the format: *one thing that works, one thing to change, one question.*
3. **Revise:** make at least two specific changes and keep a log: "Bar 6: changed G to E so it fits the C chord."
4. **Deliberate practice:** find the hardest two bars. Practise only them, slowly with a metronome at 70% of your tempo, until correct five times in a row. Then raise the tempo.
5. **Full run-throughs:** three complete performances in a row without stopping, even if you slip. Record the best.

## Understand it

**Retrieval practice** — pulling knowledge out of your memory — strengthens it more than reading it again. That is why this week starts with questions about your own piece rather than a summary of the term. Each question is a week of the course:

- **Week 1 – pulse:** does the tempo stay steady, or do you rush the exciting parts?
- **Week 2 – notation:** does every bar contain exactly the beats the time signature promises?
- **Weeks 3 and 4 – melody and reading:** is there a clear contour and a peak? Can a reader see the pitches?
- **Week 5 – scale:** do all the notes belong to your key, unless you chose otherwise on purpose?
- **Week 6 – chords:** on strong beats, does the melody note belong to the chord?
- **Week 7 – structure:** can a listener tell where the sections begin?

**Useful feedback is specific.** "It's nice" helps nobody. "In bar 9 the jump up to the high E is hard to sing in tune — could you step up to it?" gives the composer something to do. When you receive feedback, you do not have to accept it; you do have to consider it, and be able to say why you kept or changed something.

**Deliberate practice** is focused, slow work on the exact place that is weak, with immediate feedback (a metronome, a recording). Playing a piece top to bottom over and over mostly practises the parts you can already do and repeats the mistakes in the hard bars. Isolate, slow down, repeat correctly, then speed up.

**Performing is a separate skill from playing.** Practise starting confidently: breathe, count in silently ("one, two, three, four"), and begin. Practise **recovering**: if you make a mistake in a real performance, keep the pulse going and come back in on the next beat 1. An audience forgives a wrong note; they notice a stop.

**Nerves** are normal and show you care. Slow breathing — in for four beats, out for six — lowers your heart rate. Rehearse in front of one or two people before the showcase so the first audience is not the real one.

**Dynamics and expression:** check that your marks (p, f, crescendo) are actually audible in the recording. Often what feels like a big change while performing sounds tiny on playback.

## Key words

- **Retrieval practice:** recalling knowledge from memory to strengthen it
- **Deliberate practice:** slow, focused work on a specific weakness with feedback
- **Revision:** a deliberate change made to improve a piece
- **Run-through:** a complete performance without stopping
- **Count-in:** beats counted before starting so the tempo is set

## Read and watch

- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [BBC Bitesize KS3 Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zmsvr82) — BBC
- [Learning Music](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/) — Ableton

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** answer the retrieval questions with your score open next to the week's notes, and aim for one clean run-through rather than three.
- **If you already can:** revise for contrast — add a dynamic plan for the whole piece, a short introduction, and a final bar that holds a longer note — and perform it from memory.

## Learning online

Rehearsal is ideal at home. You need your score, a metronome app and your phone's recorder.

- If no classmate is available, swap recordings in the online class group, or ask a family member to give the *works – change – question* feedback; write down their exact words.
- **Evidence to upload:** your six retrieval answers, the feedback you received, your revision log (at least two changes with bar numbers), the revised score, and your best full run-through recording.
- **At the live Saturday class:** you will do a **dress rehearsal** — perform once on camera with your microphone on. Test your sound beforehand: sit about an arm's length from the phone and avoid a noisy fan behind you.

## Before the next session

Perform your piece for at least one person at home. Ask them what they remember most about it. Bring their answer.

lessons.title: Showcase: perform, listen, reflect
lessons.summary: Perform your original piece to an audience, give thoughtful responses to others' work, and reflect on how your musicianship has grown this term.
objectives: You will introduce and perform your original piece to an audience
You will respond to other musicians' work with precise, kind musical vocabulary
You will reflect on your progress across the term and set a next step
lessons.body:
Twelve weeks ago you clapped along to a pulse. Today you perform music you wrote yourself. A showcase is a celebration — and also the moment a musician learns most, because an audience shows you what your music actually does.

## What to do

1. **Prepare a 30-second introduction:** your name, the title, what the piece is about or who it is for (mention your week 9 client if you grew the jingle), and one thing to listen for.
2. **Warm up** for five minutes: breathe, hum, clap the pulse of your piece with a metronome, then run the hardest bars once slowly.
3. **Perform** your piece for the showcase audience — family, classmates, your centre, or the live online class.
4. **Listen and respond** to at least three other performances. For each, write one specific thing that worked and one question, using the term's vocabulary.
5. **Reflect:** compare your week 1 recording with today's. Write what has changed.
6. **Set a next step:** choose one course or skill to continue with next term and say why.

## Understand it

**A showcase is a performance with a purpose.** You are not proving you are perfect; you are sharing something you made and learning how it lands.

**Presenting your work.** A good introduction tells the audience how to listen: "This is a hand-washing song for the nursery class at our church. Listen for the call and response in the chorus — you can join in." It is short, warm, and gives listeners something to hold.

**Stage presence**, even on a video call: stand or sit tall, look at the audience (or the camera lens, not the screen) before you start, take one breath, count in silently, and begin. At the end, hold the last note or silence for a moment, then smile and say thank you. Do not apologise in advance — let the music speak.

**Being a good audience** is part of musicianship. Listen actively, with the same tools you used on Nigerian recordings in week 8: tempo, rhythm, melody, harmony, timbre, texture, dynamics and structure. Feedback at a showcase is **kind and specific**: "The leap up to the word 'together' in your chorus made it feel joyful" teaches the performer far more than "nice".

**Reflecting on growth.** Reflection turns experience into learning. Good reflection is:
- **Specific** — not "I improved" but "In week 1 I rushed at 80 BPM; now I hold 100 BPM for a whole piece."
- **Evidence-based** — point to recordings, scores and checks you completed.
- **Honest about difficulty** — name what was hard and what you did about it.
- **Forward-looking** — a next step you can actually take.

**Where next?** The Creative and Performing Arts division has courses that build directly on this one. If you loved singing, try **Vocal Training**; if chords made sense, **Piano** or **Guitar**; if rhythm was your favourite, **Drums**; if you enjoyed building tracks in BandLab, **Music Production**. Choir, worship teams, school bands and cultural groups in your community are all places to keep making music with others.

**Sharing safely:** only post a recording online with your parent or guardian's permission, and never alongside personal details such as your school or address.

## Key words

- **Showcase:** a public performance sharing finished work
- **Stage presence:** how a performer holds the audience's attention and confidence
- **Active listening:** listening with attention to specific musical elements
- **Reflection:** thinking back on experience to learn from it
- **Musicianship:** the shared skills of hearing, reading, making and performing music

## Read and watch

- [BandLab](https://www.bandlab.com/) — BandLab
- [BBC Bitesize KS3 Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zmsvr82) — BBC
- [Learning Music](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/) — Ableton

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** perform your piece once for a small, friendly audience, and use the reflection sentence starters: *At the start I … Now I … The hardest part was …*
- **If you already can:** perform from memory, teach the audience your chorus or response line so they sing it back, and record a short spoken programme note to go with your recording.

## Learning online

You can take part fully from home.

- **Live:** perform in the Saturday online showcase. Test your camera and sound before the class, use headphones to hear others but take them off while you perform if your device allows, and keep your metronome off during the performance unless your piece needs it.
- **If your connection is unreliable:** record your performance in advance in one take, upload it before Saturday, and your instructor will play it in the showcase. Be on the call to introduce it and to hear the response.
- **Evidence to upload:** your performance recording, your written introduction, three peer responses, and your written reflection comparing week 1 and today.
- **At the live Saturday class:** bring your week 1 recording ready to play for a "then and now" moment, if you choose to share it.

## Before the next session

Enjoy it. Then save every recording and score from this term in one folder — it is your portfolio, and next term you will want to hear how far you have come.

lessons.title: Exposure and light on a phone
lessons.summary: Take control of brightness on your phone so faces are clear and skies are not burnt white.
objectives: You will lock focus and exposure on a phone camera
You will use exposure compensation to protect highlights and faces
You will explain why a frame rate and steady light matter for exposure
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** A phone guesses the brightness of every shot. This week you stop letting it guess.

## What to do

- Film the same person in three places — in shade, in direct sun and indoors near a window — first on automatic, then with exposure locked and adjusted by you
- Compare the pairs side by side and note which details were lost on automatic
- Make one 15-second clip where the brightness does not "breathe" as people walk through the frame

## Understand it

**Exposure** is how much light reaches the camera's sensor, and so how bright the picture is. Too little and the shadows turn to muddy black (**underexposed**); too much and bright areas turn to flat white with no detail (**overexposed**, or "clipped"). Once a sky or a white shirt is clipped, no editing app can bring the detail back, because it was never recorded.

A phone sets exposure automatically by measuring the whole frame and aiming for an average grey. That works for a dull scene, but it fails in exactly the situations you meet every day in Nigeria:

- **A bright sky behind a person.** The phone darkens everything to save the sky, and the face becomes a silhouette.
- **A dark face against a white wall.** The phone darkens the shot for the wall, and the skin loses detail. Deeper skin tones need you to expose *for the face*, not for the background.
- **Someone walking from shade into sun.** The phone keeps changing its mind and the picture pumps brighter and darker. This "breathing" is one of the clearest signs of amateur video.

**Taking control.** On almost every phone, tap and hold on your subject's face until you see **AE/AF Lock** (iPhone) or a lock icon (most Android phones). Focus and exposure now stay fixed. Then slide the sun or brightness icon next to the focus box up or down — this is **exposure compensation**. Expose for the face: skin should look natural, with detail in the bright side of the cheek.

Many Android phones and free apps (Blackmagic Camera, Open Camera) offer a **Pro** or **Manual** mode with **ISO** and **shutter speed**. ISO brightens the image electronically but adds grain, so keep it low and add light instead. For video, a shutter speed of about double the frame rate (1/50 for 25 fps, 1/60 for 30 fps) gives natural movement. Under fluorescent tubes on Nigeria's 50 Hz mains, 25 fps with 1/50 also avoids flicker.

**Zebras.** Some apps show diagonal stripes on areas that are about to clip. If the stripes are on the sky, that may be acceptable; if they are on a face, bring the exposure down.

The best fix is often not a setting at all: **move the person or move yourself** so the light falls on the face and the background is not much brighter than the subject.

## Key words

- **Exposure:** how bright the image is, set by how much light reaches the sensor
- **Clipping:** detail lost in the brightest (or darkest) areas, which cannot be recovered
- **AE/AF lock:** fixing auto-exposure and auto-focus so they stop changing during a shot
- **Exposure compensation:** telling the camera to make the picture brighter or darker than it would choose
- **ISO:** electronic brightening of the image, which adds grain

## Read and watch

- [Exposure (photography)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposure_%28photography%29) — Wikipedia
- [Zebra patterning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zebra_patterning) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do only the shade/sun pair first, with a partner holding still while you practise the lock.
- **If you already can:** try the free Blackmagic Camera or Open Camera app and film the same shot at ISO 100 and ISO 1600; describe the difference in grain.

## Learning online

You can do all of this at home with one phone and one willing family member (ask first, and film only people who are happy to be filmed). Use your phone's own camera app; if you have an Android phone with no exposure slider, install Open Camera (free). Film your three automatic-versus-locked pairs, then put them side by side in CapCut or VN using split screen. **Upload:** the split-screen comparison (under one minute) and three sentences saying what the automatic setting got wrong each time. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** one screenshot of a clipped sky or a silhouetted face — yours or from any video — so we can discuss how it could have been avoided.

## Before the next session

lessons.title: Composition: thirds, headroom and lead room
lessons.summary: Place people and objects in the frame on purpose so the viewer's eye goes where you want it.
objectives: You will use the rule of thirds with your phone's grid
You will give subjects correct headroom and lead room
You will use foreground, lines and background to add depth
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Where you put things in the frame tells the viewer what matters before anybody says a word.

## What to do

- Turn on your camera grid and film six still shots around your home or centre, each using a different composition rule
- Film one person walking across the frame twice: once with lead room and once without
- Swap clips with a partner and say which shot you would cut first, and why

## Understand it

**Composition** is the arrangement of everything inside the frame. Two shots of the same place can feel calm or tense, open or trapped, simply because of where the camera points.

**The rule of thirds.** Imagine the frame divided by two lines across and two lines down, like a noughts-and-crosses board. Placing important things on those lines, or where they cross, usually looks more alive than putting them dead centre. Put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, not through the middle. Turn on the grid in your camera settings (it is called *Grid* on iPhone and most Android phones) so the lines show while you film.

The rule is a starting point, not a law. A centred frame can be powerful when you want symmetry or confrontation — a speaker at a lectern, a door at the end of a corridor. What matters is that the choice is yours, not an accident.

**Headroom** is the space between the top of a person's head and the top of the frame. Too much and they seem to sink; too little and they feel squashed. In a close-up the eyes usually sit near the top third line, and it is fine to cut off the top of the hair.

**Lead room** (also called *nose room* or *looking room*) is extra space in front of a person in the direction they are looking or moving. Someone walking left-to-right needs space on the right of frame to walk into. Take it away and they look as if they are about to hit the edge — which is useful if you *want* the viewer to feel trapped, but jarring by accident.

**Depth.** A phone screen is flat, so you create depth by layering:

- **Foreground** — something close to the lens (a plant, a market stall's edge, a shoulder) frames the subject.
- **Leading lines** — roads, gutters, fences and benches draw the eye towards the subject.
- **Background** — check it before you record. Watch for a pole "growing" out of someone's head, a bright window, or a stranger who did not agree to be in your film.

**Cropping people.** Avoid cutting a person exactly at a joint — at the knees, elbows or ankles — because it looks like an amputation. Frame just above or below.

## Key words

- **Rule of thirds:** placing key elements on imaginary lines dividing the frame into thirds
- **Headroom:** space above a person's head in the frame
- **Lead room:** space in front of a subject in the direction they face or move
- **Leading lines:** lines in the scene that guide the eye to the subject
- **Foreground:** objects nearest the camera, used to frame and add depth

## Read and watch

- [Rule of thirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_thirds) — Wikipedia
- [Lead room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_room) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** start with three shots only — thirds, headroom and lead room — and check each against the grid.
- **If you already can:** film a 20-second sequence where you break one rule on purpose for effect, and explain the effect.

## Learning online

At home, switch on the grid and film six still shots of five seconds each: rule of thirds, a centred symmetrical shot, correct headroom on a family member (with their permission), lead room on someone walking, a leading-lines shot, and a foreground-framed shot. Join them in CapCut or VN with a text label on each naming the rule. **Upload:** the 30-second labelled reel. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** one still from a film or advert you admire, with the grid drawn over it (any free drawing app works), ready to explain its composition in one minute.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Notice the headroom on the next news programme you see — is it the same for every presenter?

lessons.title: Lenses and focal length on a phone
lessons.summary: Choose between your phone's wide, main and telephoto lenses for what each one does to faces and space.
objectives: You will identify your phone's lenses and their focal-length equivalents
You will explain how distance and focal length change a face and a background
You will avoid digital zoom when it lowers quality
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Your phone probably has two or three cameras. Each one tells a different story about the same place.

## What to do

- Find out which lenses your phone has (0.5×, 1×, 2×, 3× or 5×) and note each one's equivalent focal length
- Film the same head-and-shoulders shot of a partner with each lens, moving your feet so the face stays the same size
- Film the same street or compound scene with each lens from one spot, and compare how much space each shows

## Understand it

**Focal length** describes how "zoomed in" a lens is. Film-makers describe it in millimetres, and phone makers usually give a **35 mm-equivalent** figure so lenses can be compared:

- **Ultra-wide (0.5×)** — about 13–16 mm. Shows a huge amount of the scene. Close to a face it bends features: the nose grows, the ears shrink, straight walls curve at the edges.
- **Main (1×)** — about 24–28 mm. The phone's best camera, with the largest sensor, so it is the sharpest and best in low light. A natural, slightly wide view.
- **Telephoto (2×–5×)** — about 48–120 mm, depending on the phone. Fills the frame from further away and flatters faces.

Above the highest real lens, the phone uses **digital zoom**: it simply crops and enlarges the picture, which throws away detail. If your phone has a 1× and a 3×, then 2× is a crop of the main camera and 10× is a heavy crop of the telephoto. *Walk closer* rather than pinch-zooming whenever you can.

**What really changes the look.** People say a telephoto "compresses" space and a wide lens "stretches" it. Strictly, it is the **camera's distance** that changes perspective; the lens only decides how much you see from there. But because you stand far back with a telephoto and close in with a wide lens, the results are real:

- With a **telephoto from far away**, the background looks large and close behind the person — useful for making a busy Lagos road look packed with cars, or isolating a face against a soft background.
- With a **wide lens close up**, the background looks far away and small, and the space feels big and energetic — good for a market or a dance, dangerous for portraits.

**Depth of field** is how much of the scene is sharp. Phones have tiny sensors, so nearly everything is sharp. You get the most natural background softness by using the telephoto, standing close enough for a tight shot, and keeping the background far behind the subject. "Cinematic" or "Portrait" video modes fake the blur with software; check the edges of hair and glasses, where it often fails.

**Switching lenses mid-shot** makes a visible jump in colour and sharpness, so choose the lens before you record.

## Key words

- **Focal length:** how much the lens magnifies, given in millimetres
- **35 mm equivalent:** a focal length translated so different cameras can be compared
- **Digital zoom:** cropping and enlarging the image, which loses detail
- **Perspective distortion:** stretched features caused by filming very close
- **Depth of field:** how much of the scene from near to far is in focus

## Read and watch

- [Focal length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focal_length) — Wikipedia
- [Depth of field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth_of_field) — Wikipedia
- [Pixar in a Box: virtual cameras](https://www.khanacademy.org/computing/pixar/virtual-cameras) — Khan Academy with Pixar

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** if your phone has only one lens, film the face shot from close up and then from three steps back (cropping the far one in the editor) — you will still see the perspective change.
- **If you already can:** film a "dolly zoom" attempt: walk backwards while zooming in so the face stays the same size, and describe what happens to the background.

## Learning online

Look up your phone model's camera specifications (the maker's website lists the lenses). With a family member's permission, film the same face from each lens at the same face size, and one wide scene from a fixed spot with each lens. Build two side-by-side comparisons in CapCut or VN and label each lens and its equivalent millimetres. **Upload:** both comparisons and a short note on which lens you would use for a serious interview and why. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your phone's lens list — we will build a class chart of what everyone's phones can do.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week we move the camera, so find something you can use to steady it: a small tripod, a stack of books or a bag of rice.
