lessons.title: Camera movement and stabilising
lessons.summary: Move the camera only when the movement means something, and keep it smooth when you do.
objectives: You will perform a pan, tilt, push-in and tracking shot on a phone
You will steady a phone using your body and simple home-made supports
You will decide when a movement is motivated and when to keep still
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** A moving camera is a storyteller. A shaking camera is a distraction.

## What to do

- Practise the four basic moves — pan, tilt, push-in and tracking — each three times, and keep your best take of each
- Build one home-made stabiliser and compare footage with and without it
- Film one 20-second sequence where every movement has a reason

## Understand it

**The basic moves** (named for what the camera does):

- **Pan** — the camera turns left or right from one spot, like shaking your head. Use it to reveal a place or follow someone walking past.
- **Tilt** — the camera turns up or down, like nodding. Tilting up a tall building or from shoes to face builds anticipation.
- **Push-in / pull-out** — the camera physically moves closer or further. A slow push-in towards a face draws the viewer into a thought or a feeling; a pull-out reveals where a person is, or leaves them alone.
- **Tracking** (following) — the camera moves alongside or behind a moving subject.

A **zoom** is not the same as a push-in: zooming changes the lens, not the camera's position, so the space does not change the way it does when you move. On a phone, zooming also often switches lens or crops the image. Move your body instead.

**Motivated movement.** Every move should have a reason: following action, revealing information, or showing a change in feeling. If you cannot say why the camera moves, keep it still. Static shots, held well, look confident. A good rule: begin each move on a still frame, end on a still frame, and hold both for two seconds so the editor has somewhere to cut.

**Steady habits.**

- **Two hands, elbows in**, phone close to your chest — your body becomes the tripod.
- **The ninja walk** — knees bent, heel-to-toe steps, upper body relaxed, so your legs absorb the bumps.
- **Turn from the waist** for a pan, not from the wrists, and start slowly.
- **Wide lenses hide shake** better than telephoto, so use 1× or 0.5× when walking.

**Phone stabilisation.** Most phones have **optical** stabilisation (the lens floats on tiny motors) and **electronic** stabilisation (the phone crops in and shifts the image). "Action" or "Super steady" modes crop more and can look smooth but slightly blurry in low light. Free editors (CapCut, DaVinci Resolve) can stabilise afterwards, again by cropping.

**Home-made supports:** a phone resting on a bag of rice or garri on a wall; a selfie stick held low and upside down as a counterweight; a phone taped to a skateboard, a chair with wheels or a wheelbarrow pushed slowly for a "dolly" shot; a string tied to the phone clamp and stepped on, then pulled tight upwards, which steadies it surprisingly well.

**Safety.** Never walk backwards while filming without a spotter guiding you, and never film from a moving vehicle or near traffic.

## Key words

- **Pan / tilt:** turning the camera horizontally / vertically from a fixed point
- **Push-in:** physically moving the camera closer to the subject
- **Tracking shot:** a shot where the camera moves with the subject
- **Motivated movement:** camera movement with a story reason
- **Stabilisation:** reducing shake, optically, electronically or in editing

## Read and watch

- [Tracking shot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_shot) — Wikipedia
- [Image stabilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_stabilization) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** master the pan and the push-in first; add tracking once those are smooth.
- **If you already can:** plan and film a single, unbroken 30-second "oner" that follows someone through two spaces with no cuts.

## Learning online

At home, film the four moves using a sibling or a household object as your subject (ask before filming people). Build a stabiliser from what you have — the string trick or a rice bag — and film the same walking shot with and without it. In CapCut or VN, place the two walking shots side by side. **Upload:** your four best moves labelled, and the stabiliser comparison, with a photo of your home-made rig. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your rig (or a photo of it) to demonstrate on camera, and one movement from a film that you think is motivated.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Watch the opening minute of any film and count the camera moves — could each one be explained?

lessons.title: Colour temperature and white balance
lessons.summary: Make white look white under sunshine, shade, bulbs and tubes, and keep colour consistent between shots.
objectives: You will explain colour temperature in kelvin
You will lock or set white balance on a phone
You will spot and fix mixed lighting in a scene
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Light has a colour. Your eyes hide it from you; the camera does not.

## What to do

- Film a white sheet of paper under four light sources — midday sun, shade, a warm bulb and a fluorescent tube or LED — on automatic, then with white balance set by you
- Film one person in a room with mixed light, then fix the scene by switching off or moving one source
- Match two shots of the same person filmed at different times so they cut together

## Understand it

Different light sources give off different colours. Film-makers measure this as **colour temperature**, in **kelvin (K)**:

- **About 2,700–3,200 K** — household filament or "warm white" bulbs, candles, kerosene lanterns: orange-yellow.
- **About 4,000 K** — many fluorescent tubes and "cool white" LEDs: often slightly green.
- **About 5,500 K** — midday sunshine: neutral.
- **6,500 K and above** — open shade and overcast sky: blue.

The scale feels backwards — lower numbers look *warmer* (more orange), higher numbers look *cooler* (more blue). Remember it by the flame of a gas cooker: the hottest part is blue.

**White balance** is the camera's correction that makes a white object look white under the current light. Your brain does this automatically, which is why a classroom under tubes looks normal to you but green on camera.

**The problem with automatic.** Automatic white balance (AWB) keeps re-guessing, so the colour of a shot can drift as someone in a bright red agbada walks into frame, or as clouds pass. Two shots of the same person can then look different colours and refuse to cut together. It also struggles with:

- **Mixed light** — a warm bulb inside and blue daylight through the window on the same face. One side of the face goes orange and the other blue, and no single setting fixes both.
- **Skin tones** — wrong white balance makes brown skin look grey, orange or green. Faces are what viewers judge colour by.

**Taking control.**

- In **Pro / Manual** mode (most Android phones) or apps such as Blackmagic Camera, set WB to a kelvin number or a preset (sun, cloud, bulb, fluorescent).
- On phones without manual WB, keep light consistent, and lock **AE/AF** with a neutral white or grey object in the frame before recording — some apps also offer a WB lock.
- **Fix mixed light at the source:** switch off the room light and use the window, or close the curtains and use the bulbs. Choose one colour of light for faces.
- **Use colour on purpose.** A slightly warm image feels cosy or nostalgic; a cool one feels lonely or clinical. Make that choice deliberately, not by accident.

Whatever you choose, **keep it the same for every shot in a scene**. Consistency matters more than perfection; small shifts can be matched in the edit, but mixed light on one face cannot.

## Key words

- **Colour temperature:** the colour of a light source, measured in kelvin
- **Kelvin (K):** the unit for colour temperature; lower is warmer (orange), higher is cooler (blue)
- **White balance:** the camera's correction so white looks white
- **Mixed lighting:** light of different colours falling on the same subject
- **Colour cast:** an unwanted tint over the whole image

## Read and watch

- [Color temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_temperature) — Wikipedia
- [Color balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_balance) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do only the white-paper test, and say which light gave which colour.
- **If you already can:** shoot a short scene twice — once warm (about 3,200 K look) and once cool (about 6,500 K look) — and describe how the mood changes.

## Learning online

The white-paper test needs only your phone, a sheet of paper and the lights in your home. Film five seconds under each light on automatic, then again with WB set manually (or with a free app such as Open Camera, which lets you choose presets). Put the pairs on a CapCut or VN timeline with labels. **Upload:** the labelled clip and a screenshot of one mixed-light problem you found at home and how you fixed it. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your best guess of the colour temperature of three lights in your home — we will compare answers.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week we light with what you have, so find a sheet of white card, foil or a white bedsheet.

lessons.title: Lighting with what you have
lessons.summary: Light a face beautifully with a window, a reflector and a torch — no studio needed.
objectives: You will place a subject for soft window light
You will build and use a home-made reflector for fill
You will describe key, fill and back light and what each does
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Professional lighting is mostly about where you put people. You already own the most beautiful light there is: a window.

## What to do

- Light the same person three ways using a window: facing it, side-on to it, and with their back to it
- Make a reflector and use it to fill the shadow side of the face
- Add a back light with a torch or phone light, and film a 10-second portrait with all three

## Understand it

**Hard and soft light.** A small, bright source — the bare midday sun, a phone torch, a naked bulb — makes **hard light**: sharp-edged shadows, shiny skin, squinting eyes. A large source close to the subject makes **soft light**: gentle shadows that roll off the face. Size relative to the subject is what matters. A window with sun bouncing in from outside, or a white bedsheet with light shining through it, is a large source, and it flatters every face.

**Three-point lighting** is the classic way to light a person:

1. **Key light** — the main light, usually to one side at about 45°. A window is a perfect key.
2. **Fill light** — softens the shadow side so it is not black. A **reflector** bounces some of the key back into the shadows.
3. **Back light** (rim light) — from behind and above, it puts a thin bright edge on hair and shoulders and separates the person from the background.

You do not always need all three. Facing a window gives flat, even light — good for a clear explainer. Side-on to a window gives shape and mood. The **ratio** between the bright and shadow sides of a face is a creative choice: a strong difference feels dramatic, a gentle one feels open and friendly.

**Reflectors from home:** white card or a manila folder, a white bedsheet over a chair, aluminium foil smoothed over cardboard (strong, cool bounce — use the dull side for softer), a car windscreen sunshade. Hold it on the shadow side, just out of shot, and tilt it until you see the shadows lift.

**When NEPA takes the light.** A rechargeable lamp or a phone torch is hard light. Make it soft: bounce it off a white wall or ceiling, or shine it through a white cloth or tracing paper held a safe distance from the lamp. Never cover any lamp that gets hot, and keep cloth away from candles, lanterns and generators.

**Light the eyes.** A small reflection of the light in the eyes — the **catchlight** — makes a person look alive. Without it, eyes look dull in close-ups.

**Avoid:** overhead tubes straight down (deep eye shadows, often green), a bright window behind the subject, and direct midday sun on faces. Early morning and late afternoon — the **golden hour** — give soft, warm light outdoors.

**Deeper skin tones** reward soft light and a little extra exposure on the face; a reflector adds a warm, even glow and brings out detail.

## Key words

- **Hard / soft light:** light from a small source (sharp shadows) or a large one (gentle shadows)
- **Key light:** the main light on the subject
- **Fill light:** light that softens the shadow side
- **Back light:** light from behind that separates the subject from the background
- **Catchlight:** the reflection of a light source in the eyes

## Read and watch

- [Three-point lighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-point_lighting) — Wikipedia
- [Golden hour (photography)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_hour_%28photography%29) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do only the three window positions and the reflector, and describe the change in shadows.
- **If you already can:** light a moody night scene with one bounced torch and a reflector, and keep the face readable.

## Learning online

Everything this week is at home. Ask a family member to sit for you (or use a doll or a ball as a stand-in face). Film the three window positions, then add your reflector and a torch back light. Take a photo of your setup from above, or draw a quick plan. Put the clips together in CapCut or VN. **Upload:** the three window clips, the reflector before-and-after and your final portrait, with the setup photo or plan. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your reflector — we will test everyone's live on camera and compare foil against white card.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week is about filming a conversation, so think of two people who could act out a short scene for you.

lessons.title: Coverage and continuity
lessons.summary: Film a conversation so it can be edited smoothly: the 180-degree rule, eyelines and matching action.
objectives: You will plan coverage for a two-person scene
You will keep to the 180-degree rule and correct eyelines
You will film an action from two angles so it can be cut on the move
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** A scene is not filmed in one shot. It is filmed in pieces that must fit back together.

## What to do

- Plan coverage for a 30-second two-person scene: a wide, two over-the-shoulders and two close-ups
- Film it keeping to the 180-degree rule, then film one shot that deliberately breaks it and compare
- Film one action (opening a door, handing over a phone) from two angles, repeating it the same way each time

## Understand it

**Coverage** is the set of shots you film of one scene so the editor has choices. A standard pattern for a conversation:

1. A **master shot** (wide) of the whole scene from start to finish — the safety net.
2. **Over-the-shoulder** shots of each person, from behind the other's shoulder.
3. **Close-ups** of each person for the important lines and reactions.
4. **Inserts** — details such as hands, a text message, a cup.

The editor then cuts between them as **shot-reverse-shot**. Reactions often matter more than the person speaking, so film the listener too.

**The 180-degree rule.** Draw an imaginary line through the two people talking. Keep the camera on **one side** of that line for every shot. Then person A always looks right-to-left and person B always looks left-to-right, and the viewer keeps their bearings. Cross the line and suddenly both people seem to face the same way, as if they had swapped places — the audience feels lost without knowing why. You may cross the line only by showing the move (the camera travels across it on screen) or by cutting to a neutral shot straight down the line.

**Eyelines.** In close-ups, each person should look slightly off the lens towards where the other person is — just beside the camera on the correct side. Keep the height consistent: if a child is talking to a standing adult, the child looks up and the adult looks down in every shot. Wrong eyelines make two people seem to be talking to someone else.

**Continuity** means details match from shot to shot: the cup is in the same hand, the bottle is at the same level, the scarf is on the same shoulder, the light comes from the same side. On a real production a **continuity** person notes these. On yours, take a reference photo on your phone before each new set-up.

**Match on action.** If a person reaches for a door in the wide shot, ask them to do exactly the same movement in the close-up. The editor can cut *during* the movement, and the viewer's eye follows the action straight across the cut. Overlap the action: start each take before the move and finish after it.

**Consent and comfort.** Your actors are friends giving their time — agree what will be filmed and where it will be shown, get a parent or guardian's written consent for anyone under 18, and stop when someone asks.

## Key words

- **Coverage:** all the shots filmed of one scene so it can be edited
- **Master shot:** a wide shot of the whole scene from start to finish
- **180-degree rule:** keep the camera on one side of the line between the characters
- **Eyeline:** the direction a person on screen is looking
- **Match on action:** cutting between two angles in the middle of the same movement

## Read and watch

- [180-degree rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/180-degree_rule) — Wikipedia
- [Continuity editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuity_editing) — Wikipedia
- [Shot reverse shot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shot_reverse_shot) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** film only the master and the two over-the-shoulders; add close-ups when those cut together cleanly.
- **If you already can:** add a third character to the scene and plan where the lines are as people move.

## Learning online

From home, write a six-line conversation (for example, borrowing a phone charger). Two family members can act it, with their agreement. Draw the 180-degree line on a top-down plan with your camera positions. Film the coverage, then cut it in CapCut or VN, including one match on action. **Upload:** the plan photo, the edited scene, and the deliberate line-cross shot with one sentence on how it felt. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your top-down plan — we will check each other's lines on screen.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week we look at AI tools critically; note any AI video or image you saw this week that fooled you, even briefly.

lessons.title: AI tools for film-makers, used critically
lessons.summary: Test what AI can and cannot do for a cinematographer, and use it honestly, safely and with consent.
objectives: You will test an AI tool on a real cinematography task and judge the result
You will spot common faults in AI-generated or AI-altered footage
You will apply clear rules on labelling, consent and real people's likenesses
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** AI can now plan shots, steady footage, relight faces and even generate video. A cinematographer's job is to know when it helps, when it lies, and when it must not be used.

## What to do

- Ask an AI assistant for a shot list for a scene you have already filmed, and compare it with what you actually did
- Run one of your own shaky or dark clips through an AI-assisted tool (stabilise, denoise or enhance) and compare before and after frame by frame
- Study two AI-generated videos and list every fault you can find

## Understand it

**Where AI is genuinely useful.**

- **Planning.** A chat assistant can suggest shot lists, coverage and lighting ideas, or turn a script into a first storyboard. It is a fast brainstorming partner, but it has never stood in your compound at 4 p.m. — check every suggestion against the real location, light and people.
- **Fixing footage.** Tools in DaVinci Resolve, CapCut and phone galleries use machine learning to stabilise, reduce noise, sharpen, track objects and cut out backgrounds. They save hours. They also invent detail: an "enhanced" face may gain smoother skin, different teeth or a lighter complexion than the real person. **Always compare with the original at full size.**
- **Generating shots.** Text-to-video tools can create footage from a description. Useful for a mood test or a storyboard animatic; risky in anything that claims to show real events.

**How to spot AI-made or AI-altered footage.** Look for hands and fingers that merge or change count; text and signboards that turn to nonsense; objects that melt, appear or vanish between frames; light and shadows that disagree; skin that looks waxy; people whose faces drift when they turn; physics that is "almost" right (water, cloth, a ball). Many faults only show when you step through frame by frame.

**Bias.** AI models learn from huge image collections that under-represent African faces, skin tones, places and clothing. Generated "Nigerian market" scenes can look like a stereotype; enhancement tools can lighten or smooth dark skin. As the person behind the camera, you are responsible for representing people truthfully.

**The rules this programme expects you to follow.**

1. **Label it.** If footage or a voice is AI-generated or substantially altered, say so on screen or in the description. Many platforms now require it.
2. **No real people without consent.** Never generate, swap or clone the face or voice of a real person — a classmate, a teacher, a celebrity, a politician — without their clear permission, and never of anyone under 18. A **deepfake** used to embarrass someone is bullying, and in Nigeria can break the law.
3. **Never present generated footage as a real event.** Not in a documentary, not in news, not "for a joke" that may be shared on.
4. **Protect data.** Do not upload footage of other people, especially children, to an online AI service without their permission; read where the footage goes.
5. **Your eye decides.** You choose the frame, the light and the moment. AI is a tool in your hand, not the author.

## Key words

- **Generative AI:** software that creates new images, video, audio or text from a prompt
- **Deepfake:** AI-made video or audio that makes a real person appear to say or do something they did not
- **Artefact:** a visible fault or glitch introduced by processing
- **Upscaling / enhancement:** AI that invents extra detail to make footage look sharper
- **Disclosure label:** a clear note that content is AI-generated or altered

## Read and watch

- [Deepfake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake) — Wikipedia
- [Content Credentials](https://contentcredentials.org/) — Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
- [DaVinci Resolve training](https://www.blackmagicdesign.com/products/davinciresolve/training) — Blackmagic Design

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do only the shot-list comparison and the fault-spotting, using videos your instructor shares.
- **If you already can:** write a one-page "AI policy" for a small film crew, covering when AI may be used and how it must be labelled.

## Learning online

From home, use any free AI chat assistant to generate a shot list for your Week 7 scene, and paste it next to your real plan. In CapCut (Stabilise, Enhance or Reduce noise) or the free DaVinci Resolve, process one of your own clips — never someone else's face without permission — and screenshot the same frame before and after at full zoom. **Upload:** the side-by-side shot lists with three things AI got wrong or missed, and your before/after frames with any invented detail circled. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** one AI-generated video you found online (share the link, do not download it) and the faults you spotted.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week you film a scene from a script for a community brief — think about a short message your centre or street needs to hear.

lessons.title: Shooting a scene from a script for a community brief
lessons.summary: Break a short script into shots and film it to a real brief from your centre or community.
objectives: You will break down a script into a shot list and schedule
You will run a set using a slate and a take log
You will film a complete scene that answers a community brief
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** This week you work like a real crew: a client, a brief, a script and a deadline.

## What to do

- Agree a brief with your centre or a community group: a 45–60 second scene with one clear message (for example, washing hands before eating, keeping gutters clear, safe crossing at the junction)
- Write or receive a one-page script and break it down into a shot list
- Film the scene with a slate and a take log, using everything you have learnt this term

## Understand it

**The brief** is the client's request: who the audience is, what they should think or do after watching, where it will be shown (a WhatsApp group, a screen at the centre, Instagram), how long it can be, and the deadline. Write it in five lines and get the client to agree before you write anything else. If the client is a community group, find out the languages your audience speaks; a scene in Pidgin, Yoruba, Hausa or Igbo with English subtitles may reach far more people.

**The script** uses a simple format: a **scene heading** (`EXT. COMPOUND – DAY`), short action lines in the present tense, and dialogue under each character's name. One page is roughly one minute on screen.

**The breakdown.** Read the script and mark everything you need: characters, locations, props, costume, sounds. Then write the **shot list**: number every shot, and for each give the size, angle, lens, movement and which lines it covers. Group shots by **set-up**, not by story order: film every shot from one camera position before moving, because moving lights and camera takes the most time. A wide master first, then closer coverage, as you practised in Week 7.

**On set.**

- **Slate every take.** Before each take, hold up a card (or a phone showing text) with scene, shot and take number — "Scene 1, shot 3, take 2" — and clap your hands in shot. The clap gives a sync mark if you record sound separately, and the card makes the footage easy to find.
- **Keep a take log:** shot, take, good or not, and why ("take 3 — good, but car horn at end").
- **"Roll, action, cut."** The camera starts recording and runs for two seconds *before* "action", and after "cut", to leave handles.
- **Check the playback** of the take you think is good before you move on — focus, exposure, sound and the background.
- **Use your term's skills:** locked exposure and white balance, composition with lead room, the right lens, motivated movement, soft light and the 180-degree rule.

**Location and people.** Ask permission to film at the location. Every person who appears needs to agree; for anyone under 18, a parent or guardian signs a release. Keep strangers' faces and car number plates out of shot unless they have agreed. Never film in a road or near traffic for a road-safety message — stage it safely at the roadside.

## Key words

- **Brief:** the client's description of what the video must do, for whom and by when
- **Script breakdown:** listing everything a script needs: people, places, props, sound
- **Set-up:** one camera and lighting position, from which several shots may be filmed
- **Slate:** the card and clap that identify a take and give a sync point
- **Take log:** a record of each take and whether it is usable

## Read and watch

- [Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenplay) — Wikipedia
- [Clapperboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapperboard) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use a script your instructor gives you and film it in three set-ups.
- **If you already can:** add a second location and plan the schedule so the crew finishes in two hours.

## Learning online

If you are learning from home, your "client" can be your family, your place of worship or a neighbourhood group — agree the brief with a real person and write it down. Write a one-page script in any free notes app, then the shot list. Use family members as actors with their consent (a parent or guardian signs for anyone under 18). Slate with a phone screen and a clap; keep your take log on paper. **Upload:** the brief, script, shot list, take log (photo) and your rough assembly of the scene from CapCut or VN. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your shot list, to explain how you grouped the set-ups.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Show your rough scene to the client and write down their reaction in one sentence — you will refine it into your capstone.

lessons.title: Capstone and showcase: your cinematography reel
lessons.summary: Finish your community scene, build a short reel of your best shots, and present your choices at the showcase.
objectives: You will refine your community scene using the client's feedback
You will build a 60-second reel of your best work this term
You will explain your cinematography choices to an audience
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** A cinematographer is hired on the strength of a reel and the ability to explain it. This is yours.

## What to do

- Make the changes your client asked for and finish your community scene, with subtitles
- Build a 60-second reel of your best shots from the whole term
- Present one shot at the showcase: what you wanted, what you did, what you would change

## Understand it

**Responding to feedback.** Read your client's notes and sort them into three piles: **must fix** (wrong information, someone who did not consent, an unclear message), **should fix** (a dark shot, a confusing cut) and **taste** (they prefer a different song). Fix all the first pile, most of the second, and discuss the third. If a note means a reshoot, decide whether you have time — sometimes a better edit or a different take solves it.

**What makes a strong reel.**

- **Short.** Sixty seconds of your best work beats three minutes of everything. Viewers decide in the first ten seconds, so open with your strongest image.
- **Range.** Show different skills: a well-exposed interior, a soft-lit close-up, a motivated movement, a strong composition, a clean match on action.
- **Shots, not stories.** Each clip lasts two to four seconds. Cut on movement and to the rhythm of the music.
- **Quality control.** Cut any shot that is soft, shaky or badly exposed, however much you like the moment. One weak shot lowers how people judge all the others.
- **Honesty.** Only include shots you filmed. If another member filmed a shot or AI altered it, leave it out or credit it.
- **Music you may use**, from a free library, credited.
- **A title card** at the end with your name (first name only if you prefer) and what you did — "Camera and lighting".

**Presenting your work.** At the showcase, choose one shot and talk for one minute:

1. **Intention** — what the shot needed to make the audience feel or understand.
2. **Choices** — lens, framing, light, movement, exposure, and why.
3. **Problems** — what went wrong and how you solved it on the day.
4. **Next time** — one thing you would do differently.

Speak about the image, not the equipment. Audiences remember "I put her by the window so her face had soft light and the background fell dark" far longer than a list of settings.

**Giving feedback to others.** Use "I noticed… / I felt… / I wondered…" and be specific about frames, not people.

**Safety and consent at a showcase.** Check that everyone in your reel agreed to be shown publicly. If a family has said the video may be shown only at the centre, do not post it online.

## Key words

- **Reel:** a short compilation of a film-maker's best shots, used to show their skill
- **Client feedback:** notes from the person who commissioned the work
- **Reshoot:** filming a shot again to fix a problem
- **Intention:** what a shot was meant to achieve
- **Credit:** naming the people and sources who contributed

## Read and watch

- [Cinematography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematography) — Wikipedia
- [Video accessibility: captions](https://www.w3.org/WAI/media/av/captions/) — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** make a 30-second reel of six shots, and present with a partner asking you the four questions.
- **If you already can:** make two versions of your reel — 16:9 for YouTube and 9:16 for Reels — and explain how you reframed each shot.

## Learning online

Finish your scene and reel at home in CapCut, VN or DaVinci Resolve, and add subtitles (check every auto-caption against what was said). Export at 1080p. **Upload:** the final community scene, your 60-second reel, and a one-paragraph note on the client's feedback and what you changed. **Bring to Saturday's online class (showcase):** be ready to share your screen and play one shot, then talk for one minute using the four questions. If your connection is weak, upload the clip in advance so the instructor can play it for you.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Write down one cinematography skill you want to master next term, and one film-maker whose images you want to study.

whys: A weak shot lowers how viewers judge every other shot.

lessons.title: Pre-production: brief, schedule, call sheet and consent
lessons.summary: Plan a shoot on paper so the day runs on time and everyone on camera has agreed to be there.
objectives: You will turn a request into a clear production brief
You will write a shoot schedule and a call sheet
You will prepare and use consent and release forms correctly
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Most problems on a shoot day were made the week before. This week you make the paperwork that prevents them.

## What to do

- Turn a real request into a one-page brief and get it agreed
- Write a schedule and a call sheet for a two-hour shoot
- Prepare a consent and release form, and practise explaining it to a parent and to a young person

## Understand it

**Pre-production** is everything that happens before the camera rolls. In professional video it usually takes longer than the filming itself.

**1. The brief.** One page agreed with whoever asked for the video:

- **Purpose** — what should the audience think, feel or do afterwards?
- **Audience** — who exactly? ("Parents in our area who have not heard of the Club", not "everyone".)
- **Platform and format** — WhatsApp, YouTube, a screen at an event; vertical or horizontal; length.
- **Key message** in one sentence.
- **Deadline, budget and sign-off** — who approves the final version?

**2. The plan.** A treatment or storyboard, the shot list, and a list of what you need: people, locations, props, equipment, charged batteries, empty storage, a power bank.

**3. The schedule.** Work backwards from the deadline: when you film, when the rough cut is due, when the client reviews it, when it is delivered. On the shoot day itself, plan in blocks: set-up, each scene, breaks, pack-down. Allow at least a quarter of the time for things going wrong — rain, a late arrival, no light, a generator next door. Film outdoor scenes when the light is right, and the most important shot early, while everyone is fresh.

**4. The call sheet** is the one page everybody receives the day before. It lists the date, the **call time** (when to arrive), the address and a map pin, the schedule, who is in each scene, what to wear or bring, the weather, the nearest clinic, and a contact phone number for the person in charge. If a parent is dropping a child off, they need it too.

**5. Consent and release forms.** Before you film anyone, they must understand what the video is, where it will be shown, for how long, and that they can say no. A **release form** records their agreement in writing:

- The person's name, and for anyone **under 18, a parent or guardian's name and signature** as well as the young person's own agreement.
- What will be filmed and where it will be used (the centre's social media, a competition, a screen at an event).
- Whether their full name may appear on screen.
- A date, and how to withdraw consent.

Nigeria's **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** treats a person's image and voice as personal data, so you must have a reason to hold the footage, keep it safely, and use it only as agreed. Store forms and footage in one safe place, not on a shared phone. Location owners need to agree too: a shop, a school, a market association or a church.

**Explaining consent well** means plain language, no pressure and a real choice. "If you'd rather not be on camera, that's completely fine — you can help behind the camera instead."

## Key words

- **Pre-production:** planning done before filming
- **Brief:** the agreed description of what the video must do
- **Call sheet:** the one-page plan of a shoot day sent to everyone involved
- **Call time:** the time a person must arrive on set
- **Release form:** a signed agreement allowing someone's image and voice to be used

## Read and watch

- [Call sheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sheet) — Wikipedia
- [Model release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_release) — Wikipedia
- [Pre-production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-production) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** fill in a template brief and call sheet from your instructor for a shoot at the centre.
- **If you already can:** add a risk assessment (hazards, who could be harmed, what you will do) and a wet-weather back-up plan.

## Learning online

From home, find a real request — a relative's small business, your place of worship, a school club — and write the brief in Google Docs or any notes app, then message it to them for approval. Write the schedule and call sheet for a two-hour shoot at your home or nearby. Draft a release form in plain English (and in the language your contributors speak, if different). **Upload:** the agreed brief (with the client's reply as a screenshot), the call sheet and the release form. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** be ready to role-play explaining your release form to a parent in under one minute.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week is audio: find the quietest room in your home and note what you can hear when you stand in it for one minute in silence.

lessons.title: Recording audio done right
lessons.summary: Capture clear, clean speech at the right level, and record the room tone and sounds the editor will need.
objectives: You will choose and place a microphone for clear speech
You will set recording levels that avoid distortion and noise
You will record room tone and wild sound for the edit
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Viewers will watch a soft picture, but they will skip a video they cannot hear. This week the picture is switched off and you only listen.

## What to do

- Record the same sentence five ways: phone at arm's length, phone close, clip-on mic, in a tiled room, in a room with cushions and curtains
- Set levels on a recording app and record a voice that peaks in the right range
- Record 30 seconds of room tone and three wild sounds for a scene

## Understand it

**Distance is everything.** Sound gets weaker very quickly with distance — double the distance from the mouth to the microphone and the voice drops by about a quarter in loudness, while the room's echo and noise stay the same. So the most important thing is: **get the microphone close**. A cheap clip-on (lavalier) microphone 15–20 cm below the chin beats an expensive camera at three metres.

**Types of microphone.**

- **Built-in phone mic** — fine within about 30 cm of the mouth in a quiet room.
- **Lavalier (lav)** — clips to clothing near the chest; wired ones plug into the phone, wireless ones use a small transmitter. Hide the cable under clothing, and stop it rubbing against fabric, jewellery or beads — rustle ruins takes.
- **Shotgun** — long, directional, mounted on the phone or a pole (a boom), pointed at the mouth from just out of shot.

**The room.** Hard surfaces — tiles, bare walls, glass — bounce sound and make an echo. Soft things absorb it: curtains, cushions, mattresses, a wardrobe full of clothes. Record in the softest room, and away from fans, fridges, generators, air conditioners, traffic and the mosque or church loudspeaker. Switch off the ceiling fan for each take, then switch it back on for the speaker's comfort. Outdoors, cover the microphone with a **windshield** (a foam cover or a "dead cat") — a piece of sock works in a hurry.

**Levels.** A recording app such as a voice recorder, Blackmagic Camera or the audio in your camera app shows a **meter** in decibels (dBFS). 0 dB is the ceiling: anything above it is **clipped**, and clipping sounds like crackling distortion that cannot be repaired. Aim for normal speech peaking around **−12 dB**, with loud moments no higher than about −6 dB. Too low, and when you turn it up in the edit you turn up the hiss as well. Do a test: record, then **listen back on headphones** before every interview.

**Record more than the words.**

- **Room tone** — 30 seconds of the room in silence, with everyone still. Editors use it to fill gaps and smooth cuts.
- **Wild sound** — sounds of the place recorded on their own: a gate, footsteps, the market, birds. They make a scene feel real.
- Ask your speaker to repeat a line if a motorbike or a horn went past.

**AI clean-up, critically.** Tools such as CapCut's "Reduce noise" or DaVinci Resolve's Voice Isolation can remove background hum surprisingly well. Pushed too far, they make voices sound robotic, underwater or cut off at the end of words. Treat them as a rescue, not a plan — always compare with the original, and keep the original file.

**Safety and consent.** Clipping a microphone to someone means approaching their body: ask first, explain where it goes, and let them clip it themselves where possible. A recording is personal data too — store it as safely as the video.

## Key words

- **Lavalier (lav):** a small clip-on microphone worn on clothing
- **Clipping (audio):** distortion when the level goes above 0 dB
- **Levels:** how loud the signal is recorded, shown on a meter
- **Room tone:** a recording of a room's natural silence
- **Wild sound:** sounds recorded separately from the picture

## Read and watch

- [Lavalier microphone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavalier_microphone) — Wikipedia
- [Room tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Room_tone) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do the five-way test with only the phone's mic and compare close against far.
- **If you already can:** record a two-person interview with two separate phones as recorders, sync them to the picture using a clap, and mix the result.

## Learning online

All of this works at home with your phone and a pair of earphones. Use the phone's voice recorder or a free app that shows a level meter. Record your five-way test (say the same sentence each time), a level test, 30 seconds of room tone and three wild sounds. Put them on a VN or CapCut timeline with a title before each. **Upload:** the labelled audio reel (it can be over a black screen), a screenshot of your meter peaking near −12 dB, and one sentence on which room won. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your earphones — we will listen together, and you will join with your best microphone setup so we can hear the difference live.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week is colour, so film a few shots indoors and outdoors of the same object and keep them.

lessons.title: Colour correction
lessons.summary: Fix brightness, white balance and skin tones so every shot in your video looks like it belongs together.
objectives: You will correct exposure and white balance in an editor
You will read a waveform scope to check brightness
You will match two shots so they cut together
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Correction makes footage look *right*. Grading makes it look *beautiful*. This week is about right.

## What to do

- Correct three badly balanced clips: one too dark, one too blue, one too orange
- Use a scope (in DaVinci Resolve) or the histogram (in CapCut or VN) to check each correction
- Match two shots of the same person filmed at different times so the cut is invisible

## Understand it

**Correction before grading.** Colour work happens in two stages. **Colour correction** fixes problems: exposure, white balance, contrast, and differences between shots. **Colour grading** then gives the film a look — warmer, cooler, faded, punchy. Always correct first; a stylish grade on uncorrected footage just exaggerates the mistakes.

**Work in this order:**

1. **Exposure** — set the brightest and darkest parts of the image. Blacks should be dark but not crushed into a solid block; highlights bright but not clipped.
2. **White balance** — remove colour casts. Many editors have a **temperature** slider (blue ↔ orange) and a **tint** slider (green ↔ magenta). Some have an eyedropper: click something that should be white or grey, and the editor balances to it.
3. **Contrast and saturation** — small adjustments only. Over-saturated skin looks orange or red.
4. **Match shots** — compare each shot with the one before and after it.

**Trust the scopes, not your screen.** Phone screens have different brightness and colour, and your eyes adapt to a cast within seconds. Scopes measure the picture:

- **Waveform** (DaVinci Resolve, free) — shows brightness from 0 at the bottom to 100 (or 1023) at the top, across the width of the frame. If the trace hits the top, highlights are clipped; if it piles up at the bottom, shadows are crushed.
- **Histogram** (CapCut, VN, phone photo apps) — a graph of how many pixels are at each brightness. A heap jammed against either edge means lost detail.
- **Vectorscope** — shows colour. Skin tones of every complexion fall along roughly the same line, called the **skin tone line**, between red and yellow. If a face sits well off that line, the white balance is probably wrong.

**Skin tones first.** Viewers judge colour by faces. Brown and dark skin is rich in colour and detail; wrong white balance can make it look grey, ashy, orange or green, and over-exposure flattens it. Check faces on the vectorscope, and compare to how the person really looks in daylight. Never "lighten" someone's skin as a correction — that is misrepresenting a real person.

**Matching.** Put two shots side by side (Resolve has a split-screen and "Shot Match"; in CapCut, copy and paste adjustments then tweak). Match brightness first, then the colour of a white or grey object, then the skin.

**Look-up tables (LUTs)** are preset colour transformations. A LUT made for a different camera can wreck your footage; use them after correction, gently, and check skin tones.

## Key words

- **Colour correction:** fixing exposure, white balance and consistency
- **Colour grading:** giving footage a creative look after correction
- **Waveform:** a scope showing brightness across the frame
- **Vectorscope:** a scope showing the hue and saturation of the colours
- **LUT:** a look-up table, a preset that transforms colours

## Read and watch

- [Color grading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_grading) — Wikipedia
- [Waveform monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waveform_monitor) — Wikipedia
- [DaVinci Resolve training](https://www.blackmagicdesign.com/products/davinciresolve/training) — Blackmagic Design

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** correct in CapCut or VN with the exposure and temperature sliders only, using the histogram.
- **If you already can:** after correcting, build two different grades for the same scene and explain the mood of each.

## Learning online

On a phone, use CapCut or VN's Adjust tools (brightness, contrast, temperature, tint, saturation) and turn on the histogram if your app shows one. On a laptop, the free DaVinci Resolve gives you real scopes on the Colour page. Use three of your own badly balanced clips — or film some on purpose under a bulb and in shade. **Upload:** before-and-after screenshots for all three, a screenshot of a scope or histogram for one, and the two matched shots cut together. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** one clip you could not fix, so we can work on it together on screen.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week is pacing: watch a short documentary or advert and count roughly how long each shot lasts.

lessons.title: Pacing and rhythm of the cut
lessons.summary: Control how fast your video feels by choosing when each shot starts and ends, and when to let a moment breathe.
objectives: You will tighten a rough cut by removing what the story does not need
You will vary shot length to build and release tension
You will cut to music and to speech with a deliberate rhythm
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Two editors with the same footage make two different films. The difference is mostly timing.

## What to do

- Take a two-minute rough cut and make it 25% shorter without losing the story
- Cut the same 30 seconds of footage twice: once to a fast track and once to a slow one
- Find one moment in your piece that needs to breathe, and give it space

## Understand it

**Pacing** is how fast a video feels overall. **Rhythm** is the pattern of shot lengths and cuts inside it. Neither is about speed alone: a fast video with no variation feels exhausting, and a slow one with no shape feels long.

**Tightening.** Rough cuts are almost always too long. Go through and ask of every shot and every line: *does the viewer need this to follow the story or feel the moment?*

- **Enter late, leave early.** Start each shot just before the important action and leave as soon as it is done. You do not need to see someone walk all the way to the door.
- **Trim the "air"** in interviews — the "erm", the long breath, the repeated start of a sentence — and cover the edit with B-roll.
- **Cut the second example** when two moments make the same point. Keep the stronger one.
- **Kill your darlings** — the beautiful shot that does not serve the story still goes.

A useful target: a second pass usually removes 10–25% of a rough cut, and the film gets better.

**Shot length is a tool.**

- **Short shots** (one to two seconds) build energy, excitement or tension — a football match, a market morning, a deadline.
- **Long shots** (five seconds and more) give weight, calm or emotion — someone thinking, a reveal, a sad moment. Holding on a face after an important line lets the audience feel it.
- **Change the pattern** to mark a turning point. A run of quick shots followed by one long, still shot lands with force.

**The viewer's eye.** After a cut, viewers need a moment to find what matters in the new frame. A complex wide shot needs longer than a simple close-up. If you place the important thing where the eye already was at the end of the last shot, the cut feels smooth.

**Cutting to music.** Find the **beat** (tap along) and place cuts on strong beats, but not every beat — that becomes mechanical. Cut on the first beat of a bar or phrase, and change the rhythm when the music changes. In CapCut, the **Beats** feature marks them for you; check that it found the right ones. Let the music's ending and your picture's ending land together: edit the music so it finishes on purpose rather than fading randomly.

**Cutting to speech.** Cut at the end of a thought, not mid-word. A short pause before a key line, or a reaction shot after it, gives it weight.

**Test it fresh.** Leave your edit for a few hours, then watch it in one go without stopping. Note the moments where your attention dipped — that is where to cut. Better still, watch someone else watching it.

## Key words

- **Pacing:** how fast a whole video feels
- **Rhythm:** the pattern of shot lengths and cuts
- **Rough cut / fine cut:** the first full assembly / the tightened, polished version
- **Enter late, leave early:** starting and ending shots as close to the key action as possible
- **Beat:** the regular pulse of a piece of music

## Read and watch

- [Film editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_editing) — Wikipedia
- [Montage (filmmaking)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montage_%28filmmaking%29) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** shorten a one-minute clip to 45 seconds and list three things you removed.
- **If you already can:** recut the same footage for a 15-second vertical teaser and a 90-second horizontal version, and explain the pacing of each.

## Learning online

Use any rough cut you have made this year (or the footage from your Cinematography lessons). In CapCut or VN, **duplicate the project** first so you keep the original. Make the 25% cut, then the fast-music and slow-music versions of the same 30 seconds, using free music from your editor's library or the YouTube Audio Library. **Upload:** the before and after lengths, the shortened cut, both music versions, and a list of what you removed and why. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your two music versions — classmates will guess the mood of each before you say which is which.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week is titles, thumbnails and export: collect three thumbnails that made you click on a video.

lessons.title: Titles, graphics, thumbnails and exporting for platforms
lessons.summary: Make text people can read, a thumbnail people click, and an export that looks right on every platform.
objectives: You will design readable titles and lower thirds within safe areas
You will make an honest, eye-catching thumbnail
You will choose export settings for WhatsApp, Instagram and YouTube
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** A video is judged before it plays — by its thumbnail — and after it plays, by whether it looked and sounded right on the viewer's phone.

## What to do

- Design an opening title, a lower third and an end card for your piece
- Make a thumbnail and test it at the size of a phone search result
- Export your piece for two platforms and check both on a real phone

## Understand it

**Titles and lower thirds.**

- A **lower third** shows a speaker's name and role in the lower part of the frame the first time they appear: "Amaka Obi — Tailor, Ikeja". Spell names exactly as the person spells them — ask.
- **Readable means contrast and size.** Light text on a busy background disappears. Add a soft shadow, an outline or a semi-transparent bar behind it. Aim for contrast at least 4.5:1, as you would on a web page.
- **Keep it on screen long enough** to read twice — a rough rule is one second per three words, and never under two seconds.
- **One or two fonts**, used consistently. A clean sans-serif reads best on small screens.
- **Safe areas.** Keep text away from the edges. On vertical platforms (Reels, TikTok, Status), the app covers the bottom with captions and buttons and the right side with icons — keep text in the middle area. CapCut and Resolve can show safe-area guides.

**Thumbnails.** On a phone, a thumbnail is shown about the size of a postage stamp. What works:

- **One clear subject**, often a face with a visible expression, large in the frame.
- **Three to five words at most**, big and high-contrast — or none.
- **Honest.** It must show what the video really delivers. A misleading "clickbait" thumbnail earns a click and loses the viewer's trust, and platforms push such videos down.
- Make it at **1280 × 720 pixels** (16:9) for YouTube. Use a real frame from your footage or a photo you took. Do not use an image of a person who has not consented, or a logo you do not own.

**Exporting.** The **export** (or *render*) turns your project into a single video file. Key settings:

- **Resolution and aspect ratio** — 1920 × 1080 for horizontal (16:9), 1080 × 1920 for vertical (9:16). Export at the shape you planned; do not stretch.
- **Frame rate** — the same as you filmed (usually 25 or 30 fps). Changing it can cause stutter.
- **Format** — MP4 with the **H.264** codec plays almost everywhere. H.265 (HEVC) gives smaller files but some older phones and apps struggle with it.
- **Bit rate** — how much data per second. YouTube recommends roughly 8–12 Mbps for 1080p at 25–30 fps. Higher bit rates mean bigger files, which matters on mobile data.
- **Audio** — AAC, 48 kHz. Keep dialogue consistent; platforms turn quiet videos up and loud ones down, so a clean, even mix travels best.

**Platform notes.** WhatsApp recompresses video heavily and limits file size — send a shorter, smaller export, or share as a document to keep quality. Instagram and TikTok favour vertical. YouTube keeps the best quality and lets you upload subtitles as a separate file.

**Always watch the exported file all the way through**, on a phone, with sound — exports can add glitches, missing fonts or out-of-sync audio.

## Key words

- **Lower third:** a caption in the lower part of the frame naming a speaker
- **Safe area:** the part of the frame where text will not be cut off or covered
- **Thumbnail:** the still image shown before a video plays
- **Codec:** the method used to compress video, such as H.264
- **Bit rate:** the amount of data per second of video

## Read and watch

- [YouTube recommended upload encoding settings](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1722171) — YouTube Help
- [Lower third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_third) — Wikipedia
- [Advanced Video Coding (H.264)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Video_Coding) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use your editor's text templates, then change the font, colour and timing so they are readable.
- **If you already can:** make a simple animated title (a fade and a slide) and a matching thumbnail template you can reuse for a series.

## Learning online

Make your titles in CapCut, VN or DaVinci Resolve and your thumbnail in Canva (free) or a free photo editor. Test the thumbnail by shrinking it to a small size on your phone screen — if you cannot read it, enlarge the text or cut words. Export two versions (for example 9:16 for Status or Reels, and 16:9 for YouTube) and play each one back on a phone. **Upload:** a screenshot of your lower third, your thumbnail, a screenshot of each export's settings, and one sentence on any problem you found in playback. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your thumbnail at full size and at stamp size — we will vote on which ones we would click and why.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Next week you produce a full piece to a brief: choose your topic and book your contributors now, with consent.

lessons.title: A fully produced piece, reviewed
lessons.summary: Produce a finished 60–90 second video to a real brief, from plan to export, and review it like a professional.
objectives: You will take a piece from brief to delivered file
You will run a structured review and act on the notes
You will deliver the final file with credits, subtitles and permissions in order
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** This week everything joins up: pre-production, sound, picture, colour, pacing, graphics and export — finished, reviewed and delivered.

## What to do

- Produce a 60–90 second video to a real brief agreed with a client
- Hold a review with your client and one other member, and record their notes
- Deliver a final version with subtitles, credits and every release form in place

## Understand it

**The production pipeline** you have built this term:

1. **Pre-production** — brief agreed, schedule and call sheet sent, contributors briefed, release forms signed (parent or guardian for under-18s), location permission given.
2. **Production** — sound recorded close and at the right level, room tone and wild sound captured, exposure and white balance locked, coverage and B-roll filmed, take log kept.
3. **Post-production** — logging and selecting, assembly, rough cut, review, fine cut, audio mix, colour correction, titles and subtitles, export.
4. **Delivery** — the right file in the right format to the right person, with credits and a short description, and a backup kept.

**Running a review.** Show the rough cut to your client and one fresh viewer, in one sitting, without explaining it first. Then ask:

- What is the video about, in one sentence? (If they cannot say, the message is not clear.)
- Where did your attention drift?
- Was anything confusing or wrong?
- Is everything factually correct, and is every name spelt correctly?

Write the notes down with **timecodes** — "0:42: music too loud over Mr Bello" is a note you can act on; "the sound is off" is not. Then sort the notes (as in Cinematography): must fix, should fix, taste.

**Versioning.** Save each export with a clear name — `centre-promo_v1_rough`, `_v2_fine`, `_v3_final` — never `final_final2`. Keep the project file and the original footage until the client has signed off.

**The quality-control checklist before delivery:**

- **Picture:** no black frames or flash frames between cuts; colour consistent; titles inside safe areas.
- **Sound:** speech clear and even; music under speech; no sudden peaks; checked on headphones and a phone speaker.
- **Words:** subtitles complete and checked against what was said; names spelt correctly; lower thirds on first appearance.
- **Credits and rights:** everyone who made it, everyone who appeared (as agreed), music titles and licences.
- **Permissions:** a signed release for every identifiable person; nobody shown who asked not to be.
- **Export:** right shape, frame rate and format for the platform; watched all the way through.

**Delivering well.** Send the file with a short message: what it is, its length and format, where it is meant to be posted, and the caption or description you suggest. Ask the client to confirm they have received and approved it. If the video includes children, remind the client of the agreement on where it may be shared.

**Reviewing yourself.** Professionals finish every job with a short "what went well, what I would change" note. It is how the next job is better.

## Key words

- **Pipeline:** the stages a production moves through, from brief to delivery
- **Timecode:** the position in a video, in minutes and seconds, used for precise notes
- **Fine cut:** the polished edit after review
- **Quality control (QC):** the final check before delivery
- **Sign-off:** the client's approval of the final version

## Read and watch

- [Post-production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-production) — Wikipedia
- [Video accessibility: captions](https://www.w3.org/WAI/media/av/captions/) — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** produce a 45-second version with one contributor and one location, and use the QC checklist with your instructor.
- **If you already can:** deliver three versions from the same edit — 16:9, 9:16 and a 15-second teaser — each with its own thumbnail.

## Learning online

You can make the whole piece from home: a client from your family or community, contributors who agree (with a guardian's signature for under-18s), filmed on your phone and edited in CapCut, VN or DaVinci Resolve. Run the review over a video call or by sending the rough cut privately and asking the four questions. **Upload:** the brief, the signed releases (photographed — or a note confirming they are held safely, if they include addresses), the review notes with timecodes, the final video, and your completed QC checklist. **Bring to Saturday's online class:** your final piece to screen, and your "what went well, what I would change" note.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below. Send your client the final file and ask for their sign-off in writing; keep the message.

lessons.title: What a brand really is: promise, audience and position
lessons.summary: A brand is the promise an organisation keeps to one audience, in a place in their mind that nobody else holds.
objectives: You will explain the difference between a brand and a logo
You will write a one-sentence brand promise for a real local business
You will describe a brand's audience and position against a competitor
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Before anybody draws a logo, a brand has to know what it promises and to whom. Today you take a business you already know — a bakery, a barber, a school, a keke park — and find the promise hiding inside it.

## What to do

- Choose one small business near you and one of its competitors
- Write down what each one *promises* its customers, in one sentence each
- Describe who each one is for, and what makes people pick one over the other
- Turn your notes into a one-sentence promise and a one-sentence positioning statement

## Understand it

People often say "brand" when they mean "logo". The logo is only a signature. A **brand** is the set of ideas and feelings people hold about an organisation — and it is earned by what the organisation *does*, again and again.

Three ideas sit at the centre of every brand:

- **The promise** — what you can always expect. A good promise is specific and keepable: "Fresh bread before 7 a.m., every day" is a promise; "the best bread in Nigeria" is a boast nobody can check.
- **The audience** — who the brand is for. A brand that tries to speak to everyone usually speaks to nobody. "Workers on the morning bus who need breakfast fast" is an audience; "everybody who eats" is not.
- **The position** — the space the brand holds in people's minds *compared with* its competitors. If two bukas sell the same jollof at the same price, why do people queue at one? Maybe it is cleaner, faster, or friendlier. That difference is its position.

Marketers often write a **positioning statement** like this:

> *For* [audience] *who* [need], [brand] *is the* [category] *that* [difference], *because* [reason to believe].

For example: "For students who study late, Mama Ngozi's Kitchen is the canteen that stays open until 10 p.m., because the family lives behind the shop."

Notice the **reason to believe**. Customers trust a promise when there is a fact behind it. Without one, a promise is just advertising.

Finally, a brand is kept or broken at every **touchpoint** — every moment someone meets it: the sign, the WhatsApp reply, the receipt, the way staff greet you. A beautiful logo cannot rescue a brand that keeps people waiting and is rude when they complain. That is why branding starts with behaviour and only then moves to design.

## Key words

- **Brand:** the ideas and feelings people hold about an organisation, earned by what it does
- **Brand promise:** the specific thing customers can always expect
- **Target audience:** the particular group a brand is for
- **Positioning:** the space a brand holds in people's minds compared with competitors
- **Touchpoint:** any moment where a person meets the brand

## Read and watch

- [Branding](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/branding) — Interaction Design Foundation
- [Personas](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/personas) — Interaction Design Foundation

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** pick a business your family uses every week, so you already know its promise from experience.
- **If you already can:** write positioning statements for both businesses and show where they overlap — then suggest a position the weaker one could own.

## Learning online

You can do this whole lesson from home with a phone. Your research is real life: think about shops, salons or food sellers you or your family use. If you can, ask one adult *why* they choose that place over another and note their exact words — customers often say the promise better than the business does.

- Type your two promises and positioning statements into a free tool such as Google Docs, Canva Docs or your phone's notes app.
- **Upload as evidence:** a photo or screenshot of your page with both businesses, both promises, both audiences and your positioning statement. Do not photograph people or shop staff without permission — a photo of the sign from the street is enough.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your positioning statement, ready to read aloud in 20 seconds. Classmates will guess which business it describes — if they cannot, the position is not yet clear.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Notice one brand promise you meet this week (on a bus, a billboard or a packet) and decide whether it has a reason to believe.

checks.answer: Fresh bread on the shelves before 7 a.m. daily

Speaking to everybody means no particular audience feels it is for them.

Range can help, but here the products are the same.

lessons.title: Researching a brand and writing the brief
lessons.summary: Good branding starts with research, and the research is captured in a one-page brand brief.
objectives: You will gather evidence about an audience and competitors
You will write a one-page brand brief
You will separate facts from guesses in your research
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Designers who skip research design for themselves. Today you research a real need and turn what you find into a brief — the document that keeps every later decision honest.

## What to do

- Choose a client: a real local group, or the NGG Media Lab club itself
- Ask three people from the audience the same five questions
- Collect four competitor examples and note what each does well and badly
- Write a one-page brand brief

## Understand it

A **brand brief** is the agreement between a designer and a client about what the brand must achieve. Without one, people argue about colours when the real disagreement is about the audience.

**Research comes first, and it has two parts.**

1. **Audience research.** Talk to real people the brand is for. Ask open questions — ones that cannot be answered "yes" or "no":
   - "What do you look for when you choose a ... ?"
   - "Tell me about the last time you ..."
   - "What annoys you about the ones you have tried?"

   Write down their exact words. Patterns across three or four people are worth more than one loud opinion. Never put words in their mouths with questions like "Don't you think orange is nice?"

2. **Competitor research.** Find three or four organisations that serve the same audience. For each, note its name, colours, typefaces, tone of voice and what it promises. Put them side by side. You are looking for a **gap**: if every competitor is blue and serious, a warm, friendly brand will stand out.

**Facts versus guesses.** Mark each finding as *observed* (you saw or heard it) or *assumed* (you believe it). Assumptions are fine — but they should be tested, not treated as truth.

**The brief itself** fits on one page:

| Section | What it says |
|---|---|
| Background | Who the client is and what they do |
| Problem | Why they need a brand now |
| Audience | Who it is for, with one quote from your research |
| Competitors | Who else is out there and the gap you found |
| Promise | One sentence |
| Personality | Three words, e.g. "warm, smart, local" |
| Deliverables | Logo, palette, social template, etc. |
| Must / must not | Fixed rules, e.g. "must work in black and white" |
| Deadline | When it is due |

The client signs off the brief *before* design starts. Later, when someone says "I just don't like green", you can ask: "Does green match *warm, smart, local* for our audience?" The brief turns taste into reasons.

## Key words

- **Brand brief:** a one-page agreement on what a brand must achieve
- **Open question:** a question that cannot be answered with yes or no
- **Competitor analysis:** comparing organisations that serve the same audience
- **Gap:** something the audience needs that no competitor offers
- **Assumption:** a belief that has not yet been tested

## Read and watch

- [User research](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/user-research) — Interaction Design Foundation
- [Interviewing users](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interviewing-users/) — Nielsen Norman Group

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use the NGG Media Lab club as your client — you already belong to its audience.
- **If you already can:** interview five people instead of three and add a short section to your brief on what surprised you.

## Learning online

Interviews work well by phone, WhatsApp voice note or video call — always with people you already know, and with a parent or guardian aware of who you are contacting. Never message strangers for research.

- Use a free Google Form if you want written answers; keep it to five questions and do not collect names, phone numbers or addresses — you do not need them.
- Collect competitor examples by taking screenshots of their public pages or photos of their signs. Store them in one folder.
- Build your brief in Google Docs or Canva Docs using the table above.
- **Upload as evidence:** your one-page brief, plus a screenshot of your anonymous interview notes (first names removed).
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** one quote from your research that changed your mind about something. We will share these in the first ten minutes.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Ask your client (or your mentor, for the club) to read the brief and tell you one thing they would change.

Research is exactly what helps you choose with reasons.
A tiny change will not make a brand recognisably different.

lessons.title: Naming a brand and finding its voice
lessons.summary: A good name is easy to say, spell and remember, and a brand's voice keeps it sounding like itself everywhere.
objectives: You will generate and test brand names against clear criteria
You will check that a name is not already taken
You will write the same message in your brand's voice and in a wrong voice
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** A name is the one part of a brand people say out loud, and its voice is how it sounds every time it speaks. Today you name the brand from your brief and teach it to talk.

## What to do

- Brainstorm at least twenty possible names for your brief's brand
- Score your best five against the naming checklist
- Check your top two are not already in use
- Write a voice chart and rewrite one message in your brand's voice

## Understand it

**Naming.** Names come in a few families:

- **Descriptive** — says what it does: *Lagos Phone Repairs*. Clear, but hard to protect and easy to confuse.
- **Invented** — a new word: *Kodak*. Easy to protect but needs explaining at first.
- **Evocative** — suggests a feeling: *Ọ̀rẹ́ Kitchen* (friend), *Sunrise Tutors*.
- **Founder or place** — *Mama Cass*, *Ikeja Prints*.

Brainstorm widely first — twenty bad names often hide one good one — then test the best against a checklist:

1. **Say it**: can someone say it correctly after hearing it once on the phone?
2. **Spell it**: can they type it after hearing it? Names with unusual spellings lose customers in search.
3. **Remember it**: does it stick after a day?
4. **Meaning**: does it mean anything unfortunate in Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Pidgin or English? Ask people who speak each.
5. **Available**: is it already taken?

**Checking availability** at your level means searching the name on Google and on public social pages, and — for a real business — the Corporate Affairs Commission's public search, because businesses in Nigeria are registered with the CAC. Trademarks are protected by law; using a name that is confusingly similar to an existing brand can get a business into trouble.

**Voice and tone.** A brand's **voice** is its personality in words, and it stays the same. Its **tone** adjusts to the moment — the same friend speaks gently at a funeral and loudly at a party, but is still the same person. A **voice chart** describes the voice in three traits, each with "is / is not":

| Trait | We are | We are not |
|---|---|---|
| Friendly | warm, uses first names | over-familiar or slangy |
| Clear | short sentences, plain words | childish or vague |
| Proud | celebrates members | boastful |

Test the voice by rewriting one ordinary message. *"Registration closes Friday."* becomes, in a friendly, clear voice: *"Don't miss out — sign up by Friday so we can save your seat."* A useful way to see the difference is to write it once in a wrong voice too, such as stiff and formal: *"Kindly note that registration terminates on Friday."*

## Key words

- **Descriptive name:** a name that says what the business does
- **Invented name:** a brand-new word created as a name
- **Brand voice:** the brand's consistent personality in words
- **Tone:** how the voice adjusts to a situation
- **Voice chart:** a table of voice traits with what the brand is and is not

## Read and watch

- [The four dimensions of tone of voice](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tone-of-voice-dimensions/) — Nielsen Norman Group
- [Trademarks](https://www.wipo.int/trademarks/en/) — World Intellectual Property Organization

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** start from a descriptive name, then try one evocative version of it.
- **If you already can:** test your top name with five people using the say-it-once phone test and record how many spelt it correctly.

## Learning online

From home, the phone test is easy: send a voice note saying your top two names to two family members or friends and ask them to type back what they heard. Count how many spelt each one correctly.

- Check availability with a simple web search and by searching public social media pages in a browser — you do not need an account to look. Only an adult should use the CAC public search for a real business.
- Make your voice chart in Google Docs or Canva.
- **Upload as evidence:** your scored shortlist (five names, five criteria), screenshots of your availability searches, your voice chart, and one message written in the right voice and a wrong voice.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your top name and one sentence in your brand's voice. Classmates will guess your three voice traits.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Notice one brand whose voice you like this week and write down one sentence it used.

materials.guide: Read the four dimensions (funny–serious, formal–casual, respectful–irreverent, enthusiastic–matter-of-fact) and place your brand on each.

whys: Common words, easy to hear and type.
