lessons.title: Logo design principles: simple, scalable, single-colour
lessons.summary: A strong logo is simple enough to remember, works from a tiny icon to a billboard, and survives in one colour.
objectives: You will judge logos against five design principles
You will sketch at least twelve logo ideas before choosing one
You will test your logo small, large and in black and white
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** You already know the logo types from Media Lab. Today is about the craft: what makes one logo work everywhere while another falls apart on a phone screen.

## What to do

- Judge three local logos against the five principles below
- Sketch twelve or more thumbnail ideas on paper for your brand
- Develop your best two digitally
- Test them at favicon size, poster size, in black, and reversed out in white

## Understand it

Professional designers judge a logo against a small set of principles:

1. **Simple.** Few shapes, few colours, no tiny details. If you cannot draw it from memory in ten seconds, it is too complicated.
2. **Memorable.** One clear idea — a shape, a letter, a clever detail — not five ideas fighting.
3. **Scalable.** It must still read at 16 pixels wide (the icon on a browser tab) and on a two-metre banner. Thin lines vanish when small; fine detail turns to mud.
4. **Versatile.** It works in one colour (a rubber stamp, a fax, an embroidered cap), and **reversed** — white on a dark background.
5. **Appropriate.** It fits the audience and personality in your brief. A children's charity and a law firm should not look alike.

**Sketch before you click.** Start on paper with **thumbnails** — small, quick drawings about the size of a stamp. Make at least twelve. Quantity first: the first idea is usually the most obvious one, and your competitors have probably already used it. Circle your best three.

**Go digital with vectors.** A logo should be built as a **vector** — shapes described by maths, not pixels — so it can be scaled to any size without going blurry. Formats such as SVG and PDF are vector; PNG and JPG are pixel (**raster**) images. Canva, Figma and Inkscape (free) all make vector shapes.

**Build a logo family.** Most brands need:

- the **primary logo** (full colour, the main version);
- a **one-colour version** (all black, and all white for dark backgrounds);
- a **compact version** or icon for small spaces — a profile picture is usually a circle, so check your logo fits one.

**Clear space and minimum size.** Decide how much empty space must always surround the logo (often the height of one letter), and the smallest size at which it may be printed.

**Make it yours.** Do not trace, copy or lightly change someone else's logo, and do not use a generated image you cannot explain. A logo must be original to be protected — and to be honest.

## Key words

- **Thumbnail:** a small, quick sketch used to explore many ideas
- **Scalable:** works at any size without losing clarity
- **Vector:** an image made of shapes that can be resized without going blurry
- **Raster:** an image made of pixels, such as PNG or JPG
- **Reversed logo:** a logo shown in white on a dark background

## Read and watch

- [Gestalt principles](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/gestalt-principles) — Interaction Design Foundation
- [SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/SVG) — MDN Web Docs

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** make a wordmark first — your brand name in a carefully chosen font — and add a symbol only if it helps.
- **If you already can:** design a compact icon version that still reads as a 32-pixel circle, and explain which part of the primary logo it keeps.

## Learning online

You need only paper, a pen and a free design tool. Take a clear photo of your thumbnail page in good light.

- Build your two best ideas in Canva, Figma (free) or Inkscape (free on a laptop). On a phone, Canva works well — use its shapes and text, not ready-made logo templates, so the work is yours.
- Make a **test board**: one page showing each logo at 16 px and 300 px, in black, and reversed in white on a dark square. Export it as a PNG.
- **Upload as evidence:** your thumbnail photo (at least twelve sketches) and your test board.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your test board on screen. We will do a "squint test" — everyone squints at the smallest version; if the idea disappears, it needs simplifying.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Look at app icons on your phone and pick one that works brilliantly at small size — note why.

lessons.title: Colour and type systems for a brand
lessons.summary: A brand needs a small, fixed system of colours and typefaces with clear jobs, and it must stay readable for everyone.
objectives: You will build a brand palette with exact HEX codes and roles
You will choose a type pairing and a simple hierarchy
You will check your colours pass contrast for readable text
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Choosing a favourite colour is easy. Building a *system* — where every colour and font has a job and stays readable — is what makes a brand look professional.

## What to do

- Choose a palette of one primary, one or two secondary and two neutral colours
- Write the exact HEX code and the job of each colour
- Pick one or two typefaces and set a heading/body hierarchy
- Check every text-on-background pairing for contrast

## Understand it

**Colour with roles.** A brand palette is not a rainbow. Most strong brands use:

- **One primary colour** — the one people remember (MTN's yellow, for example).
- **One or two secondary colours** — to support and add variety.
- **Neutrals** — a near-black and a near-white or light grey for text and backgrounds.
- Sometimes one **accent** for important buttons or highlights.

A helpful starting proportion is the **60–30–10 rule**: about 60% neutral or dominant colour, 30% secondary, 10% accent. It is a guide, not a law.

Give every colour an **exact code**. On screens, colours are written in **HEX** (for example `#F2B705`) or RGB. For printing, printers use **CMYK**. Writing "yellow" in a guide guarantees five different yellows.

Colours also carry meaning, and that meaning depends on culture. Green can suggest growth, money, or Nigeria itself; red can suggest energy, danger or celebration. Ask your audience, not a chart from another country.

**Readable for everyone.** About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some colour-vision deficiency, and many people read on cracked or dim phone screens in sunlight. The international accessibility guideline, **WCAG**, asks for a **contrast ratio** of at least **4.5 : 1** for normal text and **3 : 1** for large text. Yellow text on white fails badly; dark navy on white passes easily. Use a free contrast checker and test every pairing you plan to use. Never use colour alone to carry meaning — add a word or an icon too.

**Type with roles.** Choose one or two typefaces:

- A **heading** face with personality.
- A **body** face that is easy to read at small sizes — usually a clean sans-serif on screens.

Pairing a **serif** (with small "feet" on the letters) and a **sans-serif** (without) is a classic way to get contrast without clashing. Avoid pairing two decorative fonts.

Then fix a **hierarchy**: for example heading 32 pt bold, subheading 20 pt, body 12 pt regular. Check your fonts are free to use — Google Fonts are open-licensed — and that they include the characters you need, such as the dotted and accented letters in Yoruba (ẹ, ọ, ṣ) or Hausa (ɓ, ɗ, ƙ), if your brand will use them.

## Key words

- **Palette:** the fixed set of colours a brand uses
- **HEX code:** a six-character code that names an exact screen colour
- **Contrast ratio:** how different two colours are in lightness; 4.5 : 1 is the minimum for normal text
- **Serif / sans-serif:** typefaces with / without small strokes at the ends of letters
- **Type hierarchy:** fixed sizes and weights that show what to read first

## Read and watch

- [Contrast checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — WebAIM
- [Understanding contrast (minimum)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html) — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative
- [Google Fonts Knowledge](https://fonts.google.com/knowledge) — Google Fonts

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** start from your logo's main colour and add only a dark neutral and a light neutral; that is already a working palette.
- **If you already can:** add a full tint scale (e.g. 100–900) for your primary colour and note which steps pass contrast with white text.

## Learning online

Everything here works in a browser on a phone or laptop. Use Canva's colour picker or the free site coolors.co to explore, then copy the exact HEX codes. Test pairings in the WebAIM contrast checker linked below. Browse Google Fonts and type a sentence in your brand's language to preview it — check the special letters appear.

- Make a one-page **colour and type sheet** in Canva or Google Slides: swatches with HEX codes and roles, your two fonts with sizes, and a sample heading and paragraph.
- **Upload as evidence:** your sheet and screenshots of the contrast checker for your two main text pairings.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your sheet on screen. We will view everyone's palettes in greyscale to see which still hold their hierarchy.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Notice a sign or label this week that is hard to read, and work out whether contrast is the reason.

lessons.title: Writing the brand guidelines
lessons.summary: Brand guidelines are the rulebook that lets anyone use the brand correctly without asking its designer.
objectives: You will assemble a short brand guidelines document
You will write clear do and don't rules with examples
You will test your guide by having someone else follow it
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** In Media Lab you made a one-page guide. Today you write a proper short guidelines document — the kind a printer, a volunteer or a new team member can follow alone.

## What to do

- Gather your brief, name, voice chart, logo family, palette and type sheet
- Lay them out as an eight- to ten-page guidelines document
- Add at least six 'don't' examples showing misuse
- Give it to someone who has not seen your brand and ask them to make one post using only the guide

## Understand it

A brand is only as consistent as the least informed person who uses it. **Brand guidelines** (also called a style guide or brand book) exist so that a volunteer designing a flyer at midnight makes the same choices you would.

A short guide for a small organisation usually has these sections:

1. **The brand in one page** — the promise, audience, personality words and positioning from your brief.
2. **Logo** — the primary logo, the one-colour and reversed versions, the compact icon; clear space and minimum size shown with measurements.
3. **Logo misuse** — the "don'ts": do not stretch it, rotate it, change its colours, add shadows, put it on a busy photo, or redraw it. Show each one crossed out. Pictures of mistakes teach faster than sentences.
4. **Colour** — swatches with HEX (and CMYK for print), each colour's role, and the contrast-safe text pairings.
5. **Typography** — the typefaces, the hierarchy, and where to download them legally.
6. **Voice** — the voice chart and two or three before-and-after examples.
7. **Imagery** — what photos or illustrations look like: natural light? Real members (with consent)? Flat illustrations? Also what to avoid.
8. **Templates and examples** — a social post, a poster, a letterhead, showing everything working together.
9. **Contacts and files** — where to find the logo files, and who to ask.

Write rules as **instructions**, not descriptions. "The logo is navy" describes; "Use the navy logo on white or light backgrounds; use the white logo on navy" instructs. Be specific with numbers: "Leave clear space equal to the height of the letter N on every side."

**Test the guide.** The real test of a guide is whether it works without you. Give it to someone who has never seen your brand — a sibling, a classmate — and ask them to make one social post using only the guide and your files. Do not help. Every question they ask, or mistake they make, shows a gap in your guide. Fix those gaps.

Guides grow over time. Put a **version number and date** on the cover so everyone knows whether they have the latest one.

## Key words

- **Brand guidelines:** the rulebook for using a brand's identity consistently
- **Misuse examples:** pictures showing what not to do with the logo
- **Clear space:** the empty area that must surround the logo
- **Template:** a ready-made layout that keeps the brand consistent
- **Version number:** a label showing which edition of a document is current

## Read and watch

- [Design systems](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/design-systems) — Interaction Design Foundation
- [Trademarks](https://www.wipo.int/trademarks/en/) — World Intellectual Property Organization

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** aim for a six-page guide covering sections 1–6 first, and add imagery and templates after the user test.
- **If you already can:** add a print section with CMYK codes and a short accessibility section explaining your contrast and alt-text rules.

## Learning online

A presentation tool is perfect for this: Canva Presentations or Google Slides, one section per slide, exported as a PDF. Work on a laptop if you can; on a phone, build one slide at a time and preview it as a PDF before sharing.

- For your user test, send the PDF and the logo files to a family member or classmate on WhatsApp, ask them to make one post in Canva using only the guide, and ask them to send it back. Write down every question they asked.
- **Upload as evidence:** your guidelines PDF, the test post someone else made, and a short list of what you changed after the test.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your misuse page. We will vote on the most useful "don't" in the class.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Make sure your guide has a version number and date on its cover.

lessons.title: Across every touchpoint: a rebrand critique
lessons.summary: A brand is tested where people actually meet it, and studying a real Nigerian rebrand shows what changes and why.
objectives: You will map the touchpoints of a real brand
You will critique a Nigerian brand's change of identity with evidence
You will apply your own brand to three different touchpoints
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** A logo on a white page always looks fine. The real test is the shop sign in harmattan dust, the profile picture as a tiny circle, and the receipt from a cheap printer. Today you look at a real rebrand, then put your own brand through the same test.

## What to do

- List every touchpoint for one well-known Nigerian brand
- Research one Nigerian brand that has changed its identity and compare old and new
- Write a fair critique: what improved, what was lost, and why they changed
- Apply your own brand to three touchpoints of different sizes

## Understand it

**Touchpoints.** Map every place a customer meets a brand — before, during and after they buy:

- *Before:* billboards, radio jingles, social posts, a friend's recommendation, the shop sign.
- *During:* the shop, the app, the staff uniform, the packaging, the price list, the WhatsApp reply.
- *After:* the receipt, the follow-up message, the customer service line, how a complaint is handled.

Each touchpoint has its own limits. A profile picture is cropped to a circle and shown tiny; a uniform may be embroidered in one colour; a POS receipt is black thermal print. A strong identity is designed for its *hardest* touchpoint, not its easiest.

**Rebrands.** Organisations change their identity for reasons such as: a new strategy or audience, a merger, looking out of date, or a logo that does not work on phones. Many big brands have moved from shiny, 3D logos to **flat**, simpler ones, because flat designs reproduce cleanly on screens, app icons and cheap printing. For example, MTN refreshed its identity in 2022 with a flatter, simpler version of its famous yellow-and-black logo and its own typeface.

A **rebrand critique** is not "I like it" or "I hate it". It asks:

1. **Why did they change?** Look for the organisation's own announcement or reputable news coverage.
2. **What stayed?** Good rebrands keep **brand equity** — the things people already recognise, such as a colour or shape — so customers are not lost.
3. **What changed, and does it work better at the hard touchpoints?** Compare old and new as an app icon, on a sign, in one colour.
4. **Does it fit the audience and promise?**
5. **What was lost?** Sometimes warmth or character goes with the old design.

Support each point with evidence — a picture, a quote, a test — not just opinion. People will disagree; a good critique lets them see *why* you reached your view.

**Apply your own brand.** Choose three touchpoints of very different shape: a square social post, a circular profile picture, and something physical such as a T-shirt, a name badge or a sign. If your identity breaks at one of them, fix the system, not only that piece.

## Key words

- **Touchpoint map:** a list of every place people meet a brand, before, during and after
- **Rebrand:** a deliberate change to an organisation's identity
- **Brand equity:** the recognition and trust a brand has built up
- **Flat design:** simple shapes and colours without 3D effects or shine
- **Critique:** a reasoned judgement supported by evidence

## Read and watch

- [Branding](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/branding) — Interaction Design Foundation
- [MTN Group](https://www.mtn.com/) — MTN Group's official website

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** critique the brand using only questions 2 and 3 — what stayed and what changed at the app icon size.
- **If you already can:** find the organisation's own explanation of the rebrand and test whether the new identity delivers what it claimed.

## Learning online

Do your research in a browser: search for the brand's name plus "new logo" and choose sources such as the company's own website or established news outlets. Save images of the old and new identity side by side. Look at the brand's current app icon on a family member's phone, or at its signs and packets around your home.

- Create a one- or two-page critique in Canva or Google Slides with old and new side by side, each of the five questions answered, and your sources listed.
- Mock up your three touchpoints in Canva using mock-up frames — you do not need to print a T-shirt.
- **Upload as evidence:** your critique (with sources) and your three touchpoint mock-ups.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** one point where you think the rebrand improved things, and one where you think it lost something. We will hold a short, respectful debate.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Tell one adult about the rebrand you studied and ask whether they noticed the change at the time.

lessons.title: Capstone: a complete brand identity, with AI used critically
lessons.summary: You bring brief, name, logo, colour, type, voice and guidelines together into one brand, and show honestly where AI helped and where it did not.
objectives: You will present a complete brand identity for a real or realistic client
You will use an AI tool critically and record what you kept, changed or rejected
You will give and receive structured feedback
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** This is the term's capstone. Everything you built in weeks 1–7 becomes one brand package, presented as a professional would — with the reasons behind each choice.

## What to do

- Finalise every piece of your identity and fix anything your user test exposed
- Try one AI tool on one part of the work and keep an honest AI log
- Prepare a five-minute presentation
- Present, take feedback and write your reflection

## Understand it

**What a complete identity includes.** Your capstone package should contain:

1. The **brand brief** (week 2), updated if your thinking changed.
2. The **name** and its availability check, and the **voice chart** (week 3).
3. The **logo family**: primary, one-colour, reversed, compact icon (week 4).
4. The **colour and type system** with contrast evidence (week 5).
5. The **brand guidelines** PDF, versioned (week 6).
6. **Three touchpoints** showing the brand in use (week 7).

**Using AI critically.** AI tools can generate names, colour palettes, slogans and even logo-like images in seconds. Used well, they widen your options. Used badly, they produce work that is generic, unoriginal or even legally risky. Think like an editor:

- **AI does not know your audience.** It has not done your interviews. Everything it suggests must be tested against your brief.
- **AI names may already be taken.** Run the same availability checks as for your own ideas.
- **AI images can resemble existing logos** or contain garbled text, and in many countries purely machine-generated images may not be protected as anyone's original work. Never present an AI image as your final logo; at most, use one as a sketch you redraw and change substantially.
- **AI is often confidently wrong** about facts — for example, colour meanings or what a font supports. Check.
- **Be open.** Say what you used and how, just as you credit a photographer.

Keep an **AI log** with three columns: *what I asked*, *what it gave*, *what I kept, changed or rejected — and why*. A strong log often shows more rejections than acceptances; that is a sign of good judgement, not failure.

**Presenting.** Structure your five minutes as a story: the client and problem (brief), what you learned (research), the idea (promise and personality), the identity (logo, colour, type, voice), proof it works (touchpoints and user test), and what you would do next. Explain *why* for each choice — "navy because the audience said trust matters, and it passes contrast with white at 12 : 1".

**Feedback.** Use **"I like / I wonder / What if"**: one strength, one question, one suggestion. Write down what people say without arguing; decide later what to act on.

## Key words

- **Brand identity:** the full visible system: name, logo, colour, type, voice and their rules
- **AI log:** a record of what you asked an AI tool, what it produced and what you did with it
- **Generic:** ordinary and interchangeable, with nothing that marks it as this brand
- **Disclosure:** openly stating which tools and sources you used
- **Structured feedback:** feedback given in a set pattern so it is fair and useful

## Read and watch

- [Policy guidance on AI for children](https://www.unicef.org/innocenti/reports/policy-guidance-ai-children) — UNICEF
- [Trademarks](https://www.wipo.int/trademarks/en/) — World Intellectual Property Organization

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** present the six core pieces clearly; an AI log with two honest entries is enough.
- **If you already can:** add a short section on how the brand could grow — a sub-brand for a new service, or a version for a new audience.

## Learning online

You can complete and present the capstone entirely online. Gather everything into one Canva presentation or Google Slides deck and export it as a PDF as well, in case the connection drops during class.

- Use only AI tools that allow your age, and only with a parent or guardian's knowledge. Canva's built-in Magic tools, used inside a supervised or NGG-provided account, are fine. Do not upload photos of real people to any AI tool.
- Record a five-minute run-through on your phone to practise; time yourself.
- **Upload as evidence:** your capstone PDF, your AI log, and your guidelines PDF.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your deck, ready to share your screen, and a notebook for feedback. If your connection is weak, your mentor can present your PDF while you talk over audio.

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below, including the reflection. Keep your files in one folder — they are the start of your portfolio.

lessons.title: Your digital footprint
lessons.summary: Everything you do online leaves a trail that others can find, copy and keep, so you can shape it on purpose.
objectives: You will explain active and passive digital footprints
You will audit what can be found about a person or organisation online
You will write three personal rules for what you share
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Before we post for anybody, we start with ourselves. Every message, photo and search leaves a trace. Today you find out how big that trail is and how to shape it.

## What to do

- Sort a list of online actions into active and passive footprints
- Audit a fictional character's footprint from a case card
- Search a public organisation's name and note what you find
- Write your three personal sharing rules

## Understand it

Your **digital footprint** is the trail of information you leave online. It has two parts:

- **Active footprint** — what you choose to share: posts, comments, photos, profile details, reviews, messages in a group.
- **Passive footprint** — what is collected about you without you actively posting: your location from a phone, the websites you visit, what you watch and for how long, the device you use. Apps and advertisers use this to build a picture of you.

Three facts make footprints matter:

1. **Online is close to permanent.** Deleting a post does not delete screenshots, forwards or copies. A WhatsApp status disappears after 24 hours — unless someone screenshots it in the first minute.
2. **Online is searchable.** Schools, scholarship panels and employers increasingly search applicants' names. What is found can open doors or close them.
3. **Small details add up.** A school uniform in one photo, a street sign in another, a "happy birthday" post with your date of birth — together they can reveal where you live, study and when you are alone. This is called **aggregation**.

**A footprint can be positive.** A member who shares their art, a coding project or a volunteering story builds a footprint that shows who they are becoming. The goal is not to be invisible; it is to be **intentional**.

**The audit.** To check a footprint, search the name in a search engine (with quotation marks: "Ada Bello"), look at image results, and check any public profiles. Ask: *What could a stranger learn? Would I be happy for a teacher, a future employer or my grandmother to see this?*

**Before you post anything, use the THINK test:** is it **T**rue, **H**elpful, **I**nspiring, **N**ecessary, **K**ind? And add one more question of our own: *does it reveal where I am, or details about someone else who did not agree?*

**Organisations have footprints too.** When you post for NGG, a club or a business, you are adding to *their* footprint — and to the footprints of every person in your photos. That is why consent matters, which we cover next week.

## Key words

- **Digital footprint:** the trail of information a person leaves online
- **Active footprint:** what you deliberately share
- **Passive footprint:** data collected about you without you posting it
- **Aggregation:** small details combined to reveal something bigger
- **Intentional:** done on purpose, after thinking it through

## Read and watch

- [Digital citizenship](https://www.commonsense.org/education/digital-citizenship) — Common Sense Education
- [Internet Matters](https://www.internetmatters.org/) — Internet Matters (online safety advice for families)

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use the THINK test on three posts you have seen this week, then write your rules.
- **If you already can:** audit a public organisation, such as a local business, and write three suggestions to improve its footprint.

## Learning online

You do not need your own social media account for any of this. Most platforms are for people aged 13 and over; if you are younger, or have no account, work with mock-ups or with an NGG account run by staff.

For the audit, **do not search for real classmates or private people** — use the fictional case card your mentor shares in the class folder, or search a public organisation such as a museum or a well-known Nigerian business.

- Make a two-column table (active / passive) in Google Docs or on paper and sort at least ten actions.
- **Upload as evidence:** your sorted table, your case-card audit (what a stranger could learn, and from which details), and your three personal rules.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** one detail from the case card that surprised you by how much it revealed.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Sit with a parent or guardian and look together at the privacy settings of one app your family uses.

lessons.title: Privacy, consent and the age rules
lessons.summary: Platforms set age limits, Nigerian law protects children's personal data, and nobody should be posted without consent.
objectives: You will explain why most platforms are for people aged 13 and over
You will describe what Nigeria's Data Protection Act means for children, in plain words
You will plan a consent process for photos at an NGG event
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Social media runs on personal data — names, faces, locations, habits. Today you learn the rules that protect people, especially young people, and plan how NGG asks before it posts.

## What to do

- Find the minimum age in the terms of three platforms
- Match personal data examples to 'ordinary' and 'sensitive'
- Learn the key idea of the NDPA 2023 for children
- Design a photo consent plan for an NGG event

## Understand it

**Age rules.** Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat, X, YouTube and WhatsApp all set **13** as the minimum age in most countries, including Nigeria. YouTube offers YouTube Kids for younger children. The age limit is in each platform's **terms of service** — the agreement you accept when you sign up. Lying about your age breaks those terms, and the account can be closed. More importantly, the limits exist because younger children are more easily targeted by strangers, scams and advertising, and are not protected by the safety features built for teens.

Some platforms give teen accounts extra protection — private by default, limited messaging from strangers, time reminders. Those settings are there for a reason; keep them on.

**Personal data.** Personal data is any information that identifies a person: name, photo, phone number, address, school, location, ID numbers. Some data is **sensitive** — health, religion, ethnicity, biometric data such as a fingerprint — and needs even more care.

**Nigeria's law.** The **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA)** sets the rules for how organisations in Nigeria collect and use personal data, and the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)** enforces it. At your level, the key ideas are:

- Organisations must have a lawful reason to use your data, use it only for that purpose, keep it safe, and not keep it longer than needed.
- People have rights: to know what data is held about them, to have it corrected, and in many cases to have it deleted.
- **Children get extra protection.** The Act treats a person under 18 as a child, and an organisation generally needs the consent of a **parent or guardian** before it processes a child's personal data. It must also take reasonable steps to check a person's age.

**Consent in practice.** For an NGG event, that means: a written consent form signed by a parent or guardian before photos of a member are posted; a visible way for anyone to say "no photos" (for example, a coloured lanyard); never posting a child's full name with their face, school or home area; and removing a photo promptly if anyone asks. **Consent can be withdrawn** — "yes" last month is not "yes" for ever.

When in doubt, shoot hands, backs of heads, the work being made, or wide shots where nobody is identifiable.

## Key words

- **Terms of service:** the rules you agree to when you join a platform
- **Personal data:** any information that identifies a person
- **Sensitive data:** data such as health or religion that needs extra protection
- **NDPA 2023:** Nigeria's Data Protection Act, which governs how personal data is used
- **Consent:** clear, informed permission that can be withdrawn

## Read and watch

- [Nigeria Data Protection Commission](https://ndpc.gov.ng/) — the official regulator's website
- [UNICEF](https://www.unicef.org/) — children's rights, including online

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** focus on the age rules and the consent plan; summarise the NDPA in three sentences.
- **If you already can:** read the NDPC's public pages and add a short 'your rights' section to your consent plan, written for a 12-year-old.

## Learning online

You do not need your own social media account for any of this. Most platforms are for people aged 13 and over; if you are younger, or have no account, work with mock-ups or with an NGG account run by staff.

To find minimum ages, open each platform's help or safety page in a browser — no login needed. Search for "minimum age" on the help centre.

- Build your consent plan in Google Docs or Canva: the consent form wording, the "no photos" signal, the posting rules, and the removal process.
- **Upload as evidence:** a small table of three platforms and their minimum ages (with links), and your consent plan.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your consent form wording. We will combine the clearest lines from everyone's into a draft for NGG staff to consider.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Explain to a younger sibling or cousin, in two sentences, why apps have age limits.

lessons.title: Hooks and captions that get read
lessons.summary: In a fast scroll you have about a second to earn attention, so the first line must hook and the rest must be clear and useful.
objectives: You will write hooks using four proven patterns
You will structure a caption: hook, value, call to action
You will write alt text so posts work for everyone
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** People scroll past most posts in under a second. Today you learn to write the first line that stops them, and the caption that rewards them for stopping.

## What to do

- Collect five posts from public pages that made you stop, and five that did not
- Write ten hooks for one NGG event using the four patterns
- Write a full caption and its alt text
- Swap with a partner and score each other's hooks

## Understand it

**The hook** is the first line of a caption (or the first second of a video). Most platforms hide everything after the first line or two behind "...more", so the hook carries the post. Four reliable patterns:

1. **A question the reader wants answered** — "Can a 12-year-old build a website in a weekend?"
2. **A surprising number or fact** — "48 members. 3 weeks. 1 robot that actually walks."
3. **A promise of value** — "Three free tools to edit photos on your phone."
4. **A story opening** — "At 9 a.m. Tolu had never touched a camera."

Avoid **clickbait** — hooks that promise something the post does not deliver ("You won't BELIEVE what happened!"). It may get a click once; it loses trust for ever.

**The caption** then follows a simple shape:

- **Hook** — the stopping line.
- **Value** — the useful, interesting or moving part. Short sentences. One idea per line. Line breaks make it scannable on a phone.
- **Call to action (CTA)** — one clear next step: "Register by Friday — link in bio", "Save this for later", "Tell us your favourite in the comments".

Keep it in the brand's **voice**. Check every fact: date, time, place, spelling of names.

**Hashtags.** Use a few specific, relevant tags (#LagosCoding is more useful than #love). Put them at the end so they do not interrupt the message. Too many look like spam.

**Emoji** can add warmth, but screen readers read each one aloud ("rocket, rocket, rocket"), so use them sparingly and never in place of words.

**Alt text** is a written description of an image for people who use screen readers, and for when images fail to load. Describe what matters in the image for this post, in one or two sentences: "Three members in NGG T-shirts test a small wheeled robot on a classroom floor." Do not start with "Image of" — screen readers already say it is an image.

**Test before posting.** Read the caption aloud. Cover everything except the first line: would you tap "more"?

## Key words

- **Hook:** the first line or second that stops the scroll
- **Clickbait:** a hook that promises what the post does not deliver
- **Call to action:** the one next step you ask the reader to take
- **Alt text:** a written description of an image for people who cannot see it
- **Scannable:** easy to read quickly on a small screen

## Read and watch

- [How users read on the web](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-users-read-on-the-web/) — Nielsen Norman Group
- [Images tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/) — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** write five hooks, one from each of the first four patterns plus your favourite, before writing the caption.
- **If you already can:** write the same announcement for two audiences — members and parents — and explain how the hook changed.

## Learning online

You do not need your own social media account for any of this. Most platforms are for people aged 13 and over; if you are younger, or have no account, work with mock-ups or with an NGG account run by staff.

You can collect examples by browsing public pages in a web browser without logging in, or by using posts your mentor has saved in the class folder. Take screenshots and crop out other people's comments and names.

- Write your hooks and caption in your notes app or Google Docs. Create a **mock-up** post in Canva using a social post template, so it looks real without being published.
- **Upload as evidence:** your ten hooks (labelled by pattern), your finished caption with CTA, the alt text, and the Canva mock-up.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your best hook. We will do a "scroll test": hooks are shown one at a time for two seconds, and the class votes on which they would stop for.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Notice which hooks make you stop this week, and which pattern each used.

lessons.title: Short-form video: structure in sixty seconds
lessons.summary: A strong short video hooks in the first seconds, delivers one idea, and ends with a payoff and a clear next step.
objectives: You will plan a short video with a hook–value–payoff–CTA structure
You will shoot vertical video with steady framing, good light and clear sound
You will add on-screen captions so the video works with sound off
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** Short vertical video is the main language of social media now. Today you plan, shoot and edit a 30–60-second video about one thing you can teach.

## What to do

- Choose one small skill you can teach in under a minute
- Write a shot list using the four-part structure
- Shoot it vertically, using natural light and a quiet room
- Edit with captions, then watch it with the sound off

## Understand it

**One video, one idea.** The most common mistake is trying to say everything. A short video does one job: teach one trick, show one moment, answer one question.

**The four-part structure** (for a 45-second video):

| Part | Time | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Hook** | 0–3 s | Show the result first, or ask the question. "This is how to fold a paper plane that flies 10 metres." |
| **Value** | 3–35 s | The steps, quick and clear. Change the shot every 2–4 seconds to keep energy. |
| **Payoff** | 35–42 s | The satisfying result — the plane flying. |
| **CTA** | 42–45 s | One next step: "Try it and tell us your distance." |

**Shooting well with a phone:**

- **Vertical (9 : 16)**, usually 1080 × 1920 pixels. Hold the phone upright.
- **Light:** face a window; never stand with a bright window behind you, or you become a silhouette.
- **Steady:** lean on a table, use a pile of books as a tripod, or hold the phone with both elbows tucked in.
- **Sound:** a quiet room matters more than an expensive microphone. Turn off fans while recording. Keep the phone close to whoever is speaking.
- **Safe zones:** platforms cover the bottom and right edges with buttons and captions, so keep text and faces in the middle.

**Captions on screen.** A large share of people watch with the sound off. Add on-screen captions — most free editors can create them automatically, but **always correct them**: automatic captions often mangle names and Nigerian words.

**Music and copyright.** Only use music you have the right to use: the editor's own licensed library, royalty-free tracks, or music you made. A popular song from your playlist can get a video muted or removed.

**Editing.** Cut every pause and every "erm". If a shot does not add something, remove it. Check the first frame: it is often the thumbnail people see.

**Who is in it?** Film your hands, the object, or yourself only with a parent or guardian's agreement. Never film other people without their consent, and never film in a way that shows your home address, school name or location.

## Key words

- **Vertical video:** video shot upright, usually 9 : 16
- **Shot list:** a planned list of each shot in order
- **Payoff:** the satisfying result the viewer has been waiting for
- **Safe zone:** the area of the screen not covered by platform buttons
- **Royalty-free music:** music licensed so you can use it without paying per use

## Read and watch

- [YouTube Creators](https://www.youtube.com/creators/) — YouTube
- [Making audio and video media accessible](https://www.w3.org/WAI/media/av/) — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** make a 30-second video with three shots only: result, one step, result again.
- **If you already can:** make two versions with different hooks and ask five people which they would keep watching.

## Learning online

You do not need your own social media account for any of this. Most platforms are for people aged 13 and over; if you are younger, or have no account, work with mock-ups or with an NGG account run by staff.

A phone and a free editor are all you need: CapCut, the Canva video editor, or the editor built into your phone's gallery. Film only your hands and objects unless a parent or guardian agrees otherwise. You are **not** publishing this video — you are making it for class.

- Write your shot list first (in Google Docs or on paper), then film. Export at 1080 × 1920.
- Watch your edit once with the sound off: can someone still follow it?
- **Upload as evidence:** your shot list, your finished video (or a link to it in a shared Google Drive folder set to "anyone with the link"), and one sentence on your hook choice.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your video. We will watch the first three seconds of each one and decide together whether we would keep watching.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Watch three short videos this week and time how quickly each one hooks you.

lessons.title: Reading analytics: what the numbers really say
lessons.summary: Analytics show what people did with your posts; the skill is choosing the right number and comparing fairly.
objectives: You will explain reach, impressions, engagement, saves, shares and watch time
You will calculate engagement rate and compare posts fairly
You will turn a set of figures into one decision
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** In Media Lab you met reach and engagement rate. Today you go further: reading a real-looking dashboard, spotting misleading numbers, and deciding what to post next.

## What to do

- Read the sample analytics sheet your mentor shares
- Calculate the engagement rate for eight posts
- Rank them by a metric that matches the goal
- Write one decision and the evidence behind it

## Understand it

Analytics (also called **insights**) are the numbers a platform gives about your posts. Each one answers a different question:

| Metric | Answers |
|---|---|
| **Reach** | How many different accounts saw it? |
| **Impressions / views** | How many times was it seen in total? (One person can see it three times.) |
| **Engagements** | How many likes, comments, shares and saves? |
| **Saves** | Did people find it useful enough to keep? |
| **Shares** | Did people think it was worth passing on? |
| **Watch time / retention** | How long did people keep watching a video, and where did they leave? |
| **Link clicks** | Did people take the action we asked? |

**Engagement rate** lets you compare posts that reached different numbers of people:

> engagement rate = engagements ÷ reach × 100

A post reaching 2,000 with 60 engagements has a 3% rate; one reaching 400 with 40 engagements has 10%. The second post connected far better with the people who saw it, even though its raw number is smaller.

**Match the metric to the goal.** If the goal is *awareness*, reach matters. If it is *usefulness*, saves and shares matter more than likes — a save is a stronger signal than a quick tap. If it is *action* (registrations), count link clicks and actual sign-ups. Choosing the metric *after* you see the results, to make a post look good, is cheating yourself.

**Reading video retention.** A retention graph shows the percentage of viewers still watching at each second. A sharp drop in the first three seconds means a weak hook; a drop in the middle means a slow section.

**Traps to avoid:**

- **Small numbers.** With 40 views, one extra like changes the rate a lot. Look for patterns across several posts, not one result.
- **Unfair comparisons.** A post on a holiday, or one boosted with paid advertising, is not a fair comparison with an ordinary Tuesday post.
- **Vanity metrics.** Big numbers that feel good but do not connect to the goal.
- **Correlation is not cause.** "Posts with yellow did better" may be because they were all posted on Saturday.

**From numbers to a decision.** End every analysis with one sentence: *Because [evidence], next week we will [change].* For example: "Because our three tutorial reels averaged 40 saves and our event photos averaged 4, next week we will post two tutorials."

## Key words

- **Reach:** the number of different accounts that saw a post
- **Impressions:** the total number of times a post was seen
- **Engagement rate:** engagements divided by reach, times 100
- **Retention:** how much of a video viewers keep watching
- **Vanity metric:** a number that looks impressive but does not show progress towards the goal

## Read and watch

- [Google Digital Garage](https://learndigital.withgoogle.com/digitalgarage) — Google
- [YouTube Creators](https://www.youtube.com/creators/) — YouTube

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** calculate engagement rate for four posts first, then compare only those four.
- **If you already can:** plot the eight posts on a simple chart in Google Sheets and explain one pattern and one possible hidden cause.

## Learning online

You do not need your own social media account for any of this. Most platforms are for people aged 13 and over; if you are younger, or have no account, work with mock-ups or with an NGG account run by staff.

You will use a **sample analytics sheet** your mentor shares in the class folder, or anonymised figures from an NGG page — you do not need an account of your own.

- Open the sheet in Google Sheets (free, works on a phone browser or app). Add a column that calculates engagement rate with a formula such as `=C2/B2*100`.
- **Upload as evidence:** your completed sheet (or a screenshot), the ranking you chose and why, and your one-sentence decision.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your decision sentence. We will compare decisions — people often reach different conclusions from the same numbers, and we will discuss why.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Practise the formula: if a post reached 800 accounts and had 56 engagements, what is its engagement rate?

lessons.title: Community management and negative comments
lessons.summary: Managing a community means replying well, protecting people, and knowing when to respond, hide, report or escalate.
objectives: You will write replies that match a brand's voice
You will sort comments into respond, hide, report and escalate
You will draft simple community guidelines for an NGG page
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Posting is half the job; the other half happens in the comments. Today you learn to look after a community — welcoming people, handling complaints, and protecting members from harm.

## What to do

- Sort twelve sample comments into the four actions
- Write replies to four of them in NGG's voice
- Draft five community guidelines for an NGG page
- Role-play a complaint with a partner

## Understand it

A **community manager** looks after the people around a page: answering questions, celebrating members, calming problems and keeping the space safe. Good community management makes people want to come back.

**Respond quickly and in voice.** Questions and kind comments deserve replies — ideally within a day. Reply as the brand, warmly and clearly: "Thank you, Amaka! Registration is open until Friday — the link is in our bio."

**The four actions.** When a comment arrives, decide:

| Action | When | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Respond** | Questions, praise, fair complaints | "The venue changed and nobody told me!" |
| **Hide or delete** | Spam, scams, off-topic links | "Earn ₦500k a day, DM me" |
| **Report** | Harassment, hate, threats, sharing private details | Insults aimed at a member, a child's phone number |
| **Escalate** | Anything about safety, a serious complaint, the press | "Your instructor said something inappropriate" |

Always follow your organisation's own rules first. In NGG, **any concern about a child's safety goes straight to a staff member** — you do not handle it alone, argue it in public, or ask the child questions yourself.

**Handling a fair complaint — the LAST steps:**

1. **Listen** — read it fully; what actually happened?
2. **Acknowledge** — "You're right, we should have told everyone sooner."
3. **Solve** — what will you do? "We have messaged all families today."
4. **Take it offline** if details are personal — "We've sent you a private message so we can sort this out" — but never to hide a problem.

**What not to do:** argue, use sarcasm, delete fair criticism to look good, reply in anger, or reveal anyone's personal details in a reply. Screenshots last for ever.

**Trolls** are people who post to provoke. Do not feed them: one calm, factual reply if others might be misled, then hide or report if it continues.

**Look after yourself.** Reading unkind comments is hard, even when they are about a brand rather than you. Take breaks, share the load, and talk to an adult if something upsets you.

**Community guidelines** are a short public list of what is welcome and what is not — "Be kind", "No adverts", "No sharing anyone's personal details" — plus what happens if they are broken. Pinning them makes moderation fair, because everyone knows the rules in advance.

## Key words

- **Community manager:** the person who looks after the people around a page
- **Moderation:** checking and acting on what people post
- **Escalate:** pass a problem to someone with more responsibility
- **Troll:** someone who posts to provoke a reaction
- **Community guidelines:** public rules for how people should behave in a space

## Read and watch

- [How to stop cyberbullying](https://www.unicef.org/end-violence/how-to-stop-cyberbullying) — UNICEF
- [Internet Matters](https://www.internetmatters.org/) — Internet Matters

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** sort the comments and write two replies, one to praise and one to a fair complaint.
- **If you already can:** write replies for all four actions and a short note for staff explaining an escalation.

## Learning online

You do not need your own social media account for any of this. Most platforms are for people aged 13 and over; if you are younger, or have no account, work with mock-ups or with an NGG account run by staff.

Your mentor will share twelve **sample comments** in the class folder — they are invented, so there is no real person on the other end. Work on those, not on real pages.

- Make a table in Google Docs or Sheets: comment, action, reason, and your reply where you would respond.
- Role-play the complaint with a family member over a call or in person: they read the complaint, you reply aloud using LAST.
- **Upload as evidence:** your sorted table with four replies, and your five community guidelines.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** the comment you found hardest to decide about. We will discuss the grey areas together.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Look at the pinned rules or guidelines on one public community page and compare them with yours.

lessons.title: Misinformation: check before you share
lessons.summary: False information spreads faster than corrections, so pause, check the source, find better coverage and trace the claim before you share.
objectives: You will tell misinformation, disinformation and satire apart
You will use the SIFT method to check a claim
You will use reverse image search and a Nigerian fact-checker
lessons.body:
**Learn & practise.** Every forwarded message is a decision. Today you learn the habits professional fact-checkers use, so that you never become the person who spreads something false.

## What to do

- Classify six sample posts as true, false, misleading or satire
- Check two claims using the four SIFT moves
- Reverse-search one image to find where it first appeared
- Write a kind correction for a family WhatsApp group

## Understand it

**Three kinds of false or misleading content:**

- **Misinformation** — false information shared by someone who *believes* it is true. Your aunt forwarding a fake health cure is usually this.
- **Disinformation** — false information spread *on purpose* to deceive, often for money or politics.
- **Satire** — jokes in the style of news. Harmless when understood, harmful when screenshotted without the joke's context.

False content often travels faster than the truth because it is designed to cause strong feeling — fear, anger, excitement. Strong feeling is your signal to slow down.

**Warning signs:** "Forwarded many times"; urgent capitals ("SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS!!!"); no named source, or "a doctor friend said"; a too-good-to-be-true offer; a photo that seems to show today's event but looks older; a website address that copies a real one with one letter changed.

**The SIFT method** (developed by digital literacy expert Mike Caulfield):

1. **Stop.** Do not share yet. Ask: do I know this source?
2. **Investigate the source.** Who is behind it? Search the name of the website or account. Is it a real news organisation, a government body, or an anonymous page?
3. **Find better coverage.** Search the claim itself. Are reliable outlets reporting it? If something huge were true, many would be.
4. **Trace claims, quotes and media to the original.** Where did the photo or quote first appear? Was it from a different country or year?

**Reverse image search.** Google Lens, Bing Visual Search or TinEye show where else an image has appeared online. A "flood in Lagos today" photo that appeared online years ago in another country is a recycled image.

**Use fact-checkers.** Nigeria has independent fact-checking organisations, including **Dubawa** and **Africa Check**, which publish checks of claims circulating in Nigeria. Search their sites for the claim.

**Correcting kindly.** If a relative shares something false, a public "You're wrong!" rarely works. Try a private, respectful message: "I checked this one because I wanted to share it too — Africa Check says it's from 2019. Here's the link." Give the evidence, not a lecture.

**When it's your post.** If NGG posts something wrong, correct it clearly and openly — edit and say what changed. A quiet deletion leaves screenshots of the error without the correction.

## Key words

- **Misinformation:** false information shared by someone who believes it
- **Disinformation:** false information spread deliberately to deceive
- **Satire:** humour written in the style of real news
- **SIFT:** Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace to the original
- **Reverse image search:** searching with an image to find where else it appears

## Read and watch

- [Dubawa](https://dubawa.org/) — an independent Nigerian fact-checking organisation
- [Africa Check](https://africacheck.org/) — an independent African fact-checking organisation
- [News Literacy Project](https://newslit.org/) — resources on checking information

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do the Stop and Find-better-coverage moves on one claim, and one reverse image search.
- **If you already can:** check a claim in both English and a Nigerian language search, and compare what you find.

## Learning online

Everything here works in a phone browser without any social media account. Use the six **sample posts** in the class folder — do not go looking in strangers' groups. For reverse image search, open Google Lens in the Google app or images.google.com, or use tineye.com, and upload the sample image.

- Record your SIFT steps in a simple table: claim, source checked, better coverage found, original traced, verdict.
- **Upload as evidence:** your classification of the six sample posts, your two SIFT tables with the links you used, a screenshot of your reverse image search, and your kind correction message.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** the claim you checked and the single most useful link that settled it.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Next time something is forwarded to you, try just the first move — Stop — and see how often it changes what you do.

lessons.title: Capstone: an honest campaign for a community cause
lessons.summary: You plan and mock up a short social media campaign for a real community cause, with clear goals, consent, disclosure and a way to measure it.
objectives: You will plan a two-week campaign with a goal, audience, content and measures
You will apply honest disclosure for any partnership or sponsorship
You will present the campaign and evaluate it against its goal
lessons.body:
**Create & review.** This is the term's capstone. You bring together hooks, video, analytics, community care and fact-checking into one campaign for a cause that matters to your community — done honestly.

## What to do

- Choose a real cause with your team: a clean-up, a book drive, a vaccination reminder, a blood-donation day
- Write a campaign plan on one page
- Make at least four mock-up posts, including one short video
- Present your plan with how you would measure success

## Understand it

**Choose a cause with a real organiser.** Work with something genuine and local, confirmed by an adult: a community clean-up, a library book drive, a school's sports day, a health centre's reminder. Check every fact with the organiser — dates, places, what people should bring. A campaign built on a wrong date does harm.

**The one-page campaign plan:**

1. **Goal** — specific and measurable: "Get 40 families to bring books to the drive on 14 March", not "raise awareness".
2. **Audience** — who, where they are online, and what would motivate them.
3. **Key message** — one sentence everyone on the team can repeat.
4. **Content** — four to six posts over two weeks: an announcement, a "why it matters" post, a short video, a reminder, a thank-you and results.
5. **Channels** — where it will run. For many Nigerian communities, WhatsApp groups and Status matter as much as any platform.
6. **Measures** — what you will count: registrations, items collected, attendance, link clicks, shares.
7. **Risks** — consent, misinformation, negative comments — and how you will handle each.

**Honest influence and disclosure.** If a campaign is paid for, sponsored, or uses free products, the audience must be told clearly. A post that looks like a personal opinion but is really an advert misleads people. Good practice, set out by advertising regulators around the world, is to put a clear label such as **#ad** or **"Paid partnership with ..."** at the *start* of the post, not hidden among hashtags. In Nigeria, advertising is regulated by the **Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON)**. For a community cause, disclose partners too: "Books donated by ... Bookshop".

Honest influence also means:

- no fake urgency ("only 2 places left!" when there are 50);
- no invented statistics — cite where every number comes from;
- no images of people without consent, and never children's names with faces;
- no pressure on people who cannot afford to give.

**Measuring.** Before you start, write what success looks like. After, compare: did the posts with the most reach also produce the most action? What would you change? Report honestly — a campaign that missed its goal but taught you why is a useful result.

**Present** your plan, your mock-ups, your measures and your risk plan in five minutes, then take feedback using "I like / I wonder / What if".

## Key words

- **Campaign:** a planned series of messages working towards one goal
- **Key message:** the one sentence the whole campaign repeats
- **Disclosure:** clearly telling the audience about payment, sponsorship or gifts
- **ARCON:** the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria
- **Measurable goal:** a goal with a number and a date, so you can tell if it was met

## Read and watch

- [Disclosures 101 for social media influencers](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers) — US Federal Trade Commission
- [Google Digital Garage](https://learndigital.withgoogle.com/digitalgarage) — Google

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** plan four posts and one measure, and make two of the mock-ups.
- **If you already can:** add a WhatsApp broadcast plan and a results-post template, and explain how you would tell whether online activity caused real-world action.

## Learning online

You do not need your own social media account for any of this. Most platforms are for people aged 13 and over; if you are younger, or have no account, work with mock-ups or with an NGG account run by staff.

Your campaign is a **plan and mock-ups**; it will only be published if NGG staff choose to run it from a supervised NGG account, or the organiser does from theirs. Agree the cause with your mentor and get the facts from the organiser through a parent, guardian or mentor.

- Build the plan in Google Docs and the posts in Canva using social templates; make the video in CapCut or Canva and keep it under 60 seconds.
- Collaborate with teammates in a shared Canva or Google folder; label each piece with who made it.
- **Upload as evidence:** the one-page plan, four or more mock-up posts with captions and alt text, the short video, and your measures and risk plan.
- **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your presentation, ready to share your screen (and a PDF backup if your connection is weak).

## Before the next session

Complete the checks below, including the reflection. If your campaign is run for real, collect the results and bring them back — the evaluation is part of the work.

lessons.title: Contrast and accessibility: designs everyone can read
lessons.summary: Check that every word and every signal in your design can be read by people with low vision or colour blindness, not only by you on a bright screen.
objectives: You will measure the contrast of text against its background and fix anything below 4.5:1
You will test a design for colour blindness and stop relying on colour alone to carry meaning
You will redesign one of your earlier pieces so it passes both checks
lessons.body:
A design nobody can read has failed, however beautiful it looks. Somewhere in your audience is a grandmother with tired eyes, a boy who cannot tell red from green, and somebody reading your poster on a cracked phone under the Lagos sun. Today you design for all of them.

## What to do

- Open one design you made earlier in the Lab (a poster or social post).
- Check every piece of text with the WebAIM contrast checker and write down each ratio.
- Run the design through a colour-blindness simulator and note anything that disappears.
- Fix what fails, then put the before and after side by side.

## Understand it

**Contrast ratio** compares how light two colours are, from 1:1 (identical — invisible) to 21:1 (black on white). The international web accessibility standard, WCAG, sets two numbers you should know by heart:

- **4.5:1** for normal text — body copy, captions, the small print with the date and venue.
- **3:1** for large text (roughly 24px and above, or 19px bold) and for things that are not words but must be seen: the outline of a button, an icon, the line on a chart.

Contrast is about **lightness**, not hue. Red and green can be completely different colours and still have almost the same lightness, which is why red text on a green background can score below 2:1. A quick test with no tools: turn the design to greyscale (in Canva, apply the "Greyscale" filter to a copy; on a phone, take a screenshot and set it to black and white). If the words melt into the background in grey, the contrast is too low.

**Colour blindness** affects about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women. The most common kinds make reds and greens hard to separate. So:

- **Never let colour be the only signal.** A chart where "girls" is red and "boys" is green fails for those readers. Add labels, patterns or icons as well.
- **Safe pairs** usually mix a dark and a light colour from different families: dark blue with orange or yellow is readable by almost everyone. Red with green, and blue with purple, are the risky ones.
- **Test, don't guess.** A simulator shows you what the design looks like through different eyes.

Text over photographs is the commonest failure in posters. The photo has light and dark patches, so part of your headline is readable and part is not. Fix it with a solid shape behind the text, a dark overlay on the photo (about 40–60% transparent black), or by moving the text to the plainest area of the picture.

Finally, **size and weight** matter too. Thin, fancy script fonts at small sizes fail even when the colour is perfect. Keep body text plain and big enough to read at arm's length.

## Key words

- **Contrast ratio:** a number comparing the lightness of two colours, from 1:1 to 21:1
- **WCAG:** the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the international standard for readable digital design
- **Colour blindness:** difficulty telling certain colours apart, most often red and green
- **Overlay:** a see-through layer placed over a photo to make text on it readable

## Read and watch

- [Contrast checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — WebAIM
- [Understanding contrast (minimum)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html) — W3C, the people who write the standard
- [Understanding use of colour](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/use-of-color.html) — W3C

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** check just the headline and one line of small text first, and fix those two before anything else.
- **If you already can:** design a small chart or key (say, results of a class vote) that works perfectly in greyscale, using labels and patterns instead of colour.

## Learning online

Everything here works on a phone or laptop with free tools. Use the WebAIM checker in your browser: in Canva, click a colour to see its hex code (such as #1A4C8B) and paste it into the checker. For colour blindness, upload a screenshot of your design to a free online simulator such as Coblis. **Upload as evidence:** your before and after images side by side, plus a short list of the ratios you measured before and after. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** the one fix you were least sure about — we will look at it together on screen and vote on whether it now passes.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below, and keep your before-and-after pair: you will use it again in your portfolio piece.

materials.guide: Paste two hex codes in and read the ratio. Normal text needs 4.5:1; large text and icons need 3:1.

materials.title: Coblis colour-blindness simulator
materials.guide: Upload a screenshot of your design and switch between the types. Note anything that disappears.

materials.title: Understanding use of colour (W3C)

checks.prompt: Your poster uses red text on a green background. The colours look very different to you. Why might it still fail?
options: Red and green can be equally light, so contrast is low
Red and green are complementary, so they always clash when printed
Bright colours look blurry on most phone screens at night
Red text is not allowed by the WCAG standard at any size
checks.answer: Red and green can be equally light, so contrast is low
whys: Complementary colours can still contrast well in lightness; the problem is lightness, not where they sit on the wheel.
Screens are not the issue; readers with full colour vision may still struggle if lightness is similar.
WCAG sets ratios, not banned colours. Red text can pass on a light enough background.

checks.prompt: Which minimum contrast does WCAG ask for normal-sized body text?
whys: 3:1 is for large text and for icons and outlines, not normal text.
7:1 is the stricter AAA level, not the minimum.
2.5:1 is far too low; most people would struggle to read it.

checks.prompt: A chart shows girls in red and boys in green with no labels. What is the best fix?
options: Make both colours much brighter so they stand out more
Add labels or patterns so colour is not the only signal
Swap the colours so the boys are red and the girls green
Make the chart bigger so each colour covers more space
checks.answer: Add labels or patterns so colour is not the only signal

checks.prompt: Use the WebAIM contrast checker on the headline and the smallest text in one of your designs. Write down both pairs of hex codes and both ratios, and say whether each passes.
checks.rubric: Up to 4 points: two real hex pairs recorded (1); both ratios recorded correctly (1); pass or fail judged against the right threshold — 4.5:1 for small text, 3:1 for large (2).

checks.prompt: Redesign one earlier piece so every text passes 4.5:1 (or 3:1 if large) and nothing relies on colour alone. Upload the before and after side by side with one sentence naming the biggest fix.
checks.answer: A before/after pair and one sentence naming a specific change (e.g. 'added a dark overlay behind the headline').
checks.rubric: Up to 6 points: every text in the 'after' passes the right threshold (2); nothing depends on colour alone — labels, icons or patterns added where needed (2); the sentence names a real, specific fix and why (2).

lessons.title: Icons and simple illustration: vector and raster
lessons.summary: Draw clean, simple icons with free vector tools and learn when a design needs vector shapes and when it needs pixels.
objectives: You will explain the difference between vector and raster images and choose the right one for a job
You will draw a set of three matching icons in a free vector tool
You will keep a set of icons consistent in line weight, corners and size
lessons.body:
Look at the signs in a hospital, a bank app or a danfo bus park sticker: tiny pictures that say "toilet", "pay", "no smoking" in a second, in any language. Today you learn how those are made, and you draw your own.

## What to do

- Zoom right in on a photo and on a logo, and see the difference for yourself.
- Pick a theme (for example, a market stall: fish, pepper, phone credit).
- Sketch three icons on paper first, as simple as you can.
- Redraw them in Figma, Inkscape or Canva using basic shapes, with one line weight for all three.

## Understand it

There are two ways a computer stores a picture.

A **raster** image (also called a bitmap) is a grid of tiny coloured squares called **pixels**. Photos are raster. Zoom in far enough and you see the squares; stretch a small raster image and it goes blurry or blocky. Common raster formats are JPG and PNG. Raster is right for photographs and painted textures.

A **vector** image is stored as instructions: "a circle here, this size, filled blue; a line from here to there". Because it is maths, not pixels, the computer redraws it sharply at any size — the same logo works on a business card and on a billboard on Third Mainland Bridge. Common vector formats are SVG, PDF and AI. Vector is right for logos, icons, diagrams and lettering.

Free tools:

- **Figma** (browser, free account) — great for icons and layouts; works well on a laptop.
- **Inkscape** (free download for Windows, Mac and Linux) — a full vector drawing program.
- **Photopea** (browser, free) — mostly for raster editing, like Photoshop, but it can handle simple shapes.
- **Canva** — has basic shapes you can combine, though less control.

Good icons follow a few rules:

- **Simplify.** Keep only what makes the thing recognisable. A fish needs a body, a tail and an eye, not every scale.
- **Build from shapes.** Circles, rectangles, rounded rectangles and lines. Combine and cut them (Figma calls this "boolean" operations; Inkscape calls them Path → Union, Difference).
- **Be consistent.** In a set, use the same stroke (line) weight, the same corner roundness and the same overall size, drawn on the same square grid (for example 24 × 24). One thick icon among thin ones looks like a mistake.
- **Test small.** Shrink the icon to the size of a fingernail. If you cannot tell what it is, simplify again.

You can also use free icon libraries such as Google's Material Symbols, but check the licence and say where icons came from. Drawing your own is how you learn.

## Key words

- **Raster:** an image made of a grid of pixels; blurs when enlarged
- **Vector:** an image stored as shapes and lines; stays sharp at any size
- **Stroke:** the line around or through a shape, with a set thickness
- **Icon set:** a group of icons that share one style

## Read and watch

- [Vector graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_graphics) — Wikipedia overview
- [Inkscape tutorials](https://inkscape.org/learn/tutorials/) — the Inkscape project
- [Material Symbols](https://fonts.google.com/icons) — Google's free icon library, a model of a consistent set

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** draw one icon only, from two or three shapes, and get it perfectly clean.
- **If you already can:** draw a set of six for a real place you know (a clinic, a school, a market) and test them on three people who have not seen the brief.

## Learning online

On a laptop, make a free Figma account in the browser or install Inkscape. On a phone only, use Canva's shapes or Photopea in the browser, zoomed in. Draw on a 24 × 24 frame. **Upload as evidence:** a photo of your paper sketches, an image of your three finished icons side by side, and the same icons shown very small. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your icons with no labels — classmates will guess what each one means, and any one they get wrong is the one to simplify.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below and keep your vector file: you can reuse your icons in the leaflet lesson.
