lessons.title: Image editing for design: cut-outs, crops and file formats
lessons.summary: Prepare photos for a design — cut out a subject, crop with purpose, keep enough resolution — and export in the right file format.
objectives: You will cut a subject out from its background and place it cleanly in a design
You will check whether an image has enough resolution for its job
You will choose between PNG, JPG, SVG and PDF for a given use
lessons.body:
The best designs often use one strong photo — a product, a face, a plate of jollof — sitting cleanly on a simple background. Getting it there is a craft: cutting it out neatly, cropping with a purpose, and saving it so it stays sharp and loads fast.

## What to do

- Photograph a small object at home (a shoe, a drink, a fruit) against a plain wall, in good daylight.
- Cut it out in Photopea, Canva or a free background remover.
- Place it on a plain coloured background with a short headline.
- Export the design twice — once as JPG and once as PNG — and compare the size and quality.

## Understand it

**Cut-outs.** A cut-out removes the background so only the subject is left. Automatic removers are fast but check the edges: hair, fingers and shiny objects often come out ragged. In Photopea, use *Select → Subject* or the Magic Wand, then refine the edge; zoom to 200% and look around the outline. A clean photo makes a clean cut-out — a plain, contrasting background and good light save you an hour of fixing.

**Cropping with purpose.** Crop to remove distractions and to put the subject where the layout needs it, not just to fit the frame. Leave space on the side the subject faces, so it "looks into" the design. Never stretch a photo to fit — hold Shift (or lock the ratio) so it stays in proportion. A squashed face is the quickest way to make a design look amateur.

**Resolution.** A raster image only has so many pixels. To check whether it is enough, work out how big it will appear:

- For **screen**, the image should be at least as many pixels as the space it fills. A 1080 × 1080 Instagram post needs a photo at least 1080 pixels wide.
- For **print**, aim for **300 pixels per inch**. A photo printed 4 inches wide needs about 1200 pixels across.

You cannot add real detail by enlarging. If a WhatsApp-forwarded image is 640 pixels wide, it will be soft on an A4 flyer whatever you do — ask for the original.

**File formats.**

- **JPG** — best for photos on screen. Small files, but it loses a little detail each time it is saved (lossy) and cannot be see-through.
- **PNG** — best for graphics with text, flat colour, and cut-outs, because it keeps sharp edges and supports **transparency**. Files are bigger for photos.
- **SVG** — vector, for logos and icons on websites. Stays sharp at any size.
- **PDF** — the safe format to send to a printer; it keeps fonts, vectors and images together exactly as you laid them out.

Always keep your **original** file and edit a copy. Name files clearly: `mama-put-flyer-v2.png`, not `IMG_0042 final final.png`.

## Key words

- **Cut-out:** a subject with its background removed
- **Resolution:** how many pixels an image has, which sets how large it can appear sharply
- **Transparency:** see-through areas in an image, supported by PNG but not JPG
- **Lossy compression:** making a file smaller by throwing away some detail, as JPG does

## Read and watch

- [Photopea learning pages](https://www.photopea.com/learn/) — Photopea
- [Image file type and format guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Formats/Image_types) — MDN Web Docs
- [Image resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_resolution) — Wikipedia overview

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use an automatic background remover, then spend your time on placing and cropping well.
- **If you already can:** cut out something hard (hair, a bicycle, a glass bottle) by hand and compare it with an automatic tool's result.

## Learning online

All of this works in a browser: Photopea for cutting and cropping, Canva for the layout. On a phone, Canva's background remover is in its paid plan, so use Photopea in the browser or a free web remover instead. Check pixel size in Photopea under *Image → Image Size*. **Upload as evidence:** your original photo, the finished design, and a screenshot showing the file sizes of the JPG and PNG versions. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your cut-out zoomed to 200% — we will look at the edges together and fix one live.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Keep your cut-out PNG: a clean product shot is useful in the leaflet project.

lessons.title: Print versus screen: DPI, bleed and CMYK
lessons.summary: Set a design up so it prints the way it looks on screen — the right resolution, a bleed around the edge, and colours a printer can actually make.
objectives: You will explain the difference between RGB and CMYK colour and why bright screen colours can print dull
You will set up a print file with bleed, trim and a safe margin
You will export a print-ready PDF and check it before sending it to a printer
lessons.body:
Every business street in Nigeria has a print shop with a big machine and a queue. Hand them a file that is not set up properly and you get white slivers at the edges, words cut off, and colours that look muddy. Today you learn to hand over a file that prints right the first time.

## What to do

- Set up an A5 flyer (148 × 210 mm) in Canva or Inkscape with a 3 mm bleed.
- Put a background colour or photo right out to the bleed edge.
- Keep all text inside a safe margin of at least 5 mm from the trim.
- Export as a print PDF, then open it and check every edge.

## Understand it

**Screens and printers make colour differently.** A screen shines light: red, green and blue (**RGB**) mixed together. A printer puts ink on paper: cyan, magenta, yellow and black (**CMYK**). Ink can't reach some of the bright, glowing colours a screen can — electric blues, neon greens and hot pinks often print duller. Canva's free plan exports in RGB, and most print shops convert it for you, so the practical lesson is: **expect bright colours to soften**, and if a colour really matters (a brand's exact green), ask the printer for a test print.

**Resolution for print** is measured in **DPI** (dots per inch) or PPI (pixels per inch). Screens look fine at 72–150; print needs about **300**. A logo grabbed from a website is usually far too small — ask for the vector file.

**Bleed, trim and safe area.** Paper is printed on a big sheet and then cut by a guillotine that can wander a millimetre or two. So:

- **Trim line** — where the paper is meant to be cut (the finished size).
- **Bleed** — an extra strip, usually **3 mm**, beyond the trim on every side. Any background colour or photo that touches the edge must extend into it, so a slightly-off cut never leaves a white line.
- **Safe area** — a margin inside the trim, at least **3–5 mm**, where all important text and logos stay, so a slightly-off cut never slices a phone number.

In Canva: *File → Settings → Show print bleed*, and export with *PDF Print* and "Crop marks and bleed" ticked. In Inkscape, add the bleed to the page size and use guides.

**Black text.** Small text should be plain black, not a dark photo-grey or a "rich" mix, so it prints crisp.

**Proofread before printing.** On screen you forgive mistakes; on 500 copies you can't. Print one copy on a home or office printer first, at actual size, and read every word, especially phone numbers and prices.

## Key words

- **RGB:** red, green, blue — how screens make colour with light
- **CMYK:** cyan, magenta, yellow, black — how printers make colour with ink
- **Bleed:** extra image beyond the cut line so no white edge shows
- **Safe area:** the inner margin where important text must stay
- **DPI:** dots per inch, a measure of print resolution

## Read and watch

- [Bleed (printing)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleed_(printing)) — Wikipedia
- [CMYK colour model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMYK_color_model) — Wikipedia
- [Dots per inch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dots_per_inch) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** concentrate on one thing — a 3 mm bleed with nothing important near the edge.
- **If you already can:** visit or phone a local print shop and ask what file they prefer (PDF? which bleed? CMYK?), then set up your file to their exact rules.

## Learning online

You can set up and export a print PDF entirely in Canva in a browser, or in Inkscape on a laptop. If you can, print a copy at home or at a business centre and trim it with scissors on the trim line to see what bleed does. **Upload as evidence:** your print PDF, and a screenshot of it with bleed and margins showing. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your PDF opened on screen — we will run a group "printer's check": edges, safe area, resolution and spelling.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Next week you design a leaflet for a real business, so keep this print setup as your template.

lessons.title: Design for a real client: a leaflet or menu for a local business
lessons.summary: Interview a real local business, write a short brief, and design a two-page leaflet or menu that helps their customers decide and buy.
objectives: You will interview a real client and turn what they say into a written brief
You will organise lots of information — items, prices, contacts — so it is easy to scan
You will present your design to the client, take feedback and make one revision
lessons.body:
Until now you have designed for yourself and your teacher. Today you design for somebody who has to sell something: the woman who runs the buka down the road, the barber, the phone-repair stand, the church bookshop. Their customers will judge your work in three seconds, standing at a counter.

## What to do

- Choose a real small business you can reach (a family member's, a neighbour's, one near your centre).
- Ask the owner the brief questions below and write their answers down.
- Design a two-page leaflet or a menu (front and back of an A5 or folded A4).
- Show it to the owner, write down their feedback, and make one round of changes.

## Understand it

**The brief comes first.** Before you open any tool, ask:

1. What do you sell, and what do you most want people to buy?
2. Who are your customers? (Students? Office workers? Mothers on the school run?)
3. What should someone do after reading this — call, come in, order on WhatsApp?
4. What must appear? (Name, logo, address, opening hours, phone, prices.)
5. Do you have colours, a logo or photos already?

Write the answers as a one-paragraph **brief**. It protects you both: when you disagree later, you go back to what you agreed.

**Organise before you decorate.** A menu or leaflet is mostly information. Group it:

- **Sections** with clear headings — Soups, Swallow, Proteins, Drinks; or Haircuts, Beard, Kids.
- **Consistent item lines** — name, short description if needed, price lined up on the right so the eye runs down a column.
- **One highlight** — the dish or service the owner most wants to sell gets a box, a photo or bigger type. Only one; if everything is highlighted, nothing is.
- **Contacts where they can be found** — on the back or the bottom of every page, large enough to read and type into a phone.

Use what you have learnt: a grid and alignment, two typefaces at most, a palette with an accent, 4.5:1 contrast, cut-out photos, bleed and safe area.

**Fold matters.** A folded A4 becomes a front cover, an inside spread and a back. The cover must make someone pick it up; the inside does the selling; the back carries the map, phone and hours.

**Working with a client.** Present the design and explain *why* you made each choice ("the price column lines up so people compare quickly"). Then listen. Write their feedback in their words. Some requests will improve it; some ("make everything bigger and red") need a kind explanation and a compromise. Always check every price and phone number with the owner — a wrong price on 500 menus costs real money.

## Key words

- **Client:** the person or business you are designing for
- **Brief:** a short written agreement of what the design must do
- **Revision:** a changed version made after feedback
- **Spread:** two pages seen side by side when a leaflet is open

## Read and watch

- [F-shaped pattern of reading](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/f-shaped-pattern-reading-web-content/) — Nielsen Norman Group: how people scan, not read
- [Menu engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menu_engineering) — Wikipedia: how menus are designed to guide choices

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** design a one-sided price list first, with sections, aligned prices and contacts, before attempting a fold.
- **If you already can:** produce a full tri-fold leaflet and a matching social post, and ask the client to try both with customers for a week.

## Learning online

You can do the interview by phone or WhatsApp voice note — ask the five brief questions and record the answers (with permission). Design in Canva or Inkscape and send the owner a PDF or screenshots for feedback. **Upload as evidence:** the written brief, the first design, the owner's feedback in their words, and the revised design. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** the hardest piece of feedback you got and how you answered it — we will discuss real client conversations together.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. If the owner wants to print your design, do the printer's check from last lesson first.

lessons.title: A portfolio piece, with critique
lessons.summary: Choose your strongest design from the term, improve it after a structured critique, and present it as a portfolio page that explains your thinking.
objectives: You will give and receive critique that is specific, kind and useful
You will improve a finished piece in response to feedback
You will write a short case study that explains the problem, your choices and the result
lessons.body:
A designer is judged by their portfolio: a small set of their best work, each piece with a short story of how it was made. Today you start yours. One piece, done properly, is worth more than ten you are not proud of.

## What to do

- Choose your strongest design from this term (the client leaflet is a good candidate).
- Present it to a partner or small group for a structured critique (below), and give critique on theirs.
- Make the improvements you agree with.
- Build a one-page portfolio entry: the final image plus a short case study.

## Understand it

**Critique is not criticism.** Its goal is to make the work better, not to judge the person. A useful critique follows a simple structure:

1. **The designer states the goal** — "This menu should help office workers order quickly at lunch."
2. **Reviewers say what works** and why — "The prices line up, so I can compare fast."
3. **Reviewers ask questions and name problems** against the goal, not personal taste — "I couldn't find the phone number; is it on the back?" is useful. "I don't like green" is not, unless you say why it hurts the goal.
4. **The designer listens and writes it down.** Don't defend each point on the spot. Afterwards, decide which notes to act on.

A good phrase to use is "I notice… I wonder… What if…": *I notice* the headline and subheading are the same size. *I wonder* which one I should read first. *What if* the headline were twice as big?

**Before and after.** Keep your version before the critique. Showing both is powerful in a portfolio because it proves you can take feedback and improve — that's what clients and employers want to see.

**The case study.** Under your image, write 100–200 words in four short parts:

- **The problem:** who it was for and what it had to do.
- **The process:** research, sketches, the client conversation.
- **The decisions:** two or three choices and why (type, colour, layout, accessibility).
- **The result:** what happened — the owner printed it, customers used it, what you would do next.

**Present it well.** Show the work large, on a plain background. For print pieces, a photo of the real printed object on a table looks far better than a flat screenshot. Credit anyone else involved and any photos or icons you did not make.

**Where to keep it.** A free Behance or Canva website page, a shared Google Drive folder, or a simple PDF all work. What matters is that you can send someone a single link.

## Key words

- **Portfolio:** a small collection of your best work, presented with explanations
- **Critique:** structured feedback measured against the goal of the work
- **Case study:** a short written account of a project's problem, process and result
- **Iteration:** improving a design in rounds

## Read and watch

- [Design critiques](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/design-critiques/) — Nielsen Norman Group
- [Behance](https://www.behance.net/) — a free platform where designers publish portfolios; browse case studies for ideas

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** write the case study as four sentences, one for each part, and focus on a clear before-and-after.
- **If you already can:** build a three-piece portfolio page with a consistent layout and a short "about me" line, and send the link to one adult whose opinion you trust.

## Learning online

Critique works online too. Post your design in your class group (or share your screen in the live class) and ask two classmates to reply using "I notice… I wonder… What if…". Build your portfolio page free in Canva (a one-page website or PDF) or on Behance. **Upload as evidence:** your before and after images, the critique notes you received, and the link or PDF of your portfolio entry. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** a one-minute spoken presentation of your piece — the group will give one "I notice" and one "What if" each.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Keep your portfolio link safe; you will add to it every term.

lessons.title: Story structure in pictures: sequencing a photo series
lessons.summary: Arrange a small set of photographs so they tell a story in order — an opening, a build-up and an ending — without needing many words.
objectives: You will plan a picture story using establishing, detail, action and closing shots
You will put a set of images in an order that builds and resolves
You will test whether a sequence makes sense to someone who has not heard the story
lessons.body:
You already know a story has a beginning, middle and end. With pictures, the order you place them in IS the storytelling — swap two photos and the meaning changes. Today you learn to sequence, using one ordinary event: someone making a meal, fixing a bicycle, getting ready for school.

## What to do

- Choose a short real event you can photograph at home or nearby, start to finish, in under an hour.
- Take 15–25 photos using the shot types below.
- Choose the best six and arrange them in order.
- Show the six, without words, to someone who wasn't there, and ask them to tell you the story back.

## Understand it

Photo editors and film-makers build sequences from a small set of shot types. Each does a different job:

- **Establishing shot** — wide. Where are we? A whole compound, a market street, a kitchen. It sets the scene.
- **Medium shot** — a person doing something, from the waist up. Who is this, and what are they doing?
- **Detail (close-up) shot** — hands kneading dough, a spanner on a bolt, a pen on a page. Details give texture and feeling.
- **Action shot** — the moment of change: the fire catches, the chain goes on, the bus arrives.
- **Portrait or reaction** — a face that tells us how it feels.
- **Closing shot** — the result or a quiet ending: the plate served, the bicycle ridden away, an empty street at dusk.

A simple sequence of six might be: establishing → medium → detail → action → reaction → closing. That gives you a **beginning** (where and who), a **middle** (the work, the problem, the change) and an **end** (the result).

**Sequencing rules of thumb:**

- **Vary the distance.** Wide, then close, then medium. Three wide shots in a row feel flat; the change of distance keeps the eye moving.
- **Each picture must earn its place.** If two photos say the same thing, keep the stronger one.
- **Juxtaposition makes meaning.** Two images side by side make the viewer connect them. A photo of an empty water bucket next to a photo of a girl walking with a full one tells a story neither tells alone. Film-makers call this the **Kuleshov effect**: viewers read emotion into a face depending on what image comes before it.
- **End strongly.** The last picture is what people remember. Don't finish on a weak photo just because it happened last.

You don't have to follow time exactly. You can open with the strongest moment (the finished meal) and then go back to how it was made — but make it clear.

**Test it.** If a viewer can tell the story back without your explanation, the sequence works. If they get lost, find the missing step — usually an establishing shot or the action moment.

## Key words

- **Sequence:** a set of images placed in a deliberate order
- **Establishing shot:** a wide picture that shows where the story happens
- **Detail shot:** a close-up of a small, telling part of the scene
- **Juxtaposition:** placing two images together so they create meaning

## Read and watch

- [Photo-essay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photo-essay) — Wikipedia
- [Kuleshov effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuleshov_effect) — Wikipedia
- [Storyboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storyboard) — Wikipedia: how film-makers plan sequences in pictures

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** make a sequence of four: establishing, detail, action, closing.
- **If you already can:** make two different sequences from the same photos — one hopeful, one worrying — and explain how the order changed the meaning.

## Learning online

Your phone camera is enough. Ask permission before photographing anyone (see the portraits lesson). To arrange your six, put them in order in a Google Slides deck, a Canva grid or a phone collage app, numbered 1–6. **Upload as evidence:** your six-image sequence in order, a one-line label for each shot type, and the story your test viewer told back to you (in their words). **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your six photos in a *shuffled* order — classmates will try to put them back, and we will compare their order with yours.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below and keep your unused photos: an alternative image is often the fix.

materials.guide: Read the introduction. Notice that the order and the captions together carry the story.

lessons.title: Comics and photo-comics: panels, gutters and speech
lessons.summary: Tell a short story in comic form — drawn or with your own photos — using panels, gutters, speech balloons and captions.
objectives: You will use panels and gutters to control time and pace in a comic
You will add speech balloons and captions that are easy to read in the right order
You will make a one-page comic or photo-comic of six to eight panels
lessons.body:
Comics are one of the most powerful ways to tell a story: they work in any language, people of every age read them, and campaigns across Africa use them to explain health, rights and money. You don't need to draw well — a photo-comic made with friends and a phone is a real comic.

## What to do

- Write a tiny story with a problem and a turn — for example, a younger brother who keeps losing his school shoe, or a friend who nearly falls for a WhatsApp scam.
- Sketch it as six to eight rough boxes on paper (stick figures are fine). This is your thumbnail.
- Draw it properly, or act it out and photograph each panel with friends or family (with their permission).
- Assemble the page in Canva, Google Slides or on paper, and add speech balloons and captions.

## Understand it

**Panels** are the boxes. Each panel is a moment. **Gutters** are the gaps between them — and that is where the magic happens. The reader's mind fills in what happens between two panels. Scott McCloud, who wrote *Understanding Comics*, calls this **closure**: panel one shows a raised hand, panel two shows a broken plate, and the reader supplies the drop.

**Controlling time and pace:**

- **More panels for one action** slows time down (suspense).
- **One big panel** gives a moment weight — use it for the turning point.
- **A wide panel** can feel like a long pause or a big place.
- **Wider gutters** can suggest more time passing.

**Reading order.** In English-language comics we read left to right, top to bottom — a Z shape. Lay panels in a clear grid (a simple 2 × 3 or 3 × 3) so nobody reads them in the wrong order.

**Words in comics:**

- **Speech balloons** hold what characters say. The tail points to the speaker's mouth. Put the balloon of whoever speaks first at the top left, so the order of reading matches the order of speaking.
- **Thought bubbles** (cloud-shaped) show what a character thinks.
- **Captions** (boxes, usually at the top or bottom of a panel) hold the narrator's voice: "Later that day…".
- **Sound effects** (*KPAK! WHOOSH!*) are drawn as part of the picture.

**Keep words short.** A balloon of more than about 20–25 words takes over the panel. If a character has a lot to say, split it across panels. Use a clear, plain font (or neat capital letters by hand) with dark text on white balloons for contrast.

**Photo-comics.** Plan each photo like a panel: who is in it, how close, which way they face, where the balloon will go. Leave empty space for the balloon — usually above the heads. Shoot each panel two or three times so you can choose.

## Key words

- **Panel:** one box or frame in a comic, showing one moment
- **Gutter:** the space between panels where the reader imagines what happens
- **Closure:** the reader filling in the action between panels
- **Speech balloon:** the shape holding a character's words, with a tail to the speaker
- **Caption:** a box with narration rather than speech

## Read and watch

- [The visual magic of comics](https://www.ted.com/talks/scott_mccloud_the_visual_magic_of_comics) — Scott McCloud, TED talk
- [Understanding Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Understanding_Comics) — Wikipedia summary of McCloud's book
- [Speech balloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_balloon) — Wikipedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** make a four-panel strip with one speech balloon per panel.
- **If you already can:** make a full page that uses one large panel for the turning point and at least one wordless panel, and explain why.

## Learning online

On a phone or laptop, make the page in Canva (search the "comic strip" templates, or use a grid) or Google Slides with shapes for balloons. For a photo-comic, ask family at home to act; always get permission and don't post anyone's photo publicly without it. **Upload as evidence:** your paper thumbnail and the finished comic page as an image or PDF. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your comic with the balloons blanked out — classmates will guess what each character says, and we will compare with your words.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Keep the comic — it is a good candidate for a portfolio piece.

materials.title: The visual magic of comics (TED)
materials.guide: Watch how McCloud explains what happens 'between' panels. Find one place in your comic where the gutter does the work.

materials.title: Speech balloon

checks.prompt: Panel one shows a boy kicking a ball towards a window. Panel two shows the boy's mother holding broken glass. What is the reader doing in the gutter between them?

Imagining the ball breaking the window
Skipping a missing panel by mistake
Waiting for the sound effect to appear
checks.answer: Imagining the ball breaking the window
whys: There is no caption — the reader works it out alone.
Nothing is missing; the gap is deliberate.
The reader doesn't need a sound effect to understand it.

checks.prompt: Two characters speak in one panel. Where should the first speaker's balloon go?
options: Top left, so it is read first
Bottom right, near the edge of the panel
In the centre, over the faces
Anywhere, as long as the tail points to them
checks.answer: Top left, so it is read first

checks.prompt: You want the moment a character makes a big decision to feel important. What is the strongest choice?
options: Give it one large panel
Fill it with as many words as possible
Make the gutter around it disappear
Put it in very small text at the bottom
checks.answer: Give it one large panel

checks.prompt: Make a one-page comic or photo-comic of six to eight panels with a problem and a turn. Upload your thumbnail sketch and the finished page.
checks.answer: Thumbnail plus finished 6–8 panel page with readable balloons and captions.
checks.rubric: Up to 8 points: clear story with a problem and a turn (2); panels read in an obvious order (2); balloons short, readable and in speaking order (2); at least one deliberate choice about pace — a big panel, a wordless panel or a sequence that slows time (2).

lessons.title: Infographics that tell a true story with data
lessons.summary: Find real numbers from a trustworthy source and turn them into a clear, honest infographic with one main message.
objectives: You will find data from a reliable source and credit it properly
You will choose the right chart for your message and draw it honestly
You will design an infographic with one clear headline and no misleading tricks
lessons.body:
Numbers can move people — but only if they understand them, and only if they are true. A good infographic takes real data and makes one point obvious at a glance. A bad one confuses or, worse, lies. Today you make one that is clear *and* honest.

## What to do

- Pick a question you care about: how many children are in school in your state? How much has the price of bread changed? How many people use mobile money?
- Find the numbers from a reliable source (see below) and write down where they came from.
- Decide your **one** main message in a single sentence.
- Design a portrait infographic (for a phone screen or A4) with a headline, one to three charts or figures, and a source line.

## Understand it

**Start with a trustworthy source.** Good places include the National Bureau of Statistics (nigerianstat.gov.ng), UNICEF and the World Bank, Our World in Data, and reports from universities or major newspapers that cite their sources. A number in a viral WhatsApp image with no source is not data. Always note **who** collected it, **when**, and **what exactly** was measured.

**One message.** Write your headline as a sentence that states the finding: "More girls than ever are finishing primary school in Nigeria" is better than "Education statistics". Everything on the page supports that one sentence.

**Choose the right chart:**

- **Bar chart** — compare amounts between groups (states, years, items).
- **Line chart** — show change over time.
- **A single big number** with a short explanation — when one figure is the story ("1 in 3").
- **Icon array** — show a proportion with little figures (10 people, 3 coloured in). Very clear for "1 in 3" and good for audiences who find charts hard.
- **Pie chart** — only for parts of one whole, and only with two to four slices. Otherwise use bars.

**Honesty rules.** These are the classic ways charts mislead — never do them:

- **A bar chart whose axis doesn't start at zero.** Bars are read by length; cutting the bottom off makes a small difference look huge.
- **Cherry-picking years** to hide a pattern you don't like.
- **3D effects** that distort sizes.
- **Comparing things that aren't comparable** — totals for a big state against a small one, when the fair comparison is per person.
- **Pictures scaled by height and width** when the number only doubled — a doubled sack drawn twice as tall *and* wide looks four times bigger.

**Design it clearly.** Big headline, plenty of space, labels directly on the bars instead of a separate legend, colour used for meaning (one highlight colour for the point you are making, grey for the rest), and contrast of at least 4.5:1. Finish with a **source line**: "Source: National Bureau of Statistics, 2023."

## Key words

- **Infographic:** a visual that explains information or data quickly
- **Axis:** the line along the side or bottom of a chart showing the scale
- **Proportion:** a part compared with the whole, such as 1 in 4
- **Source line:** a short credit saying where the data came from

## Read and watch

- [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/) — free, well-sourced charts on almost every global topic
- [Misleading graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misleading_graph) — Wikipedia: the tricks to avoid, with examples
- [National Bureau of Statistics](https://www.nigerianstat.gov.ng/) — Nigeria's official statistics

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** make an infographic with one big number, one sentence and one icon array.
- **If you already can:** make two versions of one chart — one honest and one misleading — and explain exactly what makes the second misleading.

## Learning online

Find data in your browser at Our World in Data (each chart has a "Download" tab with the numbers and source). Build charts in Google Sheets or Canva's chart tool, then lay out the infographic in Canva. If your data needs a calculation (for example per 100 people), show your working in a notes box. **Upload as evidence:** the finished infographic, a screenshot or link to your data source, and your one-sentence message. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** your infographic and one number you were not sure how to show — we will try two chart types for it together.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below. Keep your source links: a claim without a source is not finished.

Start the axis at zero; bars are read by length
Turn it into a pie chart of the two years

A pie chart is for parts of one whole, not change over time.

lessons.title: The ethics of images: consent, dignity and honesty
lessons.summary: Decide what you should and should not photograph, publish and edit — so that the people in your pictures are respected and your audience is told the truth.
objectives: You will explain informed consent and the extra care needed with children and vulnerable people
You will recognise images that strip people of dignity, such as 'poverty imagery', and choose a respectful alternative
You will tell the difference between an honest edit and a misleading one, and caption truthfully
lessons.body:
A camera gives you power: the power to decide how somebody is seen by strangers, perhaps for ever. You have already learnt to ask before taking a portrait. Today goes further — what you choose to show, how you show it, and what you change afterwards.

## What to do

- Read the three scenarios below and decide, with a partner or on your own, what you would do in each.
- Look through some news, charity or social posts about Africa and find one image you think respects its subject and one you think does not.
- Rewrite a caption or redesign a post so it treats its subject with dignity.
- Write your own five-line code of ethics for your photography.

## Understand it

**Informed consent** means the person understands what the photo is for, where it will appear, and that they can say no — and then agrees. A nod while you're already shooting is not informed consent. For **children**, you need a parent or guardian's permission as well as the child's own agreement. Be extra careful with people who are sick, grieving, in trouble with the law, or in a crisis: they may not be able to say no freely. Remember that once something is online, you cannot fully take it back.

**Dignity.** For decades, images of Africa sent abroad have often shown people only as victims — a crying child with flies, a mother in a queue for food — with no name and no voice. This is sometimes called **"poverty porn"**: images that use suffering to provoke pity or donations while stripping people of their dignity and complexity. The Kenyan writer Binyavanga Wainaina mocked it in *How to Write About Africa*; the Nigerian writer Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie calls it **the danger of a single story**: show people only one way, again and again, and that becomes all anyone thinks they are.

Questions to ask before you publish a picture of someone:

- Would they be happy to see this picture of themselves? Would I be, if it were me?
- Do I know their name, and have I used it where appropriate?
- Does the picture show them as a person with agency — working, deciding, laughing — and not only as a problem?
- Does it tell the whole story, or only the saddest part?

Showing hardship is not wrong — some stories must be told. The difference is whether the person is treated as a partner in telling their story or as a prop.

**Honest editing.** Adjusting light, contrast and colour, cropping out a distraction, and straightening are generally honest — they help show what was there. Adding or removing objects or people, combining photos, or changing what happened is **manipulation**. For news or a documentary story, it's dishonest. For art or advertising, it's acceptable **only if** you don't pretend it is real. A crop can also lie: cutting out the police officer who was helping, so it looks like they were attacking, changes the truth.

**Honest captions.** A caption says who, what, where and when, and it must be true. Don't guess a stranger's story. "A woman sells tomatoes at Mile 12 market, Lagos, on Saturday" is honest. "A desperate mother struggles to feed her children" when you don't know that is fiction.

**Scenarios to discuss:** (1) A crowd gathers around a road accident and someone asks you to film it. (2) An NGO asks you to photograph the "poorest-looking" children in a school for its brochure. (3) Your friend wants you to remove a stranger from the background of a news photo "because it looks better".

## Key words

- **Informed consent:** agreement given by someone who understands what the image is for and knows they can refuse
- **Dignity:** being treated as a whole person who deserves respect
- **Poverty imagery:** pictures that show people only as helpless victims, to provoke pity
- **Manipulation:** changing an image so it no longer shows what really happened

## Read and watch

- [The danger of a single story](https://www.ted.com/talks/chimamanda_ngozi_adichie_the_danger_of_a_single_story) — Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, TED talk
- [How to write about Africa](https://granta.com/how-to-write-about-africa/) — Binyavanga Wainaina, Granta
- [Code of ethics](https://nppa.org/code-ethics) — National Press Photographers Association

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** focus on the three scenarios and say clearly what you would do and why.
- **If you already can:** find a charity campaign that shows its subjects with dignity and one that doesn't, and write a short comparison of the choices each made.

## Learning online

You can do this lesson entirely from home. Watch the Adichie talk on your phone (it has subtitles), and look for example images on news or charity websites — don't screenshot private people's social posts. **Upload as evidence:** your answers to the three scenarios, your before-and-after caption or post, and your five-line code of ethics. **Bring to the live Saturday class:** the image you found that you think does *not* treat its subject with dignity, and be ready to explain why — we will debate a few together, respectfully.

## Before the next session

Complete the check below, and stick your code of ethics somewhere you will see it whenever you pick up a camera.

materials.guide: Watch the whole talk. Write down one 'single story' about your own community that images often tell.

materials.title: How to write about Africa (Granta)
materials.guide: A satire: everything it 'recommends' is what NOT to do. List three tips and turn each into a rule for your photos.

materials.title: NPPA code of ethics
materials.guide: Read the list of standards used by professional news photographers. Borrow two for your own code.

checks.prompt: Which of these is an honest edit for a news photo?
options: Removing a bystander who 'spoils' the picture
Brightening a photo taken in poor light so faces can be seen
Adding a second photo's sky to make it more dramatic
Cropping out the person who was helping so the scene looks worse
checks.answer: Brightening a photo taken in poor light so faces can be seen
whys: Removing a real person changes what happened.
Combining photos creates a scene that never existed.
A crop that changes the meaning is dishonest even though nothing was added.

checks.prompt: An NGO asks you to photograph the 'poorest-looking' children for a brochure. What is the most respectful response?
options: Do it, because the money raised will help them
Offer to show them learning, with consent
Photograph them but blur every face afterwards
Refuse ever to work with any NGO again
checks.answer: Offer to show them learning, with consent

checks.prompt: For a photo of a 12-year-old to appear on a public poster, whose permission do you need?
options: Only the child's own agreement
Only the class teacher's permission
A guardian's and the child's
Nobody's, if the event was public
checks.answer: A guardian's and the child's

checks.prompt: Choose one of the three scenarios in the lesson. In 120–200 words, say what you would do, and explain your reasons using at least two ideas from the lesson (consent, dignity, honesty, a single story).
checks.rubric: Up to 6 points: a clear decision (1); at least two lesson ideas used accurately (2); considers the person in the picture, not only the photographer (2); recognises any difficulty or trade-off honestly (1).

checks.prompt: Rewrite a caption or redesign a post about a person so it treats them with dignity and tells the truth. Upload the before and after, plus your five-line code of ethics.
checks.answer: Before and after caption/post and a personal five-line code.
checks.rubric: Up to 6 points: the after version names or respects the subject and avoids pity-only framing (2); caption is factual — who, what, where, when — with no invented story (2); the code has five clear, practical rules (2).

lessons.title: Needs, wants and a saving goal you can actually reach
lessons.summary: Sort your spending into needs and wants, then build a saving goal with a date, an amount and a weekly plan.
objectives: You will sort real spending into needs and wants and explain the difference
You will turn a wish into a saving goal with an amount, a deadline and a monthly target
You will track a month of money in a simple Google Sheet
lessons.body:
Most money trouble does not start with a big mistake. It starts with lots of small ones nobody wrote down: a ₦500 snack here, ₦1,000 of data there, a "just this once" that happens every week. Today you will see where your money goes, decide what matters, and set a goal you can reach.

## What to do

- List everything you spent money on in the last two weeks — snacks, data, transport, airtime, gifts, church or mosque offering, school things. Guess where you must, but write it down.
- Mark each line **N** (need) or **W** (want). Argue with a partner about the hard ones.
- Choose one thing you want to buy or do in the next three to six months and price it properly.
- Build a saving goal in Google Sheets: income, needs, wants, savings, and a running total towards the goal.

## Understand it

A **need** is something you must have to live, learn or stay safe: food, transport to school, basic toiletries, the data you need for schoolwork. A **want** makes life nicer but you could manage without it: a new phone case, extra snacks, paid game items. Many things are both — you *need* shoes, but you *want* the ₦45,000 pair when a ₦15,000 pair does the job. The need is the shoe; the difference in price is the want.

**A worked example.** Chidinma gets ₦6,000 a month from her parents and earns about ₦2,000 a month braiding her cousins' hair, so her income is **₦8,000**. She checks her spending:

| Category | Monthly |
|---|---|
| Needs (transport top-up, data for school, toiletries) | ₦3,500 |
| Wants (snacks, music app, small treats) | ₦2,000 |
| Savings | ₦2,500 |
| **Total** | **₦8,000** |

She wants a scientific calculator and two revision books costing **₦15,000** in total, and she wants them in **six months**. ₦15,000 ÷ 6 = **₦2,500 a month** — exactly what she is saving. If she wanted them in four months she would need ₦15,000 ÷ 4 = ₦3,750 a month, so she would have to cut wants by ₦1,250 or earn more.

**What makes a goal reachable?** It is *specific* (a calculator and two named books, not "save money"), it has a *price* you checked, it has a *date*, and it breaks into a *monthly or weekly amount* you can see you can manage. Write the goal where you will see it.

**Pay yourself first.** Move the savings amount aside the day money arrives — into a separate envelope, a savings pocket in a banking app your parent controls, or a family member who keeps it for you. What is left is what you can spend. People who save "whatever is left at the end of the month" usually find nothing is left.

**Prices move.** In Nigeria prices have risen quickly in recent years, so recheck the price of your goal every month and adjust the plan if it has gone up.

## Key words

- **Need:** something required to live, learn or stay safe
- **Want:** something nice to have that you could manage without
- **Saving goal:** a target amount, for a stated purpose, by a stated date
- **Pay yourself first:** setting savings aside as soon as money arrives, before spending
- **Budget:** a plan for how income will be split between spending and saving

## Read and watch

- [Personal finance](https://www.khanacademy.org/college-careers-more/personal-finance) — Khan Academy
- [Budgeting help](https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/everyday-money/budgeting) — MoneyHelper (UK government-backed)
- [Get started with Google Sheets](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6000292) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** use only three columns — what, how much, N or W — for one week before building the full sheet.
- **If you already can:** add a chart of needs vs wants vs savings, and a second goal with a different deadline.
- **If you have no regular income:** plan with money you receive for birthdays or festivals, or plan a family goal with a parent.

## Learning online

You can do all of this at home with a phone. Open Google Sheets (free with a Google account; use a parent's supervised account if you are under 13) and make four columns: *Date, Item, Amount (₦), Need or Want*. Add a goal box at the top: goal, price, deadline, months left, and a formula `=B2/B4` for the monthly amount. **Upload as evidence:** a screenshot of your sheet with at least ten real entries and your goal box filled in (hide anything private). **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** one item you could not decide was a need or a want — we will vote on a few.

## Before the next session

Keep tracking every naira for seven days. Then answer the checks below and note the one want you could cut to reach your goal faster.

lessons.title: Simple interest and compound growth, in naira
lessons.summary: See how simple interest and compound interest grow ₦100,000 differently, and why time and inflation both matter.
objectives: You will calculate simple and compound interest by hand and in Google Sheets
You will explain why compound growth speeds up over time
You will use the rule of 72 and compare an interest rate with inflation
lessons.body:
If you save ₦100,000 and a bank pays you 10% a year, how much do you have after three years? There are two different answers, and the difference between them is one of the most important ideas in money.

## What to do

- Work through the ₦100,000 example below with a pen first, then check every number in Google Sheets.
- Build a table showing years 0 to 10 for both simple and compound interest side by side.
- Add a line chart of both columns and describe the shape in one sentence.
- Find a real savings or treasury bill rate advertised in Nigeria this month and compare it with the latest inflation figure.

## Understand it

**Interest** is the price of money. When you save, a bank pays you interest for using your money; when you borrow, you pay interest.

**Simple interest** is paid only on the amount you started with (the **principal**).
Interest each year = principal × rate. On ₦100,000 at 10%: ₦10,000 every year.

| Year | Simple interest balance | Compound interest balance |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | ₦100,000 | ₦100,000 |
| 1 | ₦110,000 | ₦110,000 |
| 2 | ₦120,000 | ₦121,000 |
| 3 | ₦130,000 | ₦133,100 |
| 5 | ₦150,000 | ₦161,051 |

**Compound interest** is paid on the principal *and* on interest already earned. Year 1: 10% of ₦100,000 = ₦10,000, so ₦110,000. Year 2: 10% of ₦110,000 = ₦11,000, so ₦121,000. Year 3: 10% of ₦121,000 = ₦12,100, so ₦133,100. After three years compound is ₦3,100 ahead; after five it is ₦11,051 ahead, and the gap keeps widening. The formula is **balance = principal × (1 + rate)^years**. In Sheets, with principal in B1, rate in B2 (as 10%) and years in B3: `=B1*(1+B2)^B3`.

**The rule of 72.** Divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double with compounding. At 10%, 72 ÷ 10 ≈ 7.2 years. At 6%, about 12 years. It is an estimate, but a good one for everyday rates.

**Compounding works against you on debt.** A loan app charging interest on unpaid interest grows the same way — which is why small loans can become big ones quickly.

**Inflation is the other half of the story.** If your savings earn 10% but prices rise 20% in the same year, your ₦110,000 buys *less* than your ₦100,000 did. The **real return** is roughly the interest rate minus inflation — here about −10%. Nigerian inflation has often been well above 20% in recent years, so always compare the rate you are offered with the latest figure published by the National Bureau of Statistics. Growth you cannot spend is not the same as growth you can.

## Key words

- **Principal:** the amount of money you start with
- **Simple interest:** interest calculated only on the principal
- **Compound interest:** interest calculated on the principal plus interest already earned
- **Rule of 72:** 72 divided by the yearly rate gives roughly the years to double
- **Real return:** growth after taking inflation into account

## Read and watch

- [Interest tutorial](https://www.khanacademy.org/economics-finance-domain/core-finance/interest-tutorial) — Khan Academy
- [Compound interest calculator](https://www.investor.gov/financial-tools-calculators/calculators/compound-interest-calculator) — Investor.gov (US SEC)
- [Compound interest explained](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/compoundinterest.asp) — Investopedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do only the three-year table by hand, then type it into Sheets and check each number matches.
- **If you already can:** add a column where interest is compounded monthly (rate ÷ 12, periods × 12) and compare the result after five years.
- **If maths worries you:** use the Investor.gov calculator to check your answers — the idea matters more than the speed.

## Learning online

At home you need only Google Sheets and a calculator. Put the principal, rate and years in cells B1–B3 so you can change them, build the year-by-year table with formulas (simple: `=$B$1+$B$1*$B$2*A6`; compound: `=$B$1*(1+$B$2)^A6`) and insert a line chart. **Upload as evidence:** a screenshot or share link (set to "anyone with the link can view") showing the ten-year table and chart. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** the real Nigerian savings rate you found, where you found it, and the inflation figure you compared it with.

## Before the next session

Change your sheet's rate to 20% and the years to 10, and write down how many times larger the compound balance is than the simple one. Then try the checks below.

lessons.title: Pricing a product: cost-plus, competitor and value
lessons.summary: Work out what a product really costs to make, then set a price using cost-plus, competitor and value thinking.
objectives: You will calculate the full cost of one unit, including hidden costs
You will set a price with cost-plus, check it against competitors and adjust for value
You will tell markup and margin apart
lessons.body:
Many young sellers price by feel: "others sell for ₦500, so I'll sell for ₦500." Sometimes that works. Sometimes it means selling at a loss without knowing. Today you will price a real product the way a business does — starting from cost, then looking outward.

## What to do

- Choose a product you could make or resell: zobo, chin chin, bead bracelets, phone accessories, printed T-shirts.
- List every cost for one batch, including the ones people forget (packaging, transport, gas, data for adverts).
- Work out cost per unit, then a cost-plus price, then check two or three competitors' prices.
- Decide your final price and write two sentences justifying it.

## Understand it

**Step 1: the full cost of one unit.** Take zobo. One batch makes 20 bottles:

| Cost | Amount |
|---|---|
| Zobo leaves, ginger, pineapple, sugar | ₦4,000 |
| 20 bottles at ₦100 each | ₦2,000 |
| Gas and transport to market | ₦1,000 |
| **Total batch cost** | **₦7,000** |

Cost per bottle = ₦7,000 ÷ 20 = **₦350**. If you forget the bottles and gas, you would think it costs ₦200 and price far too low.

**Step 2: cost-plus pricing.** Add a **markup** — a percentage on top of cost. With a 40% markup: ₦350 × 1.40 = ₦490. Round to a sensible price: **₦500**.

**Markup is not margin.** Markup is profit as a share of *cost*; **margin** is profit as a share of the *price*. At ₦500, profit per bottle is ₦500 − ₦350 = ₦150. Markup = 150 ÷ 350 ≈ 43%. Margin = 150 ÷ 500 = 30%. Mixing these up is a classic mistake: if someone says "I want a 40% margin," the price must be ₦350 ÷ 0.60 ≈ ₦583, not ₦490.

**Step 3: competitor pricing.** Look at what similar products sell for nearby. If other sellers at the school gate charge ₦400–₦600, ₦500 sits in the middle. If they all sell at ₦300, your cost is too high for that market — find cheaper bottles, make bigger batches, or sell somewhere else.

**Step 4: value-based pricing.** Ask what the customer thinks it is *worth*. Ice-cold zobo sold straight after a football match on a hot afternoon is worth more to that buyer than warm zobo at 8 a.m. Better packaging, a reliable taste, delivery, or a cause (some profit goes to the centre's trip) can all support a higher price. Value pricing only works if the customer can see the difference.

**Putting it together.** Cost sets the **floor** (never price below cost for long), competitors show the **range**, and value tells you where in — or above — that range you can sit. Check also how many you can realistically sell: 30 bottles at ₦150 profit is ₦4,500; 10 bottles at ₦250 profit is only ₦2,500.

## Key words

- **Unit cost:** the total cost of a batch divided by the number of units
- **Markup:** profit as a percentage of cost
- **Margin:** profit as a percentage of the selling price
- **Cost-plus pricing:** setting price by adding a markup to unit cost
- **Value-based pricing:** setting price by what customers believe the product is worth

## Read and watch

- [Cost-plus pricing](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/cost-plus-pricing.asp) — Investopedia
- [Markup](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/m/markup.asp) — Investopedia
- [Google Sheets function list](https://support.google.com/docs/table/25273) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** price one product only, and use the zobo table as a template.
- **If you already can:** add a "what if" cell for batch size and see how the unit cost falls when you make 40 bottles instead of 20.
- **If you cannot visit a market:** use prices from Jumia, Jiji or WhatsApp status adverts as your competitor check, and say where they came from.

## Learning online

You can do this at home with a phone. In Google Sheets, list your batch costs in column B, put the number of units in a separate cell, and calculate unit cost, cost-plus price (`=unitcost*(1+markup)`), profit per unit and margin. Search online marketplaces or ask two sellers you know for competitor prices. **Upload as evidence:** a screenshot of your pricing sheet with your final price and a two-sentence justification typed beneath it. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your final price and the one hidden cost you nearly forgot.

## Before the next session

Ask one possible customer what they would pay for your product, without telling them your price first. Note their answer and compare it with your calculation.

lessons.title: Reading a simple profit and loss and balance sheet
lessons.summary: Read and build a one-month profit and loss account and a balance sheet for a small snack business, and check they make sense.
objectives: You will calculate gross profit and net profit from a month of trading
You will list assets, liabilities and equity and check that the balance sheet balances
You will explain what each statement tells an owner or lender
lessons.body:
Two pieces of paper tell you most of what you need to know about a small business. The **profit and loss** account answers "did we make money this month?" The **balance sheet** answers "what do we own, what do we owe, and what is left for the owner?" Today you will read both for a real-sized business.

## What to do

- Work through Ada's Snacks below and check every total with a calculator.
- Rebuild both statements in Google Sheets with formulas, not typed totals.
- Change one number (for example, rent goes up by ₦10,000) and see which totals move.
- Write three sentences telling Ada what her statements say.

## Understand it

**Ada's Snacks** sells puff-puff, meat pies and drinks from a stall near a school in Ibadan. Here is her **profit and loss account (P&L)** for March:

| | ₦ |
|---|---|
| Sales (revenue) | 180,000 |
| Cost of goods sold (flour, oil, meat, drinks bought for resale) | (95,000) |
| **Gross profit** | **85,000** |
| Stall rent | (20,000) |
| Transport | (12,000) |
| Packaging | (8,000) |
| Phone and data | (5,000) |
| **Total expenses** | **(45,000)** |
| **Net profit** | **40,000** |

**Gross profit** = sales − cost of goods sold = ₦180,000 − ₦95,000 = ₦85,000. It tells Ada whether her products earn more than they cost to make. **Net profit** = gross profit − running expenses = ₦85,000 − ₦45,000 = ₦40,000. That is what the business actually earned for the month. Brackets mean money going out.

Her **balance sheet** on 31 March:

| Assets (what the business owns) | ₦ | Liabilities (what it owes) | ₦ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cash | 60,000 | Loan from her aunt | 50,000 |
| Stock of ingredients | 25,000 | Owed to flour supplier | 15,000 |
| Chest freezer | 120,000 | **Total liabilities** | **65,000** |
| **Total assets** | **205,000** | **Equity (owner's share)** | **140,000** |

The rule that always holds: **assets = liabilities + equity**. ₦205,000 = ₦65,000 + ₦140,000. Equity is not a pile of cash — it is the part of the assets that belongs to Ada once every debt is paid.

**The difference between the two.** The P&L covers a *period* (March); the balance sheet is a *snapshot* on one day (31 March). A profitable month adds to equity; a loss shrinks it. If Ada takes ₦30,000 of profit home for herself, cash and equity both fall by ₦30,000 — and the sheet still balances.

**What a lender looks at.** If Ada asked a microfinance bank for a loan, they would ask: is net profit steady month to month? Is there enough cash to meet the repayments? Are liabilities already large compared with assets? Statements turn "my business is doing fine" into evidence.

## Key words

- **Revenue:** the total money from sales in a period
- **Gross profit:** revenue minus the direct cost of what was sold
- **Net profit:** gross profit minus running expenses
- **Asset:** something the business owns that has value
- **Liability:** money the business owes to someone else
- **Equity:** assets minus liabilities: the owner's share

## Read and watch

- [Accounting and financial statements](https://www.khanacademy.org/economics-finance-domain/core-finance/accounting-and-financial-stateme) — Khan Academy
- [Balance sheet](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/balancesheet.asp) — Investopedia
- [Profit and loss statement](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/p/plstatement.asp) — Investopedia

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** build only the P&L first; add the balance sheet once the profit numbers match.
- **If you already can:** make a second month where sales drop by 20% and expenses stay the same, and calculate the new net profit.
- **If you run a small business already:** build statements for your own last month, but keep the file private.

## Learning online

Everything here works at home in Google Sheets. Type the P&L lines in column A and amounts in column B, then use `=B2-B3` for gross profit and `=SUM()` for expenses. On a second tab build the balance sheet and add a check cell: `=IF(total_assets=total_liabilities+equity,"Balances","Check again")`. **Upload as evidence:** a view-only link or screenshot of both tabs, including the check cell. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your three-sentence message to Ada and the "what if" change you tested.

## Before the next session

Find one more cost Ada has probably forgotten (hint: does she pay anyone to help at busy times?) and decide whether it belongs in cost of goods sold or expenses.

lessons.title: Cash flow versus profit: why profitable businesses still fail
lessons.summary: Track cash month by month to see how a profitable order can still leave a business unable to pay its bills.
objectives: You will build a simple monthly cash-flow forecast
You will explain why profit and cash are not the same
You will suggest practical ways to fix a cash gap
lessons.body:
"But we made a profit!" is one of the saddest sentences in business. A business can win a big order, earn good profit on paper, and still close because it ran out of cash before the customer paid. Today you will see exactly how that happens — and how to stop it.

## What to do

- Follow Tunde's tailoring order through three months in the table below.
- Rebuild the cash-flow table in Google Sheets with formulas for each closing balance.
- Highlight any month where cash goes below zero.
- Test two fixes — a deposit, and cheaper or later payment for fabric — and record what changes.

## Understand it

**Tunde's order.** Tunde runs a small tailoring business in Aba. A school orders **50 uniforms at ₦6,000 each = ₦300,000**. Fabric and materials cost **₦3,800 per uniform = ₦190,000**, paid to the supplier up front. His workshop rent is **₦20,000 a month**. The school will pay **when the uniforms are delivered at the end of month 3** — in full, but not before. Tunde starts with **₦180,000** in the bank.

**Profit over the three months:** ₦300,000 − ₦190,000 − (3 × ₦20,000) = **₦50,000**. A good job.

**Cash, month by month:**

| Month | Opening cash | Cash in | Cash out | Closing cash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ₦180,000 | ₦0 | ₦210,000 (fabric + rent) | **−₦30,000** |
| 2 | −₦30,000 | ₦0 | ₦20,000 | **−₦50,000** |
| 3 | −₦50,000 | ₦300,000 | ₦20,000 | ₦230,000 |

Check: ₦180,000 start + ₦50,000 profit = ₦230,000 end. The profit is real — but in month 1 Tunde cannot pay for all the fabric, and in month 2 he cannot pay rent. Without help, the business stops before it ever gets paid.

**Why profit and cash differ.** Profit counts a sale when it is *made*; cash counts it when the money *arrives*. Costs are often paid before customers pay. Buying equipment uses cash today but is spread over years in the accounts. Customers who pay late, stock sitting unsold, and loan repayments all affect cash without changing profit in the same way.

**Fixes that work.**
- **Ask for a deposit.** If the school pays 50% (₦150,000) at the start, month 1 closes at ₦180,000 + ₦150,000 − ₦210,000 = ₦120,000, month 2 at ₦100,000, and month 3 at ₦100,000 + ₦150,000 − ₦20,000 = ₦230,000. Same profit, no crisis.
- **Pay suppliers later**, or in stages, if they agree.
- **Stage the work:** deliver and invoice 25 uniforms at a time.
- **Keep a cash buffer** for at least one or two months of fixed costs.
- **Borrow carefully**, knowing the interest cost and the repayment dates.

A **cash-flow forecast** — the table above, done *before* you accept the order — is how owners see the gap coming. It is one of the most useful sheets any small business can keep.

## Key words

- **Cash flow:** money actually coming into and going out of the business over time
- **Cash-flow forecast:** a month-by-month prediction of cash in, cash out and closing balance
- **Deposit:** part of the price paid up front, before the work is finished
- **Cash buffer:** spare cash kept to cover costs when income is late
- **Working capital:** the cash a business needs to keep running day to day

## Read and watch

- [Cash flow](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/cashflow.asp) — Investopedia
- [Working capital](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/w/workingcapital.asp) — Investopedia
- [Conditional formatting](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/78413) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** copy the table exactly and get your closing balances to match before testing fixes.
- **If you already can:** extend to six months and add a second order that starts in month 2.
- **If you know a business owner:** ask them how long their customers usually take to pay, and use that in your forecast.

## Learning online

At home, build this in Google Sheets with columns *Month, Opening, In, Out, Closing*. Closing is `=B2+C2-D2`, and next month's opening is `=E2`. Use **Format → Conditional formatting** to turn negative closing cash red. Copy the tab to test the deposit fix. **Upload as evidence:** a screenshot showing the original forecast with red months, and your fixed version with no red. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** which fix you would choose if you were Tunde, and one reason the school might refuse it.

## Before the next session

Think of a business near you that sells on credit ("pay me next week"). Write down one way that habit could cause a cash gap, and try the checks below.

lessons.title: Scams, Ponzi schemes and staying safe with mobile money
lessons.summary: Learn to spot 'too good to be true' investments and protect your mobile money, PIN and OTP from fraudsters.
objectives: You will recognise the warning signs of a Ponzi scheme or investment scam
You will use simple maths to test whether a promised return is believable
You will apply five habits that keep mobile money and bank apps safe
lessons.body:
"Invest ₦10,000 today and get 30% every month." Messages like this circulate on WhatsApp and Telegram every week in Nigeria. Many families have lost savings to schemes that looked convincing for a while. Today you learn to check the maths, spot the pattern, and protect your accounts.

## What to do

- Collect (or recall) one investment advert or "opportunity" message you have seen. Do not click any links in it.
- Test its promised return with the maths below.
- Score it against the red-flag checklist.
- Write a short, kind message you could send to a relative who is about to join a scheme like it.

## Understand it

**How a Ponzi scheme works.** Early members are paid "profits" using money from new members, not from any real business. It looks successful while new money keeps arriving. When joining slows down, it cannot pay, withdrawals are "paused", and most people — especially later joiners — lose their money. **MMM Nigeria** froze payments in December 2016 after millions of Nigerians had joined. In 2025, the crypto trading platform **CBEX** stopped withdrawals and many users lost funds. The names change; the pattern does not.

**Test the maths.** 30% a month sounds modest. Compounded for a year: 1.3¹² ≈ **23.3**. So ₦10,000 would become about ₦233,000 in twelve months. No honest business, bank or stock market reliably does that. Compare: Nigerian treasury bills and savings accounts pay a yearly rate, not a monthly one. If a monthly promise is higher than what a bank pays in a year, stop.

**Red flags checklist.**
1. **Guaranteed** high returns, especially "per month" or "per week".
2. Money comes mainly from **recruiting** others; referral bonuses are pushed hard.
3. **Vague** business: "forex", "crypto arbitrage", "AI trading" with no detail you can check.
4. **Pressure**: "only today", "slots are closing".
5. **Not registered.** Investment schemes offered to the public must be registered with the **Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Nigeria**, which publishes warnings about unregistered operators.
6. **Withdrawals are delayed** or need an extra "fee" to unlock.

**Mobile money and bank app safety.**
- **Never share your PIN, OTP or password** — not with "bank staff", not with a "customer care" number from social media. Banks do not ask for them.
- **Check credits in your app, not in an SMS.** Fake credit alerts are a common trick at shops and for online sellers.
- **Protect your SIM.** If your phone suddenly loses network for no reason, call your network provider: a **SIM swap** can let fraudsters receive your OTPs.
- **Do not let others use your account** to "receive money for them". You could be helping to move stolen funds.
- **Report quickly.** Contact your bank through its official number or app; fraud can be reported to the EFCC, and investment scams to the SEC.

Being careful is not being rude. A real opportunity will still be there tomorrow, after you have checked it.

## Key words

- **Ponzi scheme:** a fraud that pays earlier members with money from newer members
- **OTP:** one-time password sent to your phone to approve a transaction
- **SIM swap:** a fraud where someone moves your number to their SIM to receive your codes
- **Fake credit alert:** a forged message claiming money has arrived in your account
- **SEC Nigeria:** the regulator that registers and supervises investment schemes

## Read and watch

- [Securities and Exchange Commission Nigeria](https://sec.gov.ng/) — SEC Nigeria
- [Ponzi schemes](https://www.investor.gov/protect-your-investments/fraud/types-fraud/ponzi-scheme) — Investor.gov (US SEC)
- [Economic and Financial Crimes Commission](https://www.efcc.gov.ng/) — EFCC Nigeria

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** focus on the six red flags and the PIN/OTP rule; those two alone prevent most losses.
- **If you already can:** use Google Sheets to show how a ₦10,000 deposit grows at 30% a month for 12 months, and chart it next to a bank's yearly rate.
- **If someone in your family has lost money:** you do not have to share that story. If you do, keep names out of it.

## Learning online

This lesson works fully from home. Use your phone to visit the SEC Nigeria website and look for its investor alerts or warnings; note one name it has warned about. In Google Sheets, put ₦10,000 in B1 and `=B1*1.3^A2` beside months 1 to 12 to see the "30% a month" promise grow. **Upload as evidence:** your red-flag scorecard for one real advert (screenshot with any phone numbers or links blacked out) and the 12-month growth table. **Never click a scam link to collect evidence.** **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** the kind message you drafted for a relative — we will practise saying it out loud.

## Before the next session

Show the PIN/OTP rule to one adult at home and check together that your bank or mobile money app has a strong PIN that is not a birthday. Then answer the checks below.

lessons.title: Asking a good question of data
lessons.summary: Turn a vague worry into a question data can answer, and plan exactly which data you need to answer it.
objectives: You will rewrite vague questions into specific, answerable ones
You will name the data, the time period and the measure an answer needs
You will write a one-page question plan before collecting anything
lessons.body:
Most data projects go wrong before anyone opens a spreadsheet. Somebody asks "how are we doing?", a lot of numbers get collected, and nobody can say what they mean. Good analysts start with a good question. Today you will learn to write one.

## What to do

- Read the tuck-shop example below.
- Take three vague questions from your own life — school, the centre, your family business, football — and rewrite each one so data could answer it.
- Choose your best question and write a question plan: the decision it helps, the data needed, where it comes from, and what answer would change your mind.
- Swap plans with a partner and try to find one thing that is still unclear.

## Understand it

**Vague:** "Is the centre's tuck shop doing well?"
Doing well compared with what? Measured how? Over what time?

**Better:** "Which three items earned the most money at the tuck shop on Saturdays in October, and did zobo sales fall after the price went up on 12 October?"

That question names **what** is measured (money earned, number sold), **who or what** each record is about (one sale), **when** (Saturdays in October, before and after 12 October), and **which comparison** matters (before vs after the price rise). You can now see what data you need: a record of every sale with its date, item, quantity and price.

**A checklist for a good data question.**
1. **It serves a decision.** "Should we keep the zobo price at ₦400?" is a decision; the question exists to help make it.
2. **It is specific.** It names the measure, the group and the time.
3. **It is answerable** with data you can actually get, legally and safely.
4. **It is fair.** It does not assume the answer ("prove the price rise was a mistake").
5. **It says what would change your mind.** "If zobo sales fall by more than a quarter after the rise, we lower the price." Deciding this *before* you look stops you bending the result afterwards.

**Kinds of question.** *Descriptive* questions ask what happened ("how many members attended each Saturday?"). *Comparative* questions ask how groups differ ("did Ikeja and Yaba centres have different attendance?"). *Relationship* questions ask whether two things move together ("do members who attend more score higher in checks?"). Relationship questions are the hardest to answer fairly — we come back to them in week 6.

**Where data comes from.** Records you already keep (a sales book, an attendance register), a short survey (Google Forms), observation (counting people in a queue), or public data (the National Bureau of Statistics, Our World in Data). Every source has limits: a survey only hears from people who answer it; a sales book only records what someone remembered to write.

**Privacy matters.** If your data is about people, collect only what you need, do not collect names unless you must, and ask permission. A good question rarely needs anyone's phone number.

## Key words

- **Data question:** a question specific enough that data can answer it
- **Measure:** the thing being counted or recorded, such as naira earned or people attending
- **Record:** one row of data about one thing, such as one sale
- **Decision:** the choice the answer will help someone make
- **Bias:** anything that pushes an answer away from the truth

## Read and watch

- [Designing studies](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/designing-studies) — Khan Academy
- [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/) — University of Oxford / Global Change Data Lab
- [Create a survey with Google Forms](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6281888) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** rewrite one question really well instead of three quickly.
- **If you already can:** design the Google Form that would collect your data, with no question that collects more than you need.
- **If your question is about people:** check your plan with an instructor before you collect anything.

## Learning online

At home, write your question plan in a Google Doc with five headings: *Decision, Question, Data needed, Source, What would change my mind*. If your question needs a survey, draft it in Google Forms but **do not send it** until your instructor has checked it. **Upload as evidence:** your question plan (link set to view-only, or a PDF) showing the vague question and your improved version. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your vague question and your improved one, ready to read aloud for the class to test.

## Before the next session

Look at one news story that uses a number. Write down the question the journalist was really answering, and whether it was clear.
