lessons.title: Cleaning messy data in Google Sheets
lessons.summary: Find and fix duplicates, blanks and inconsistent spellings in a real-looking sign-up list without losing the original.
objectives: You will find duplicates, blanks and inconsistent entries in a dataset
You will use TRIM, PROPER, UNIQUE, COUNTBLANK and Remove duplicates to clean it
You will keep a cleaning log so others can trust your work
lessons.body:
Real data is messy. People type "Lagos", "lagos", "Lagos " and "LAG" for the same place. Someone submits a form twice. A cell is left empty. If you analyse the mess, you get wrong answers that look right. Analysts often spend more time cleaning than analysing — today you learn why, and how.

## What to do

- Make a copy of the messy sign-up list your instructor shares (or type the 15-row sample described below).
- **Duplicate the tab and name it RAW.** Never clean the only copy.
- Find every problem: duplicates, blanks, extra spaces, different spellings, numbers stored as text.
- Fix them on a CLEAN tab and write each fix in a cleaning log.

## Understand it

Imagine a sign-up sheet for a coding taster day with columns *Name, Age, Centre, Phone given (Y/N)*. Typical problems:

**1. Inconsistent spellings.** "Ikeja", "ikeja", "IKEJA", "Ikeja " (with a space) are four different values to a spreadsheet, so a count by centre splits one centre into four.
- `=TRIM(C2)` removes extra spaces at the start and end.
- `=PROPER(TRIM(C2))` also makes it "Ikeja".
- `=UNIQUE(C2:C100)` lists every distinct value so you can *see* all the spellings at once. Then use **Edit → Find and replace** to fix nicknames like "Yaba Ctr" → "Yaba".

**2. Duplicates.** The same person submitted twice. Use **Data → Data cleanup → Remove duplicates**, choosing the columns that identify a person. Be careful: two different children can share a name. Check before deleting — that is why you kept RAW.

**3. Blanks.** `=COUNTBLANK(B2:B100)` tells you how many ages are missing. Do not invent them. Decide: leave blank and say so, ask the person, or exclude that row from age calculations only. Write down which you chose.

**4. Numbers stored as text.** An age typed as "12 yrs" cannot be averaged. Look for numbers aligned to the left, or use `=ISNUMBER(B2)`. Fix "12 yrs" to 12.

**5. Impossible values.** An age of 112 or 1.2 is probably a typo. Flag it with conditional formatting (*age less than 8 or greater than 18*) and check with the source instead of guessing.

**Data validation stops it next time.** On the form or sheet, use **Data → Data validation** to give Centre a dropdown list and Age a number range. Cleaning is a cure; validation is prevention.

**The cleaning log.** A short table — *What I found, How many rows, What I did, Why* — makes your work trustworthy. Example: "Centre: 6 spellings of Ikeja → 'Ikeja' (9 rows), using PROPER(TRIM()) and Find and replace." Anyone can check it, and you can undo a mistake.

## Key words

- **Raw data:** the original, untouched data as it was collected
- **Duplicate:** a record that appears more than once
- **Whitespace:** invisible spaces that make two values look the same but differ
- **Data validation:** rules that limit what can be entered in a cell
- **Cleaning log:** a record of every change made to the data, and why

## Read and watch

- [Google Sheets function list (TRIM, PROPER, UNIQUE, COUNTBLANK)](https://support.google.com/docs/table/25273) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Data validation](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/186103) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Conditional formatting](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/78413) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** fix one column completely (Centre) before touching any other.
- **If you already can:** use `=COUNTIF(A:A,A2)>1` in a helper column to flag possible duplicates before removing anything, and explain each one.
- **If you only have a phone:** the Google Sheets app supports all of these formulas; Remove duplicates is easier on a laptop or in the browser's desktop view.

## Learning online

At home, open the shared messy file (or build your own 15-row sample with at least three spellings of one centre, two duplicates and two blanks). Duplicate the tab as RAW, clean on a CLEAN tab, and add a LOG tab. **Use invented names only** — never real children's details. **Upload as evidence:** a view-only link with all three tabs, or screenshots of the before and after plus your log. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** the trickiest problem you found and how you decided what to do about it.

## Before the next session

Look at any form you have filled in recently. Which field would you add validation to so that the data arrives cleaner?

lessons.title: Averages, and when the mean misleads
lessons.summary: Calculate mean, median and mode, and see how a single outlier can make the mean tell the wrong story.
objectives: You will calculate the mean, median and mode of a small dataset by hand and in Sheets
You will identify outliers and explain their effect on the mean
You will choose the most honest average for a given question
lessons.body:
"The average member gets ₦8,389 pocket money a week." That sounds like a lot — and in the example below, only one person actually gets more than ₦4,500. The word *average* can hide as much as it shows. Today you will learn which average to use, and when.

## What to do

- Work out the mean, median and mode of the pocket-money data below by hand.
- Check your answers in Google Sheets with AVERAGE, MEDIAN and MODE.
- Remove the outlier and recalculate. Write down what changed and what did not.
- Collect a small dataset of your own (minutes of travel to the centre, say) and decide which average to report.

## Understand it

Nine members' weekly pocket money, sorted from smallest to largest:

**₦2,000 · ₦2,500 · ₦3,000 · ₦3,000 · ₦3,000 · ₦3,500 · ₦4,000 · ₦4,500 · ₦50,000**

**Mean** — add them up and divide by how many there are.
Total = ₦75,500. Mean = ₦75,500 ÷ 9 ≈ **₦8,389**. In Sheets: `=AVERAGE(A2:A10)`.

**Median** — the middle value when the data is sorted. With 9 values, the middle is the 5th: **₦3,000**. With an even number of values, take the mean of the middle two. In Sheets: `=MEDIAN(A2:A10)`.

**Mode** — the value that appears most often: **₦3,000** (three times). In Sheets: `=MODE(A2:A10)`.

**The outlier.** ₦50,000 is far from the rest — an **outlier**. It drags the mean up to ₦8,389, a figure higher than what eight of the nine members receive. Remove it and the mean of the other eight is ₦25,500 ÷ 8 = **₦3,187.50**, while the median stays at **₦3,000** (the mean of the 4th and 5th values, both ₦3,000). The median did not even notice.

**Which average to use?**
- Use the **median** when data is skewed or has outliers: incomes, house prices, journey times, follower counts. This is why statistics offices usually report *median* household income.
- Use the **mean** when values are fairly even and you need totals to work (mean score × number of learners = total points).
- Use the **mode** for categories or the "most common" choice: most popular shirt size, most chosen snack.

**Always look at the spread too.** Two classes can both have a mean score of 60%: one where everyone scored 55–65, and one where half scored 20 and half scored 100. The **range** (largest − smallest) and a quick chart show which. `=MAX(A2:A10)-MIN(A2:A10)` gives the range.

**Do not delete outliers to make results look neat.** Check whether the value is a mistake (₦50,000 typed instead of ₦5,000?). If it is real, keep it, and choose an average that tells the truth about the typical case — then mention the outlier.

## Key words

- **Mean:** the total divided by the number of values
- **Median:** the middle value when the data is sorted
- **Mode:** the value that appears most often
- **Outlier:** a value far away from the rest of the data
- **Range:** the largest value minus the smallest; a simple measure of spread

## Read and watch

- [Summarizing quantitative data](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/summarizing-quantitative-data) — Khan Academy
- [Google Sheets function list (AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MODE)](https://support.google.com/docs/table/25273) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** sort the numbers on paper first; the median is much easier to see once they are in order.
- **If you already can:** calculate the interquartile range with `=QUARTILE(A2:A10,3)-QUARTILE(A2:A10,1)` and explain why it ignores outliers.
- **If you collect data from friends:** ask for rounded figures and no names.

## Learning online

At home, type the nine values into Google Sheets and calculate all three averages and the range. Then gather 8–12 values of your own — journey minutes, hours of sleep, data bundle prices — from family or friends (no names). **Upload as evidence:** a screenshot showing both datasets with AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MODE and range, and one sentence saying which average you would report for your own data and why. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** one real-life place you have seen an "average" that might have been misleading.

## Before the next session

Find an advert or news report that uses the word "average". Decide whether it is probably the mean or the median, and whether that choice helps or hides the truth.

lessons.title: Pivot tables: summarise hundreds of rows in seconds
lessons.summary: Use a Google Sheets pivot table to total sales by item and by day, and check the result by hand.
objectives: You will build a pivot table with rows, columns, values and a filter
You will check a pivot table's totals against a hand calculation
You will answer a business question using a pivot table
lessons.body:
The tuck shop has 400 rows of sales from October. "Which item made the most money on Saturdays?" would take an hour with a calculator. A **pivot table** answers it in about thirty seconds — and lets you ask the next question straight away.

## What to do

- Open the sample sales data (columns: Date, Day, Item, Quantity, Price, Total).
- Before building anything, total the six-row example below by hand.
- Create a pivot table that sums Total by Item, then add Day as columns.
- Use the pivot table to answer three questions your instructor gives you, and one of your own.

## Understand it

**Six rows to start with:**

| Day | Item | Qty | Price | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sat | Zobo | 3 | ₦300 | ₦900 |
| Sat | Puff-puff | 10 | ₦50 | ₦500 |
| Sun | Zobo | 2 | ₦300 | ₦600 |
| Sat | Chin chin | 4 | ₦200 | ₦800 |
| Sun | Puff-puff | 6 | ₦50 | ₦300 |
| Sun | Chin chin | 1 | ₦200 | ₦200 |

By hand: Zobo = ₦900 + ₦600 = **₦1,500**; Chin chin = ₦800 + ₦200 = **₦1,000**; Puff-puff = ₦500 + ₦300 = **₦800**. Grand total **₦3,300**. By day: Saturday ₦2,200, Sunday ₦1,100.

**Building the pivot table.**
1. Click anywhere in the data, then **Insert → Pivot table**, and choose *New sheet*.
2. In the editor, add **Item** under **Rows**.
3. Add **Total** under **Values**, summarised by **SUM**.
4. Add **Day** under **Columns** to split each item's total by day.
5. Add a **Filter** (for example, Date is in October) to focus the summary.

Your pivot should show exactly the numbers you worked out by hand. If it does not, something is wrong in the data — often a misspelt item ("Zobo " with a space shows as a separate row) or a number stored as text. That is why you clean first.

**Other useful summaries.** Change SUM to **COUNTA** to count how many sales each item had, or **AVERAGE** to see the typical sale size. Put **Quantity** in Values instead of Total to see units rather than naira. Sort the rows by value (descending) to put the best seller on top.

**Pivot tables do not change your data.** They are a view of it. When the data changes, the pivot updates. You can safely experiment: drag fields in and out until the summary answers your question.

**From numbers to a sentence.** A pivot table is not the answer; the sentence is. "Zobo earned the most (₦1,500 of ₦3,300, 45%), and Saturday brought in twice Sunday's sales" is something a manager can act on.

## Key words

- **Pivot table:** a tool that summarises data by grouping and totalling it
- **Rows / Columns:** the fields used to group the summary down and across
- **Values:** the numbers being summarised, such as a SUM of sales
- **Filter:** a rule that limits which records are included
- **Grand total:** the overall total across every group

## Read and watch

- [Create and use pivot tables](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/1272900) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Customise a pivot table](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/7572895) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Google Sheets function list](https://support.google.com/docs/table/25273) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** build the six-row pivot first and match it to the hand totals before using the big dataset.
- **If you already can:** add a calculated field for profit (Total minus cost) and find the most profitable item rather than the best seller.
- **If you are on a phone:** pivot tables can be viewed in the app but are much easier to build in a browser in desktop mode.

## Learning online

At home, copy the sample sales file into your own Google Drive (or type at least 30 rows of invented sales). Build the pivot on a new sheet, then write your answers in a text box or cells beside it. **Upload as evidence:** a view-only link or screenshots showing the pivot (items in rows, days in columns, SUM of Total) and your four answered questions written as full sentences. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** the question you asked of the data yourself and the answer the pivot gave.

## Before the next session

Think of a list you keep — football results, money you spend, songs you play. Which pivot table would summarise it best? Write the rows, columns and values you would choose.

lessons.title: Choosing the right chart, and spotting a misleading one
lessons.summary: Match the chart to the question, build an honest chart in Google Sheets, and spot the tricks that make charts lie.
objectives: You will choose between bar, line, pie, scatter and histogram for a given question
You will identify four common ways charts mislead
You will redraw a misleading chart honestly
lessons.body:
A chart can make a point in one second — which is why it can also mislead in one second. Today you will learn to choose the chart that fits the question, and to catch the tricks people use, on purpose or by accident.

## What to do

- For each of the five questions your instructor gives, choose a chart type and say why.
- Build one honest chart from your pivot-table data from last week.
- Study the two misleading charts in the example below and say exactly what is wrong.
- Find a misleading chart online or in an advert and redraw it honestly.

## Understand it

**Match the chart to the question.**

| Question | Chart |
|---|---|
| Which item sold most? (compare categories) | **Bar or column chart** |
| How did attendance change each week? (change over time) | **Line chart** |
| What share of sales was each item? (parts of a whole, few parts) | **Pie chart**, only with 2–5 slices |
| Do longer study hours go with higher scores? (relationship) | **Scatter chart** |
| How are journey times spread out? (distribution) | **Histogram** |

In Google Sheets, select the data, then **Insert → Chart**, and change the type in the Chart editor. Give every chart a title that states the point, label both axes with units (₦, minutes, members), and name the source.

**Four ways charts mislead.**

1. **A cut-off axis.** Two centres had 98 and 102 sign-ups. If the vertical axis starts at 95, the bars are 3 and 7 units tall, so one looks more than twice the other — but the real difference is 4 sign-ups, about 4%. Bar charts should start at zero. (Line charts sometimes may not, if clearly labelled.)
2. **Cherry-picked time.** Showing only the three months when sales rose hides the six months before when they fell. Ask: why does the chart start *there*?
3. **3D and odd shapes.** 3D pies make front slices look bigger than they are. Pictures scaled in both width and height make a doubling look like a quadrupling.
4. **Uneven intervals or two axes.** Gaps between dates that are not equal, or two different vertical axes on one chart, can make two lines appear to move together when they do not.

**An honesty checklist** before you share a chart:
- Does the axis start at zero (for bars)?
- Are the units and source labelled?
- Is the time period fair and stated?
- Would the chart still give the same message to someone who disagrees with you?

**Fewer things, more clearly.** One chart, one message. If a chart needs a paragraph to explain, it is probably the wrong chart — or two charts pretending to be one.

## Key words

- **Bar chart:** compares amounts across categories using bar length
- **Line chart:** shows how a value changes over time
- **Scatter chart:** plots pairs of values to show a possible relationship
- **Histogram:** shows how often values fall into ranges
- **Truncated axis:** an axis that does not start at zero, exaggerating differences

## Read and watch

- [Types of charts and graphs in Google Sheets](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/190718) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Add and edit a chart](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/63824) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Displaying and describing data](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/displaying-describing-data) — Khan Academy

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** master bar and line charts first; they answer most everyday questions.
- **If you already can:** build the misleading and the honest version side by side and present both.
- **If you have colour-blind classmates:** avoid red-green pairs and label lines directly instead of relying on a colour key.

## Learning online

At home, use your pivot table from last week (or any small dataset) to make one honest chart in Google Sheets with a title, labelled axes and a source. Then search a news site or social media for one chart you think misleads, take a screenshot, and rebuild it honestly in Sheets with the same numbers. **Upload as evidence:** your honest chart, the original misleading screenshot, and your redrawn version, with two sentences explaining the trick. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your misleading chart, ready to show — the class will try to spot the trick before you explain it.

## Before the next session

Look through one day's news or social media and count how many charts you see. Check one of them against the honesty checklist.

lessons.title: Drawing a fair conclusion: correlation, causation and how sure you are
lessons.summary: Decide what your data really shows, tell correlation from causation, and say honestly how confident you are.
objectives: You will explain the difference between correlation and causation with examples
You will identify a hidden third factor that could explain a pattern
You will write a conclusion that states how sure you are and why
lessons.body:
"Members who attend more Saturdays score higher in their checks — so attending makes you smarter." Maybe. Or maybe the most motivated members both attend more *and* study more at home. The final step of analysis is the hardest: saying what your data shows, and no more.

## What to do

- Use `=CORREL()` on the sample data (Saturdays attended vs average check score) to measure how strongly they move together.
- List at least two other explanations for the pattern.
- Write a conclusion using the confidence ladder below.
- Return to the question you wrote in week 1 and draft your final answer to it.

## Understand it

**Correlation** means two things tend to move together. **Causation** means one actually makes the other happen. Correlation is easy to find; causation is hard to prove.

**Classic examples.**
- Ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in hot months. Ice cream does not cause drowning: **hot weather** (a **confounder**, or hidden third factor) drives both.
- In Nigeria, umbrella sales and malaria cases both rise in the rainy season. Umbrellas do not spread malaria; the rains bring both more umbrellas and more mosquitoes.

**Measuring correlation.** In Google Sheets, `=CORREL(A2:A31,B2:B31)` gives a number between −1 and 1. Close to **1**: as one rises, the other tends to rise. Close to **−1**: as one rises, the other tends to fall. Close to **0**: no straight-line relationship. A scatter chart lets you *see* it — always look, because one outlier can create or hide a correlation.

**Three questions before you claim a cause.**
1. **Could something else explain both?** (Motivation, family support, distance from the centre.)
2. **Could it run the other way?** Perhaps members who already score well enjoy sessions more, so they attend more.
3. **Could it be chance?** With 8 members, a pattern can appear by luck. With 300, less so. Small samples make for weak conclusions.

The best way to test a cause is an **experiment**: change one thing for one group but not a similar group, and compare. Hospitals test medicines like this. You can too: try a new snack price at one stall and keep the old price at a similar stall for two weeks.

**The confidence ladder.** Choose words that match your evidence:
- *"The data shows…"* — a direct description ("Saturday sales were ₦2,200, Sunday ₦1,100").
- *"There is a strong pattern that…"* — a clear correlation in a decent-sized sample.
- *"This suggests… but other explanations are possible, such as…"* — correlation with plausible confounders.
- *"We cannot tell from this data whether…"* — too little data, or the wrong kind.

**A fair conclusion has four parts:** the answer to the question, the key number, how sure you are (with the reason), and what would make you more sure. Example: "Members who attended 10 or more Saturdays averaged 74% in checks, against 58% for others (r = 0.62, 30 members). This suggests attendance helps, but motivated members may simply do both. A fairer test would compare members who attend similarly but differ in one thing we can change." That is honest — and far more useful than a confident guess.

## Key words

- **Correlation:** two measures tending to move together
- **Causation:** one thing directly making another happen
- **Confounder:** a hidden third factor that affects both measures
- **Sample size:** how many records the conclusion is based on
- **Experiment:** a fair test that changes one thing and compares with a group where it did not change

## Read and watch

- [Describing relationships in data](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/describing-relationships-quantitative-data) — Khan Academy
- [Spurious correlations](https://www.tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations) — Tyler Vigen
- [Google Sheets function list (CORREL)](https://support.google.com/docs/table/25273) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** concentrate on the ice-cream and umbrella examples, then find one of your own.
- **If you already can:** design a small fair experiment for your week-1 question, with a comparison group and a time period.
- **If your data is about people:** be careful with conclusions about groups — never single out an individual.

## Learning online

At home, use the sample attendance-and-score data (or 20+ rows of your own non-personal data, such as daily temperature and cold-drink sales from a shop owner who agrees). Calculate `=CORREL()`, insert a scatter chart, and write your four-part conclusion. Browse the Spurious Correlations site and pick a favourite silly example. **Upload as evidence:** your scatter chart, the CORREL value, and your written conclusion using the confidence ladder. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your final answer to your week-1 question, in one minute — this is the term's showcase.

## Before the next session

Next time you read "X linked to Y" in a headline, ask the three questions from this lesson before you believe that X causes Y.

lessons.title: What HR does, and how work is organised in Nigeria
lessons.summary: Map the people lifecycle that HR looks after, and learn the basic rules that shape work in Nigeria at a youth level.
objectives: You will describe the stages of the people lifecycle and what HR does at each
You will name key Nigerian bodies and rules that shape employment, without giving legal advice
You will map how people join, grow in and leave a team you know
lessons.body:
Every organisation is made of people, and somebody has to make sure they are found fairly, welcomed properly, paid correctly, helped to grow and treated with respect. That is **Human Resources** (HR), sometimes called *People* or *People and Culture*. Today you will see what the job really involves — and the rules it works within in Nigeria.

## What to do

- Draw the people lifecycle (below) as a circle on paper or in Google Slides.
- For each stage, write one thing HR does and one thing that goes wrong when it is done badly.
- Choose a team you know — the centre's volunteers, a church choir, a football club, a family business — and map how people join, grow and leave it.
- Read the Nigerian context section and note two rules you did not know.

## Understand it

**The people lifecycle.** HR's work follows a person through their time with an organisation:

1. **Plan** — work out what roles are needed and what they involve.
2. **Attract and recruit** — advertise fairly and reach a wide pool of people.
3. **Select** — interview and choose fairly, using clear criteria.
4. **Onboard** — welcome and train the new person so they can do the job.
5. **Develop and reward** — feedback, training, pay, recognition, promotion.
6. **Support and protect** — wellbeing, safety, resolving conflict, handling complaints.
7. **Leave well** — resignation, retirement or dismissal handled fairly, with an exit conversation and records kept properly.

When HR is done well, few people notice. When it is done badly, it shows: good people leave, arguments go unresolved, someone is paid late, or a child is put at risk.

**HR also keeps records** — contracts, pay, leave, training, incidents — and must keep personal data private. Nigeria's **Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for how organisations handle people's personal information.

**Work in Nigeria: the basics.** This is general information for learning, not legal advice.
- The **Labour Act** sets basic rules for many workers: written terms of employment, wages, hours and rest, and rules about the work of young people.
- The **National Minimum Wage Act 2024** set the national minimum wage at **₦70,000 a month**.
- The **Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment** oversees labour matters; many workers are represented by trade unions such as those in the Nigeria Labour Congress.
- The **Child's Rights Act 2003** (adopted by most states) protects children from exploitative or dangerous work. School and safety come first.
- Many workers in Nigeria are in the **informal sector** — market traders, artisans, drivers, apprentices — where written contracts are rare. Good HR habits (clear agreements, fair pay on time, respect) matter there too, even in a two-person business.

**Volunteers are people too.** NGG relies on volunteers. They are not paid, but they still need a clear role, a welcome, training, safeguarding checks and thanks. Volunteer management uses almost every stage of the lifecycle.

**Careers in HR** include recruiter, HR officer or generalist, learning and development officer, payroll officer and employee relations adviser. In Nigeria, the **Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria (CIPM)** is the professional body for HR.

## Key words

- **Human Resources (HR):** the work of finding, supporting, developing and looking after people in an organisation
- **People lifecycle:** the stages from planning a role to someone leaving it
- **Onboarding:** welcoming and preparing a new person to do their role
- **Informal sector:** work without formal registration or written contracts, common in Nigeria
- **Minimum wage:** the lowest monthly pay the law allows for covered workers

## Read and watch

- [The ILO in Nigeria](https://www.ilo.org/regions-and-countries/africa/nigeria) — International Labour Organization
- [Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria](https://www.cipmnigeria.org/) — CIPM
- [International Labour Organization](https://www.ilo.org/) — ILO

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** focus on the seven lifecycle stages; the Nigerian rules can be revisited later.
- **If you already can:** interview an adult who has worked in a formal job and ask which lifecycle stage their employer did best and worst.
- **If someone you know works informally:** map their 'lifecycle' too — how did they find the work, learn it, and get paid?

## Learning online

At home, draw your lifecycle circle in Google Slides, Canva or on paper (photograph it). Add one HR action and one 'what goes wrong' for each stage, then a second slide mapping a team you know. Visit the ILO's Nigeria page and note one area of work it supports. **Upload as evidence:** your two slides or photographs. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** the lifecycle stage you think the team you mapped does worst, and one improvement you would suggest.

## Before the next session

Ask one adult how they got their first job or role. Which lifecycle stages did they go through, and which were missing? Then answer the checks below.

lessons.title: Writing a fair job or volunteer advert
lessons.summary: Write a clear, inclusive advert for a volunteer role that attracts a wide range of good applicants.
objectives: You will separate essential from desirable requirements for a role
You will remove words and requirements that unfairly put people off
You will write and test a complete volunteer advert
lessons.body:
An advert decides who applies — and who never does. "Young, energetic graduate needed, must own a car" quietly shuts out older people, people without degrees and people who take the bus, even if none of those things matter for the job. Today you will write an advert that is clear, honest and fair.

## What to do

- Pick a real role: Saturday registration helper at the centre, social-media volunteer, tuck-shop assistant, junior coding mentor.
- Write down what the person will actually do each week.
- Split requirements into **essential** (cannot do the role without) and **desirable** (nice to have).
- Write the advert, then test it with the fairness checklist and a partner.

## Understand it

**What a good advert contains.**
1. **Role title** that says what it is: "Saturday Registration Volunteer", not "Ninja Rockstar".
2. **Purpose** in one sentence: why the role matters.
3. **What you will do** — four or five bullet points of real tasks.
4. **What you need** — essential requirements only, each one truly needed.
5. **Nice to have** — desirable skills, clearly marked as optional.
6. **Practical details** — time commitment, place, start date, whether it is paid, any expenses covered.
7. **What you will gain** — training, experience, a reference.
8. **How to apply and by when**, plus who to contact with questions.
9. **A fairness and safety statement**: everyone is welcome to apply; reasonable adjustments are available; roles with children need safeguarding checks.

**Essential vs desirable.** For a Saturday registration volunteer:
- *Essential:* arrives reliably by 9:30 a.m. on Saturdays; can use a phone or tablet to tick names; friendly with children and parents.
- *Desirable:* speaks Yoruba as well as English; has used Google Sheets.
- *Not needed at all:* a university degree, a car, being "young".

**Words that put people off.** Research on job adverts has found that some wording discourages groups from applying. Watch for:
- **Age words:** "young", "fresh", "digital native" (unfair to older applicants).
- **Gendered words or roles:** "he will", "salesman", "strong man needed". Use "you" and neutral titles.
- **Unnecessary requirements:** "must have a degree" for a role that does not need one; "must own a laptop" when the centre can lend one.
- **Jargon:** "leverage synergies across verticals". Write as you would speak to a friend.
- **Long wish lists.** People who meet seven of ten points often do not apply. Keep "essential" short.

**Accessible format.** Use plain language, short sentences, bullet points and a readable font size. If the advert is an image on WhatsApp, also post the text so screen readers can read it.

**Honesty protects everyone.** Do not promise pay, certificates or trips that are not certain. If the role is unpaid, say so. A misleading advert wastes applicants' time and damages trust in the organisation.

## Key words

- **Essential requirement:** something a person must have to do the role
- **Desirable requirement:** something helpful but not required
- **Inclusive language:** wording that welcomes people of every background
- **Reasonable adjustment:** a change that removes a barrier for someone, such as a disabled applicant
- **Safeguarding check:** a check that someone is safe to work with children

## Read and watch

- [Recruitment](https://www.acas.org.uk/recruitment) — Acas (UK workplace advice service)
- [CIPD — the professional body for HR and people development](https://www.cipd.org/) — CIPD
- [Hemingway Editor (readability checker)](https://hemingwayapp.com/) — Hemingway

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** start from the nine-part structure and fill each part with one or two lines.
- **If you already can:** write two versions — a full advert and a 60-word WhatsApp version — that say the same essentials.
- **If you speak another Nigerian language:** translate the key points and check they still sound welcoming.

## Learning online

At home, write the advert in Google Docs using the nine headings. Paste it into the free Hemingway Editor website to check readability, and simplify long sentences. Ask one family member who is *not* your target applicant to read it and tell you if anything puts them off. **Upload as evidence:** your final advert, the list of essential vs desirable requirements, and one change you made after the fairness check. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your advert's first two lines to read aloud — we will test whether they make people want to read on.

## Before the next session

Find one real job advert online and mark any words or requirements that seem unfair. Then complete the checks below.

lessons.title: Interviewing and fair selection
lessons.summary: Plan a structured interview with clear criteria and a scoring sheet, and learn how bias creeps into choosing people.
objectives: You will write structured interview questions linked to the role's criteria
You will build a scoring rubric so every candidate is judged the same way
You will name common biases in selection and one way to reduce each
lessons.body:
Interviews feel like a way to "get a sense" of someone. But that gut feeling is often bias: we tend to like people who remind us of ourselves, went to our school or speak like us. **Structured interviews** — the same questions, the same scoring, for everyone — are one of the most reliable ways to choose fairly.

## What to do

- Use the advert you wrote last week. List the three or four essential criteria.
- Write one or two questions for each criterion, including at least one **behavioural** question.
- Build a scoring sheet in Google Sheets: a 1–4 scale with a description of each score.
- Role-play an interview in threes: candidate, interviewer, observer. Swap roles.

## Understand it

**Start from the criteria.** If the role needs *reliability, friendliness with children, and basic tablet use*, every question should help you judge one of those — nothing else.

**Kinds of question.**
- **Behavioural:** "Tell me about a time you had to be somewhere on time every week. How did you manage it?" Past behaviour is a good guide to future behaviour.
- **Situational:** "A parent arrives angry because their child's name is not on the list. What would you do?"
- **Skills:** "Here is a list on a tablet — please find Amaka Obi and mark her present."

Encourage full answers with the **STAR** shape: **S**ituation, **T**ask, **A**ction, **R**esult. Younger candidates may need a prompt: "What did *you* do next?"

**A scoring rubric.** For each criterion, describe each score before the interviews start:

| Score | Friendliness with children |
|---|---|
| 1 | No example, or an example showing impatience |
| 2 | A vague example, little detail |
| 3 | A clear example of being kind and patient |
| 4 | A clear example plus how they adapted to a child's needs |

Each interviewer scores **alone** first, then the panel discusses. Add up scores per candidate in Sheets (`=SUM(B2:D2)`). The decision should follow the scores — and if the panel overrides them, write down why.

**Common biases and fixes.**
- **Affinity bias** — favouring people like us. *Fix:* use the rubric; have a mixed panel.
- **Halo effect** — one good thing (a confident smile, a famous school) colours everything. *Fix:* score each criterion separately.
- **First impressions** — deciding in the first minute. *Fix:* score only after the full answer.
- **Name or accent bias** — judging by ethnicity, region or how someone speaks. *Fix:* focus on evidence; some organisations remove names when shortlisting.
- **Contrast effect** — a candidate seems better or worse because of who came just before. *Fix:* score against the rubric, not against each other, until the end.

**Questions you must not ask.** Questions about religion, ethnicity, marital status, pregnancy plans, family wealth or health (unless directly relevant and handled properly) are unfair and can be discriminatory. Ask only what the role needs.

**Be kind to every candidate.** Explain how the interview works, give them time, and tell everyone the outcome — including those who were not chosen, with a short piece of useful feedback if they ask.

## Key words

- **Structured interview:** an interview where every candidate gets the same questions and scoring
- **Behavioural question:** a question asking about what someone actually did in the past
- **STAR:** Situation, Task, Action, Result — a shape for full answers
- **Rubric:** a scoring guide that describes each level in advance
- **Affinity bias:** favouring people who seem similar to ourselves

## Read and watch

- [Recruitment, including interviews](https://www.acas.org.uk/recruitment) — Acas
- [CIPD — people professionals' body](https://www.cipd.org/) — CIPD
- [Get started with Google Sheets](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6000292) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** write three questions only, one per criterion, and a simple 1–4 score for each.
- **If you already can:** add a short practical task to the interview and a rubric for it.
- **If you are nervous about role-play:** start as the observer, using the bias list as your checklist.

## Learning online

At home, write your questions in Google Docs and your scoring sheet in Google Sheets (criteria across the top, candidates down the side, a total column). Run a practice interview over a video call or with a family member playing the candidate, and score it honestly. **Upload as evidence:** your question list, your rubric with a description for each score, and one completed practice scoring sheet (use an invented candidate name). **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your best behavioural question — we will run mini-interviews in breakout rooms.

## Before the next session

Think of a time you judged someone quickly on a first impression. Which bias from today was it, and was the first impression right?

lessons.title: Onboarding a new team member
lessons.summary: Plan a new volunteer's first day, first week and first month so they feel welcome, safe and able to do the job.
objectives: You will explain why the first weeks decide whether people stay
You will design a first-day, first-week and first-month onboarding plan
You will build a checklist and a welcome message for a new team member
lessons.body:
Think about your first day at a new school or club. Did someone show you where things were and introduce you, or were you left to work it out? People decide very quickly whether they belong. **Onboarding** is how an organisation makes that decision an easy "yes".

## What to do

- Pick the role from your advert in week 2.
- List what a new person must *know*, must *have* and must *meet* to do it.
- Plan the first day, first week and first month in a simple table.
- Build an onboarding checklist in Google Sheets with a tick box for each item and the name of the person responsible.

## Understand it

**Onboarding is more than paperwork.** It has four parts, sometimes called the four Cs:
1. **Compliance** — the rules and forms: safeguarding policy, code of conduct, consent, emergency contacts, photo permissions.
2. **Clarification** — what the role is, what good looks like, who to ask.
3. **Culture** — how things are done here: values, how people talk to each other, what happens on a typical Saturday.
4. **Connection** — relationships: a buddy, introductions, being included in the team chat.

Many organisations do the first well and forget the last three. People rarely leave because a form was missing; they leave because they felt lost or alone.

**Before day one.** Send a welcome message with the date, time, address, what to wear, what to bring, who will meet them and a phone number to call if they are lost. Prepare anything they need: a name badge, a login, a tablet.

**Day one.**
- Someone meets them by name at the gate.
- A short tour: toilets, first-aid kit, fire exits, where to sit, where water is.
- Introductions to the team and their **buddy** — an experienced volunteer they can ask "silly" questions.
- **Safeguarding briefing**: who the safeguarding lead is and what to do if a child tells them something worrying.
- One small, real task they can complete successfully.

**First week (or first few Saturdays).** Shadow the buddy, then do the task with support, then alone with a check. Short check-in at the end of each session: "What went well? What was confusing?"

**First month.** A 15-minute conversation with their lead: is the role what they expected? What training would help? Set one goal for the next month.

**A worked checklist (part):**

| Item | When | Who | Done |
|---|---|---|---|
| Welcome WhatsApp message sent | 3 days before | Volunteer lead | ☐ |
| Safeguarding policy read and signed | Before day one | New volunteer | ☐ |
| Buddy assigned and introduced | Day one | Volunteer lead | ☐ |
| First-month check-in | Week 4 | Volunteer lead | ☐ |

In Google Sheets, use **Insert → Checkbox** for the Done column and `=COUNTIF(D2:D20,TRUE)/COUNTA(A2:A20)` to show the percentage complete.

**Measure it.** Ask new people after a month: "How welcome did you feel, from 1 to 5?" and "What one thing should we add?" Then improve the plan.

## Key words

- **Onboarding:** the process of welcoming and preparing a new team member
- **Buddy:** an experienced team member who supports a newcomer
- **Compliance:** the forms, policies and checks that must be completed
- **Shadowing:** watching an experienced person do the task before trying it
- **Check-in:** a short conversation to see how someone is getting on

## Read and watch

- [Inductions](https://www.acas.org.uk/inductions) — Acas
- [Add and use checkboxes](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/7684717) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [CIPD — people development](https://www.cipd.org/) — CIPD

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** plan day one in detail and leave the first month as three bullet points.
- **If you already can:** create a one-page welcome guide in Google Docs or Canva for the role.
- **If you have just joined NGG yourself:** use your own first weeks as research — what helped, what was missing?

## Learning online

At home, build your onboarding checklist in Google Sheets with columns *Item, When, Who, Done* (checkboxes) and a percentage-complete formula. Draft the welcome message in Google Docs or WhatsApp notes (do not send it). **Upload as evidence:** your day-one / week-one / month-one plan, the checklist screenshot with at least ten items, and your welcome message. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** the one 'connection' idea you think would make the biggest difference to a nervous new volunteer.

## Before the next session

Ask someone who started a new job, school or club recently what made their first day better or worse. Add one idea to your plan.

lessons.title: Giving and receiving feedback with SBI
lessons.summary: Use the Situation–Behaviour–Impact model to give feedback that is specific, fair and useful, and practise receiving it well.
objectives: You will give feedback using Situation, Behaviour and Impact
You will tell the difference between describing behaviour and judging a person
You will practise receiving feedback calmly and choosing what to do with it
lessons.body:
"You're lazy." "Good job!" Neither tells the person what to do next. Feedback only helps if it is specific enough to act on and fair enough to be heard. The **SBI model** — Situation, Behaviour, Impact — is a simple way to make it both.

## What to do

- Learn the three parts of SBI from the examples below.
- Rewrite five vague pieces of feedback into SBI form.
- In pairs, give each other one piece of positive SBI feedback and one improvement, about a real task from this term.
- Practise the receiving steps: listen, ask, thank, decide.

## Understand it

**SBI**, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership, has three parts:

- **Situation** — when and where. "During registration last Saturday, around 9:45…"
- **Behaviour** — what the person *did* or *said*, as a camera would record it. "…you greeted each family by name and showed new parents where to sit…"
- **Impact** — the effect on you, the team or others. "…which meant the queue moved quickly and two parents told me they felt welcome."

**Behaviour, not character.** "You were disrespectful" is a judgement about the person. "You looked at your phone while Chidi was presenting" is behaviour. People can change behaviour; being labelled makes them defensive.

**Improvement feedback in SBI:**
"In Thursday's planning call (S), you joined 20 minutes late without sending a message (B). We waited to start, so we ran out of time to agree the rota (I)."
Then add a **question or request**: "What would help you let us know next time?" This turns it into a conversation, sometimes called **SBI-I** (with *Intent* or *Inquiry*).

**Positive feedback matters as much.** Specific praise tells people exactly what to keep doing. "Good job" is pleasant but vague; "When the projector failed (S), you switched to the whiteboard without fuss (B), and the session carried on with no time lost (I)" teaches everyone what good looks like.

**Timing and place.** Give feedback soon, while it is fresh. Praise can be public; improvement feedback is usually private. Check your own mood: if you are angry, wait until you can be calm and fair.

**Receiving feedback well** is a skill too:
1. **Listen** without interrupting or defending yourself.
2. **Ask** to understand: "Can you give me an example?"
3. **Thank** the person — feedback takes courage.
4. **Decide** what to do. You do not have to agree with all of it, but take time to consider it before rejecting it.

**Feedback across ages and roles.** In many Nigerian settings, younger people are taught not to correct elders. SBI helps here: describing a situation and its impact respectfully ("When the session started late, the children got restless") is very different from criticising someone. If in doubt, ask permission first: "Can I share something I noticed?"

**Safeguarding comes first.** If feedback concerns someone's safety or a child being hurt, do not handle it as ordinary feedback — tell the safeguarding lead.

## Key words

- **Feedback:** information about how someone's actions affected others or the work
- **Situation:** the specific time and place something happened
- **Behaviour:** what someone did or said, described without judgement
- **Impact:** the effect the behaviour had
- **Judgement:** a label about a person's character rather than a description of what they did

## Read and watch

- [Closing the gap between intent and impact (SBI)](https://www.ccl.org/articles/leading-effectively-articles/closing-the-gap-between-intent-vs-impact-sbii/) — Center for Creative Leadership
- [Center for Creative Leadership](https://www.ccl.org/) — CCL
- [Mental health information](https://www.mind.org.uk/) — Mind

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** write positive SBI feedback only today; improvement feedback can come next week.
- **If you already can:** practise SBI-I, adding a genuine question, and notice how the other person responds.
- **If speaking up is hard for you:** write your feedback first and read it out, or send it in writing using the same three parts.

## Learning online

At home, rewrite the five vague statements your instructor shares (or these: "Nice work", "You're always late", "That was rude", "Great presentation", "Be more serious") into SBI form in a Google Doc. Then record a short voice note or video (under one minute) giving SBI feedback to a family member or friend about something they really did — with their permission. **Upload as evidence:** your five rewrites, and either the recording or a written script of the feedback and how they responded. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** one piece of positive SBI feedback for a classmate's work this term — we will share these in the session.

## Before the next session

Notice one moment this week when someone gives you feedback. Practise the four receiving steps and write down what you decided to do with it.

lessons.title: Resolving conflict and looking after wellbeing
lessons.summary: Use a calm, step-by-step approach to resolve disagreements in a team, and know how to look after your own and others' wellbeing.
objectives: You will describe five ways people respond to conflict and when each fits
You will use a step-by-step process to help two people resolve a disagreement
You will recognise signs that someone is struggling and know where to signpost them
lessons.body:
Wherever people work together, they will disagree: about the rota, about who did the most work, about a careless comment. Conflict is normal. What matters is whether it is handled early and fairly — or left to grow until good people walk away. Today you learn to do the first.

## What to do

- Read the five conflict styles and think of when you have used each one.
- In threes, role-play a conflict from the scenarios your instructor gives (two people in conflict, one helper using the steps below).
- Make a wellbeing signpost card for your team: who to talk to and how to reach them.
- Reflect on what helped the conversation and what made it harder.

## Understand it

**Five ways people respond to conflict** (from the Thomas–Kilmann model):
- **Competing** — "my way". Useful in an emergency; damaging if used all the time.
- **Accommodating** — "your way". Kind when the issue matters more to them; harmful if you always give in.
- **Avoiding** — "not now". Fine for trivial issues or to cool down; problems grow if never addressed.
- **Compromising** — "meet in the middle". Quick and fair-seeming, but both sides lose something.
- **Collaborating** — "let's find what works for both". Takes longer, but often gives the best result.

No style is always right. Good team members choose deliberately rather than by habit.

**Positions and interests.** Ada says, "I'm not doing the 8 a.m. registration shift any more." That is her **position**. Ask why: she has to take her younger brother to lessons first. That is her **interest**. Once interests are on the table, solutions appear: she could take the 10 a.m. shift and swap with someone who prefers mornings.

**Five steps to help resolve a disagreement:**
1. **Calm and private.** Find a quiet moment; agree to listen without interrupting.
2. **Each person explains** what happened and how it affected them — using "I" statements: "I felt left out when…" rather than "You always…".
3. **Find the interests** behind each position. The helper summarises: "So what matters to you is…"
4. **Generate options** together. Aim for several before choosing.
5. **Agree and check.** Write down who will do what, and agree a date to see if it is working.

If the conflict involves bullying, harassment, discrimination or safety, it is **not** a matter for peer mediation. Report it to the lead or safeguarding officer straight away.

**Wellbeing.** People do their best work when they are rested and supported. Signs someone may be struggling: withdrawing from the team, changes in mood, missing sessions, saying they cannot cope. You are not expected to be a counsellor. You can:
- **Notice** and **ask** privately: "You seem quieter than usual — are you okay?"
- **Listen** without judging or rushing to fix it.
- **Signpost** to a trusted adult: a parent, the centre lead, a school counsellor, a faith leader the person trusts.
- If someone is in danger or talks about harming themselves, **tell a trusted adult immediately**, even if they asked you to keep it secret.

**Look after yourself too.** Sleep, food, movement, time with people you like, and saying no when your load is too heavy are not luxuries. A team where people can say "I need a break" is a stronger team.

## Key words

- **Conflict style:** a typical way of responding to disagreement
- **Position:** what someone says they want
- **Interest:** the underlying reason or need behind a position
- **Mediation:** a neutral person helping others reach agreement
- **Signposting:** pointing someone to the right person or service for help

## Read and watch

- [Conflict and resolution](https://www.acas.org.uk/conflict-and-resolution) — Acas
- [Tips for everyday living](https://www.mind.org.uk/information-support/tips-for-everyday-living/) — Mind
- [Support for young people](https://www.youngminds.org.uk/young-person/) — YoungMinds

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** focus on 'I' statements and the difference between positions and interests.
- **If you already can:** act as the helper in a role-play and practise summarising each person's interests accurately.
- **If any of today's topics are difficult for you personally:** you can step out of the role-play and talk to your instructor instead.

## Learning online

At home, write a short conflict scenario between two volunteers (invented names) and script how a helper would take them through the five steps. Make a wellbeing signpost card in Canva or Google Docs: three trusted people or places a member could go to, how to reach them, and one self-care idea. Do not include anyone's private phone number without their permission. **Upload as evidence:** your scripted scenario and your signpost card. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your scenario — we will act out a few in breakout rooms, and you can choose to be the observer.

## Before the next session

Think about your own most common conflict style. Write down one situation this week where a different style might have worked better.

lessons.title: Processes and flowcharts
lessons.summary: Map a real process as a flowchart with start, steps, decisions and end, and use it to spot confusion and waste.
objectives: You will describe a process as inputs, steps and outputs
You will draw a flowchart using standard symbols
You will use a flowchart to find a step that causes delay or confusion
lessons.body:
Every organisation runs on processes — the repeated steps that turn something in into something out. Registration, ordering stock, paying volunteers' transport, closing up after a session. When a process lives only in one person's head, it breaks the day that person is absent. Drawing it is the first step to running it well.

## What to do

- Choose a process you know: Saturday check-in at the centre, buying and selling at the tuck shop, getting a lesson ready.
- Write its steps on sticky notes or in a list, one action per note.
- Turn the list into a flowchart with the standard symbols, including at least one decision.
- Walk through it with a partner, acting it out, and mark any step that is unclear, repeated or slow.

## Understand it

**What is a process?** A sequence of steps that turns **inputs** (materials, information, people) into **outputs** (a product, a service, a decision). Check-in at the centre: inputs are arriving members and the attendance list; the output is a list of who is present and children safely inside.

**Flowchart symbols.**
- **Oval** — start and end ("Member arrives", "Member seated").
- **Rectangle** — an action ("Find name on list").
- **Diamond** — a decision with yes/no branches ("Name on list?").
- **Parallelogram** — input or output of information ("Record time of arrival").
- **Arrows** — show the order.

**A worked example: Saturday check-in.**
1. *Start:* member arrives at the gate.
2. Volunteer asks name.
3. *Decision:* is the name on today's list?
   - **Yes** → tick name and record time → hand name badge → member goes to the hall.
   - **No** → *Decision:* is the member registered for NGG at all?
     - **Yes** → add to today's list → continue as above.
     - **No** → call the parent or guardian and the centre lead → member waits in the safe waiting area.
4. *End:* member seated, or waiting safely.

Drawing it shows things a list hides. Here, the "not on the list" branch has no time limit — a child could wait a long time. The flowchart prompts a question: *who decides, and how quickly?*

**Good flowchart habits.**
- One action per box, starting with a verb: "Check", "Record", "Call".
- Every decision diamond has exactly two labelled exits.
- Flow from top to bottom or left to right.
- Name the **owner** of each step if several people are involved (a **swimlane** flowchart gives each person their own lane).
- Keep it to one page. If it is bigger, split it into sub-processes.

**What to look for once it is drawn.**
- **Waiting** — places where someone or something sits idle.
- **Rework** — loops where work goes back to be redone.
- **Hand-offs** — every time a task passes to a new person, information can get lost.
- **Missing exits** — decisions with no "no" path, or a path that leads nowhere.

A flowchart is also a training tool: a new volunteer can follow it on day one. Pair it with a short written procedure and the process no longer depends on one person.

## Key words

- **Process:** a repeated sequence of steps turning inputs into outputs
- **Flowchart:** a diagram of a process using standard shapes and arrows
- **Decision point:** a step where the path splits depending on a yes/no answer
- **Swimlane:** a flowchart layout giving each person or team their own lane
- **Hand-off:** the moment a task passes from one person to another

## Read and watch

- [What is a flowchart?](https://asq.org/quality-resources/flowchart) — ASQ (American Society for Quality)
- [diagrams.net — free flowchart tool](https://app.diagrams.net/) — draw.io
- [Insert drawings in Google Docs](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/179740) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** map a short process with one decision, such as making tea or charging a phone.
- **If you already can:** draw a swimlane flowchart showing who owns each step.
- **If you have no computer:** draw on paper with a ruler and photograph it clearly.

## Learning online

At home, use the free diagrams.net website (no account needed — choose "Device" to save) or Google Drawings to build your flowchart; on a phone, paper and a clear photo work fine. Choose a process from your home or centre, such as preparing for a Saturday session. **Upload as evidence:** your flowchart image with at least eight steps and one decision, plus two sentences naming the step most likely to cause delay or confusion. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your flowchart, ready to share on screen — a classmate will try to follow it without your help.

## Before the next session

Watch one process happen in real life this week — at a shop, a bus park or at home — and note one step that seemed slow or unclear.

lessons.title: Queues and bottlenecks: the canteen line
lessons.summary: Find the slowest step in a queue, calculate how many people it can serve, and test fixes that actually shorten the line.
objectives: You will time each step of a queue and identify the bottleneck
You will calculate the capacity of a process from the bottleneck
You will test whether a proposed fix moves the bottleneck
lessons.body:
Break time. Sixty hungry students, thirty minutes, one canteen. Some wait so long they never eat. Is the answer more staff, a bigger room, or something else? Operations gives you a way to answer with numbers instead of guesses.

## What to do

- Time each step of a real queue (the canteen, a bank, a tuck shop, registration) for at least ten people. Use a phone stopwatch.
- Work out the average time per person at each step.
- Find the bottleneck and calculate how many people per hour the queue can serve.
- Propose two fixes and calculate what each would change.

## Understand it

**The canteen line.** At a school in Lagos, each student goes through three steps:

| Step | Average time per student |
|---|---|
| 1. Order and pay | 30 seconds |
| 2. Serve food | 45 seconds |
| 3. Collect drink | 20 seconds |

**The bottleneck** is the slowest step: serving food at 45 seconds. However fast the other steps are, the line can only move as fast as its slowest station. Students pile up in front of the server and the drinks person waits idle.

**Capacity.** In 30 minutes there are 30 × 60 = 1,800 seconds.
- Order and pay could handle 1,800 ÷ 30 = **60** students.
- Serve food can handle 1,800 ÷ 45 = **40** students.
- Drinks could handle 1,800 ÷ 20 = **90** students.

So the whole canteen serves at most **40** students in a 30-minute break. With 60 students arriving, **20** go without — unless something changes.

**Fix 1: a faster till.** Making ordering quicker does nothing; it is not the bottleneck. Students reach the server sooner and wait there instead. *Improving a step that is not the bottleneck does not increase output.*

**Fix 2: a second server.** Two servers together handle one student every 22.5 seconds on average. Now serving can handle 1,800 ÷ 22.5 = 80 students. The bottleneck **moves** to order and pay (60 students). The canteen now serves all 60. The 10 seconds saved per student at the serving station has become the new spare time.

**Fix 3: pre-ordering.** Students order and pay the day before; on the day, the food is plated in advance. That shortens *both* order-and-pay and serving times.

**Other queue ideas.**
- **Spread arrivals:** stagger break times by class, so 30 arrive at once instead of 60.
- **One queue, several servers** is usually fairer and faster than a separate queue for each server.
- **Make waiting easier:** shade, a menu to read while waiting, a clear sign showing the queue.
- **Measure again** after every change. The real test is the new timing, not the idea.

**Utilisation.** If drinks takes 20 seconds but a student only arrives every 45 seconds, the drinks person is busy 20 ÷ 45 ≈ 44% of the time. Very high utilisation (near 100%) means long queues build quickly; very low means you might move that person to the bottleneck.

## Key words

- **Queue:** a line of people or items waiting to be served
- **Bottleneck:** the slowest step, which limits the whole process
- **Capacity:** the most a process can handle in a given time
- **Cycle time:** the average time one step takes per person or item
- **Utilisation:** the share of time a person or machine is busy

## Read and watch

- [Bottleneck](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/bottleneck.asp) — Investopedia
- [Queuing theory](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/q/queuing-theory.asp) — Investopedia
- [Google Sheets function list (AVERAGE)](https://support.google.com/docs/table/25273) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** time just one step for ten people and calculate its capacity per hour.
- **If you already can:** model the queue in Google Sheets so changing a step time updates every capacity and shows the bottleneck automatically with `=MIN()`.
- **If you cannot get to a real queue:** time your family serving dinner, or use the canteen numbers above.

## Learning online

At home, time a real queue you can safely watch — a shop, a filling station, family members at a water tap — or time steps in a home routine such as getting three people's plates served. Put the times into Google Sheets: one column per step, `=AVERAGE()` per step, then capacity `=1800/average` for a 30-minute window. Do not film or photograph strangers. **Upload as evidence:** your timing sheet with averages, capacities and the bottleneck highlighted, plus your two fixes and what each changes. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your bottleneck and your best fix — we will test each other's fixes with the numbers.

## Before the next session

Next time you are in a queue, guess the bottleneck before you reach the front. Were you right?

lessons.title: Quality checks and checklists
lessons.summary: Build a checklist and a simple check sheet so a product or service comes out right every time, and measure the defect rate.
objectives: You will write a clear checklist for a repeated task
You will record defects on a check sheet and calculate a defect rate
You will design one mistake-proofing step that stops an error happening
lessons.body:
Pilots, surgeons and engineers use checklists — not because they are careless, but because even skilled people forget steps when they are busy or tired. Quality is not luck; it is a system. Today you build one for a product or service you know.

## What to do

- Choose a repeated task: bottling zobo, preparing a lesson room, packing an online order, setting up a laptop for a class.
- Write a checklist of the critical steps.
- Use a check sheet to tally defects over a batch (real or from the example).
- Calculate the defect rate and design one mistake-proofing change.

## Understand it

**Quality** means meeting the standard the customer expects, every time. There are two broad approaches:
- **Quality control** — check the finished product and catch problems before the customer does.
- **Quality assurance** — design the process so problems are less likely in the first place.

Good operations use both, but prevention is cheaper than inspection.

**A good checklist:**
- Covers only the **critical** steps — the ones that, if missed, cause real problems. Long checklists get skipped.
- Uses short, clear actions: "Lid tightened — turn test", not "Ensure appropriate closure".
- Says **when** it is used (before, during or after) and **who** signs it.
- Is tested on real people and improved.

**Example: zobo bottling checklist (before sealing each crate).**
☐ Bottles washed and rinsed with clean water
☐ Zobo strained — no leaves in the bottle
☐ Filled to the line on the label
☐ Lid tightened — turn test
☐ Label straight, date written
☐ Crate stored in the cool box

**A check sheet** is a tally of what goes wrong, so you can see patterns. In one batch of **120** bottles:

| Defect | Tally | Count |
|---|---|---|
| Underfilled | IIII | 4 |
| Loose lid | I | 1 |
| Label missing date | I | 1 |
| **Total defective** | | **6** |

**Defect rate** = defective ÷ total × 100 = 6 ÷ 120 × 100 = **5%**. Underfilling is the biggest problem (4 of 6 defects, about 67%). That is where to focus first — a principle sometimes called the **80/20 rule** or **Pareto**: a few causes usually create most of the problems.

**Mistake-proofing** (Japanese: *poka-yoke*) changes the process so the mistake is hard or impossible to make. For underfilling: a marked jug that holds exactly one bottle's worth, or a line painted on the funnel. For missing dates: a date stamp you set each morning instead of writing by hand. Mistake-proofing beats "be more careful" every time.

**Quality in services.** For a Saturday session, defects might be "projector not working at start", "no attendance list printed", "first-aid kit not restocked". A 'room ready' checklist done 30 minutes before the start prevents most of them.

**Track it over time.** In Google Sheets, record the defect rate for each batch and plot it on a line chart. If the rate drops after your mistake-proofing change, you have evidence it worked.

## Key words

- **Quality control:** checking outputs to catch defects
- **Quality assurance:** designing the process so defects are less likely
- **Defect rate:** defective items as a percentage of the total
- **Check sheet:** a simple tally form for recording problems as they occur
- **Poka-yoke:** mistake-proofing: designing a step so an error is hard to make

## Read and watch

- [Check sheet](https://asq.org/quality-resources/check-sheet) — ASQ
- [Mistake-proofing (poka-yoke)](https://asq.org/quality-resources/mistake-proofing) — ASQ
- [Pareto chart](https://asq.org/quality-resources/pareto) — ASQ

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** write a five-item checklist and test it once.
- **If you already can:** draw a Pareto chart of your defects in Google Sheets (sorted column chart) and add a cumulative percentage line.
- **If you do not make a product:** use a service such as cleaning a room or preparing a lesson; defects are things that went wrong.

## Learning online

At home, pick a task you repeat — making breakfast for the family, packing your school bag, washing plates — and write a checklist in Google Docs. Use it for five days and keep a check sheet of anything that went wrong. In Google Sheets, calculate your defect rate (`=defects/total*100`). **Upload as evidence:** your checklist, your five-day check sheet, the defect rate, and your mistake-proofing idea with a photo or sketch. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your mistake-proofing idea — the class will vote on the cleverest.

## Before the next session

Look for one example of mistake-proofing in everyday life (a plug that only fits one way, a car that beeps when a seat belt is off). Note it for the next session.

lessons.title: Inventory basics: reorder points and FIFO
lessons.summary: Calculate when to reorder stock so you never run out, and rotate it first-in, first-out so nothing expires on the shelf.
objectives: You will calculate a reorder point from daily use, lead time and safety stock
You will apply first-in, first-out (FIFO) to stock with expiry dates
You will build a Google Sheets stock tracker that flags when to reorder
lessons.body:
Run out of pure water at the tuck shop on a hot Saturday and you lose sales and disappoint people. Order too much and it ties up cash and takes up space — and some products expire. **Inventory management** is the art of having enough, but not too much, at the right time.

## What to do

- Pick three products sold at the tuck shop, a family shop or a market stall you know.
- For each, estimate daily sales, how long the supplier takes to deliver, and a safety stock.
- Calculate a reorder point for each and put them into a Google Sheets tracker.
- Rearrange (or plan) a shelf so the oldest stock is sold first.

## Understand it

**Why stock matters.** Too little stock (**stock-out**) loses sales and customers. Too much stock (**overstock**) ties up cash you could use elsewhere, needs space and risks spoilage or damage. The goal is a sensible middle.

**The reorder point.** Reorder when stock falls to a level that will last until the new delivery arrives, plus a cushion:

**Reorder point = average daily use × lead time (days) + safety stock**

*Example: pure water at the tuck shop.*
- Sells on average **6 bags a day** (each bag holds 20 sachets).
- The supplier takes **2 days** to deliver after you order — the **lead time**.
- Keep **4 bags** of **safety stock** for unusually hot days or late deliveries.

Reorder point = 6 × 2 + 4 = **16 bags**. When the count drops to 16, order. During the 2-day wait you expect to sell 12, leaving 4 as cushion when the delivery arrives.

**How much to order?** A simple approach: enough to last a set period. If you reorder weekly, order about 6 × 7 = 42 bags, adjusted for space, cash and how fast it spoils. Bigger orders may get a better price but need more cash and storage.

**FIFO — first in, first out.** Sell the oldest stock first. When a new delivery arrives, put it **behind** the existing stock on the shelf. This matters for anything with an expiry date: drinks, bread, medicines, snacks. If new stock is placed in front, older items sit at the back until they expire and must be thrown away — that is money in the bin.

*Example:* the shelf has 10 packs of biscuits expiring 15 March. 20 new packs arrive expiring 30 April. Under FIFO, the 15 March packs move to the front; the new ones go behind.

**Stock counts.** Write down what you have at the end of each day. In Google Sheets:

| Item | In stock | Daily use | Lead time | Safety | Reorder point | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pure water (bags) | 14 | 6 | 2 | 4 | `=C2*D2+E2` → 16 | REORDER |
| Biscuits (packs) | 30 | 5 | 3 | 5 | 20 | OK |

The Status column uses `=IF(B2<=F2,"REORDER","OK")`, and conditional formatting turns "REORDER" red.

**Shrinkage.** If your count is lower than your sales records say it should be, stock has been lost, damaged or taken. A regular count against records catches this early.

## Key words

- **Inventory (stock):** goods held to sell or use
- **Lead time:** the time between placing an order and receiving it
- **Safety stock:** extra stock kept to cover unexpected demand or delays
- **Reorder point:** the stock level at which a new order should be placed
- **FIFO:** first in, first out: sell or use the oldest stock first

## Read and watch

- [First in, first out (FIFO)](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/f/fifo.asp) — Investopedia
- [Inventory management](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/i/inventory-management.asp) — Investopedia
- [Conditional formatting](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/78413) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** calculate the reorder point for one product only, using the pure-water numbers as a model.
- **If you already can:** add a "days of stock left" column (`=B2/C2`) and an order quantity for a week's supply.
- **If you do not know real figures:** ask a shop owner politely, or estimate sensibly and say they are estimates.

## Learning online

At home, choose three items your household buys regularly (rice, bread, toothpaste, data bundles) or that a family shop sells. Estimate daily use, how long it takes to buy more, and a safety stock. Build the tracker in Google Sheets with the reorder-point formula, an IF status column and red conditional formatting. Check your kitchen or store cupboard: is the oldest stock at the front? **Upload as evidence:** your tracker screenshot and a before-and-after photo (or description) of a shelf arranged FIFO. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** the item you would most likely run out of, and the reorder point you calculated for it.

## Before the next session

Update your tracker's stock count each day for a week. Did any item reach its reorder point?
