lessons.title: Logistics and delivery in Lagos
lessons.summary: Plan deliveries across Lagos by choosing routes, batching orders and costing each drop, while keeping customers informed.
objectives: You will plan a delivery route that accounts for traffic and time windows
You will calculate cost per delivery and show how batching lowers it
You will design a simple delivery process with tracking and proof of delivery
lessons.body:
In Lagos, a 15-kilometre trip can take 25 minutes at 6 a.m. or two hours at 6 p.m. A small business selling online lives or dies on whether its deliveries arrive on time, in good condition and at a cost that leaves some profit. That is **logistics** — moving things to where they are needed.

## What to do

- Take five invented orders spread across Lagos (for example Yaba, Surulere, Ikeja, Lekki Phase 1, Ajah).
- Use Google Maps to estimate travel time between them at two different times of day.
- Plan a route that batches orders sensibly, and calculate the cost per delivery.
- Write the five messages a customer would receive from order to delivery.

## Understand it

**What logistics covers.** Getting goods from supplier to business (*inbound*) and from business to customer (*outbound*): transport, routes, timing, packaging, storage and information about where things are.

**Lagos realities to plan for.**
- **Traffic** varies hugely by time and day; mornings into the Island and evenings off it are slowest. Bridges (Third Mainland, Carter, Eko) are pinch points.
- **Rain** slows everything and can flood some roads.
- **Transport options:** dispatch riders on motorbikes, cars, tricycles, buses, BRT, and ferries on some routes. Lagos State restricts commercial motorbikes in many areas and on highways, so check which routes riders can legally use.
- **Addresses** can be hard to find; a landmark ("opposite the filling station") and a phone call often matter more than a street number.

**Batching saves money.** A dispatch rider charges ₦2,500 per single trip from Yaba to Surulere. Sending four separate riders to four nearby addresses costs 4 × ₦2,500 = **₦10,000**. One rider on a planned route covering all four might charge **₦5,000**, which is ₦5,000 ÷ 4 = **₦1,250 per delivery** — half the cost. The trade-off: the last customer waits longer, so batch orders that are close together and promise realistic times.

**Planning a route.**
1. Group orders by area (Mainland vs Island; north vs south).
2. Avoid crossing the same bridge twice.
3. Respect **time windows** ("must arrive before 2 p.m.").
4. Use Google Maps' "depart at" or "arrive by" option to estimate travel time at the real hour.
5. Build in a buffer: if Maps says 50 minutes, plan for at least an hour.

**Cost per delivery** includes more than the rider's fee: packaging, phone calls, any failed delivery (the customer was not in, so the rider goes twice), and refunds for damaged goods. If an item sells for ₦6,000 with ₦1,500 profit before delivery, a ₦2,500 delivery fee you absorb turns it into a ₦1,000 **loss**. Either charge delivery, set a minimum order for free delivery, or batch.

**Keeping customers informed.** A good delivery process has clear messages:
1. Order confirmed (with expected delivery day).
2. Dispatched (rider's name and expected time).
3. Rider nearby (call or message).
4. Delivered — with **proof of delivery** (a photo at the door or the customer's confirmation).
5. Follow-up: "Did everything arrive well?"

**Payment on delivery** is popular but risky: riders carry cash, and customers can refuse at the door. Many businesses ask for payment by transfer before dispatch, and confirm it in the banking app — not by an SMS screenshot.

## Key words

- **Logistics:** planning and managing how goods move from one place to another
- **Batching:** grouping several deliveries into one trip
- **Time window:** the period in which a delivery must arrive
- **Proof of delivery:** evidence that the customer received the goods
- **Failed delivery:** a delivery attempt where the customer could not receive the goods

## Read and watch

- [Logistics](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/l/logistics.asp) — Investopedia
- [Get directions and show routes](https://support.google.com/maps/answer/144339) — Google Maps Help
- [Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority](https://lamata-ng.com/) — LAMATA

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** plan for three addresses on the Mainland only.
- **If you already can:** compare total cost and time for single trips versus one batched route in a Google Sheets table.
- **If you live outside Lagos:** do the same exercise for your own city, naming its real pinch points.

## Learning online

At home, open Google Maps (app or browser), enter the five areas as stops, and use "depart at" to compare 7 a.m. with 1 p.m. Record the times in Google Sheets and calculate single-trip and batched costs. Draft the five customer messages in Google Docs. **Upload as evidence:** a screenshot of your planned route, your cost comparison table, and the five messages. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** your route and the biggest risk you spotted (a bridge, a time window, a hard-to-find address).

## Before the next session

Notice one delivery you or your family receive this week. Which of the five customer messages did you get, and which were missing?

lessons.title: Continuous improvement with PDCA and the 5 Whys
lessons.summary: Find the root cause of a recurring problem with the 5 Whys, then test a fix with a Plan–Do–Check–Act cycle.
objectives: You will use the 5 Whys to move from a symptom to a root cause
You will run a small Plan–Do–Check–Act cycle with a measurable target
You will report what changed using before-and-after data
lessons.body:
The best operations are never finished. They improve a little, every week, because the people doing the work notice problems and fix the causes — not just the symptoms. Today you learn two simple tools for that, and use them on a real problem.

## What to do

- Choose a recurring problem from your centre, school or home: sessions starting late, tablets uncharged, the tuck shop running out of change.
- Ask "Why?" five times (or until you reach a cause you can act on).
- Plan a small test of a fix with a measurable target.
- Run it for at least two weeks, record the results, and decide what to do next.

## Understand it

**The 5 Whys.** Ask why a problem happens, then ask why *that* happens, and so on. Each answer should be a fact you can check, not a guess or a blame.

*Problem: Saturday sessions start, on average, 15 minutes late.*
1. **Why?** The room is not ready at 10:00.
2. **Why?** The projector and laptops are set up only after the instructor arrives.
3. **Why?** Only the instructor has the cupboard key.
4. **Why?** The spare key was lost last term and never replaced.
5. **Why?** No one owns the job of checking equipment and keys.

The **symptom** is lateness. The **root cause** is that no one owns equipment readiness. "The instructor should come earlier" would treat the symptom and burn out one person. A fix at the root: a cut spare key held by the volunteer lead, and a named volunteer who sets up from 9:30 using a checklist.

**Rules for good 5 Whys.** Focus on the process, not on blaming a person. Check each answer with evidence. There may be more than one branch — follow the most important one first. Five is a guide, not a law.

**PDCA — Plan, Do, Check, Act.** A cycle for testing improvements, popularised by W. Edwards Deming:
- **Plan:** state the problem, the root cause, the change, and a **measurable target**. "Start within 5 minutes of 10:00 on at least 3 of the next 4 Saturdays."
- **Do:** make the change on a small scale. Record what happens.
- **Check:** compare results with the target and the baseline. Before: average start 10:15 over four weeks. After: 10:02, 10:04, 10:12, 10:03 — three of four within 5 minutes; average 10:05.25, about 10:05.
- **Act:** if it worked, make it standard (add it to the procedure and onboarding). If not, learn why and start a new cycle with a different change.

**Small and often beats big and rare.** A small test is cheap, quick and safe to fail. Many small cycles add up — this is the Japanese idea of **kaizen**, continuous improvement.

**Measure before you change.** Without a **baseline** you cannot tell whether things improved. Record a few weeks of data first if you can — even a simple Google Sheet with *Date, Planned start, Actual start, Minutes late* (`=(C2-B2)*1440` gives minutes when both are times).

**Bringing the term together.** Your flowchart (week 1) shows the process; your queue timings (week 2) show where it is slow; your checklist (week 3) holds the standard; your stock tracker (week 4) keeps supplies flowing; your delivery plan (week 5) reaches the customer. PDCA is how you keep improving all of them.

## Key words

- **Symptom:** what you can see going wrong
- **Root cause:** the underlying reason that, if fixed, stops the problem recurring
- **5 Whys:** asking 'why?' repeatedly to move from a symptom to a root cause
- **PDCA:** Plan, Do, Check, Act: a cycle for testing improvements
- **Baseline:** measurements taken before a change, for comparison
- **Kaizen:** continuous improvement through many small changes

## Read and watch

- [PDCA cycle](https://asq.org/quality-resources/pdca-cycle) — ASQ
- [Root cause analysis](https://asq.org/quality-resources/root-cause-analysis) — ASQ
- [Lean Enterprise Institute](https://www.lean.org/) — LEI

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** do the 5 Whys on paper with a partner and plan one PDCA cycle without running it yet.
- **If you already can:** add a run chart (line chart of the measure over time, with the change date marked) to your Check stage.
- **If your problem involves other people:** ask them to help with the 5 Whys — they often know causes you cannot see.

## Learning online

At home, pick a recurring problem in your household routine (leaving late for school, phone never charged, running out of drinking water) and do the 5 Whys in a Google Doc. Record a baseline for a few days in Google Sheets, then run a two-week PDCA test and record the results. **Upload as evidence:** your 5 Whys chain, your PDCA plan with a measurable target, and your before-and-after data with a short Act decision. **Bring to the live Saturday online class:** a two-minute summary of your improvement — this is the Operations showcase for the term.

## Before the next session

Keep your PDCA test running. At the end of two weeks, decide: adopt, adapt or abandon — and say why.
